section: Author’s Note to the August 2024 Edition
text:
Author’s Note to the August 2024 Edition
2024 marks the fifth year of existence for “The Live Textbook of Physical Chemistry.” Faithful to my initial intent, the textbook has evolved substantially from its humble beginnings, and it continues to evolve to this day. Five years is a long time in education, and much has happened during this period, including a pandemic that forced everyone to online teaching and learning, and the rise of generative AI in many fields, including education and Academia. I have big plans for the next phase of the book’s evolution, but due to time constraints and the ever-increasing demands of academic duties, I had to postpone them for now. As such, the structure of the textbook has largely remained unchanged. If and when I will have time to restructure my entire courses, as well as the textbooks that go with them, I will present a true “Second Edition” of “The Live Textbook,” but this is not it yet.
What I did have time to do, however, was to bring “The Live Textbook” up to the standards of a true academic textbook. Since its inception, I was well aware that there was a glaring omission: exercises. This summer, I finally had the opportunity to add new review sections at the end of every chapter, each containing practice problems and study questions. These new sections are designed to help readers verify their understanding of each chapter’s content. More importantly, they are intended for my students to test their knowledge before exams. For this reason, they follow the same style as the questions I have used in my exams over the past five years. In fact, several of these questions and exercises are taken directly from previous exams. I can’t promise that the same questions will be in future exams, but familiarizing with them will give a student the edge over students that decide to ignore them.
Finally, I am not pretending to have been unaware of the emergence of AI, generative models, and their impact on education, so I’ve tried to put them to a good use. In the past five years, I specifically used ChatGPT and Claude to rewrite some sections of this textbook, and I have made it clear when that was the case. These tools were especially valuable this summer for the new exercises and questions sections, where I abundantly used them to help supplement my existing materials with newly generated ones. I made sure the AI didn’t hallucinate and to fix it when it did, so hopefully, everything is consistent. I must confess that I would not have met the deadline for the beginning of the semester without this new technology. Hopefully, this serves as a good example of how AI can be incorporated into the classroom.
Additionally, in the summer of 2026, I have reworked all of the pictures in the textbook to add alt-text descriptions. This is important for accessibility and it is (hopefully) compliant with the new Government directives on online accessibility for education.
As usual, if you spot any mistakes, I encourage you to reach out to me at the contacts listed above.

title: The Live Textbook of Physical Chemistry 1
text:
How to Use This Book
If you are a student in my course, please read this book carefully, since everything that will be in your exams is explained here! Since this book is specifically tailored for the CHM 3001 course at Florida Tech, there are no superfluous parts. In other words, everything in it might be subject to question in the quizzes and the final exam.

Definitions and worked examples are numbered (e.g., Definition 1.1, Example 4.1) and are set apart from the rest of the text in boxes, blue for definitions and green for examples. Notes are highlighted in this format (indented, and following a grey vertical bar). Please study the definitions carefully since they are fundamental concepts that will be used several times in the remainder of the text, and they will be subject to quizzes and exams. Worked examples are essential for cementing the concepts, and you should attempt to solve them first without looking at the solution. Even if you were able to solve an example on your own, always read the solution after, since it might contain additional explanations expanding the main concepts in the text.

Navigating the book should be straightforward. On each page, there is a useful sidebar on the left that gives you an overview of all chapters, with a few important tools at its top. Arrows to move between chapters are at the bottom of each page. If you are old-school and prefer a pdf, you can download a printout by clicking on the corresponding icon at the top of the sidebar. If you are really old-school and prefer a printed book, the best solution is to download the pdf and print it yourself. It is a LaTeX book, and I can promise you it will look good on paper. However, I cannot provide physical copies to each student. In the sidebar, you will find a useful search box that is capable of searching the entire book. The most adventurous will find there a link to the raw GitHub source code. Feel free to head to the GitHub repository of this book and fork it.
For my students, each chapter of this book represents one week of work in the classroom and at home. The sidebar on the left will reflect your syllabus, as well as the main structure of the class on Canvas. The book is a live document, which means it will be updated throughout the semester with new material. While you are not required to check it every day, you might want to review each week’s chapter before the lecture on Friday.

title: The Live Textbook of Physical Chemistry 1
text:
How This Book Is Organized
The book is divided into four parts:

Part I, The Laws of Thermodynamics (chapters 1–6), builds the laws of thermodynamics with the simplest systems possible, mostly an ideal gas in a cylinder, and without chemical reactions. Along the way, we introduce heat, work, internal energy, enthalpy, and entropy, and the zeroth, first, second, and third laws. Part I ends with the definition of the standard state and with a first look at a chemical reaction.
Part II, Chemical Thermodynamics (chapters 7–10), applies the laws to chemical reactions: the heat of reactions (thermochemistry), the thermodynamic potentials, the Gibbs energy, and chemical equilibrium.
Part III, Phase Equilibria and Solutions (chapters 11–13), uses the same tools for real gases, for the phase transitions of pure substances, and for mixtures.
Part IV, Chemical Kinetics (chapter 14), leaves equilibrium behind and asks how fast reactions go.

Many textbooks place thermochemistry right after the first law, since the heat of a reaction requires only the enthalpy. In this book, thermochemistry opens Part II instead, after the entropy. This way, all the laws are in place when we meet our first reactions, and we can ask the real chemical question from the start: not only how much heat a reaction releases, but whether it happens at all. Answering this question leads us directly to the thermodynamic potentials, which then appear as the tool that solves a concrete problem rather than as abstract definitions. The title of the book reflects the same structure: the first three parts tell us which way a process goes, and the last one tells us how fast.

title: The Live Textbook of Physical Chemistry 1
text:
A Note on Units
In general, we will use SI units or some of their multiples throughout the textbook, lectures, and exercises. For example, temperatures will be measured in kelvin (\(\text{K}\)), energetic terms will be measured in either joules (\(\text{J}\)) or kilojoules (\(\text{kJ}\)), while volumes will be measured in cubic meters, or more often in liters (\(\text{L}\)), where \(1\,\text{L} = 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3\). An important exception is made for pressures, which will be measured in bars (\(\text{bar}\)). This exception is not completely unjustified, since bar is still an (unconventional) multiple of the SI unit of pressure, pascal (\(\text{Pa}\)), where \(1\,\text{bar} = 10^5\,\text{Pa}\). This choice is made to retain a reasonable similarity with the unit atmosphere (\(\text{atm}\)) which is extensively used in several other chemistry textbooks \((1\,\text{atm} = 1.013\,\text{bar})\) and in previous physical chemistry courses.
We will generally also try to avoid conversion between units, except for some trivial conversion between degrees Celsius (°C) and Kelvin, with the conversion factor being an addition of \(273.15\,\text{K}\). Other unconventional conversions might happen in some of the exercises, with the conversion factors always reported within the exercise itself. Additionally, we will avoid unnecessary conversion between the average atmospheric pressure and bars by setting \(P_{\text{atm}} = 1\,\text{bar},\) rather than \(P_{\text{atm}} = 1\,\text{atm} = 1.013\, \text{bar},\) an approximation that is mostly inconsequential, at least at the scale of the problems that we treat here.

A Note on the Use of AI
The November 2026 revision of this book was prepared with the help of Claude Code (Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5), an AI assistant. The book, its structure, its scope, and its approach to teaching thermodynamics and kinetics are my own, developed over several years of teaching this course. In the revision, I used the AI as an assistant: to proofread the text, to rephrase passages, to draft new sections, figures, examples, and review questions following my outline and instructions, and to write the code for the computed figures. Every change was reviewed, corrected or rewritten, and approved by me, and I take full responsibility for the content of the book, including any remaining errors.

This live open textbook is distributed under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 License. The Python scripts that generate the figures are available under the MIT License. The first version of the book was funded in 2021 by the Florida Tech Open Educational Resources Grant Program, a collaboration of the Teaching Council, eEducation, and the Evans Library. That grant planted the seed; the current edition has since grown well beyond it, with a new structure, new chapters and sections, and new figures throughout.

title: 1  Introduction to Thermodynamics
text:
1.1 Calculus for Physical Chemistry: Slicing and Gluing
Why does a match burn once we strike it, while the ashes never turn back into a match? Why does salt dissolve in water but sand does not? How much heat do we get from burning a liter of gasoline, and how much of it can we actually turn into work? And when a reaction stops, why does it stop where it does, and not sooner or later? Every chemist faces questions like these, and thermodynamics is the part of physical chemistry that answers them. The remarkable thing is that thermodynamics answers them without knowing anything about molecules. It works only with quantities that we can measure in the lab, such as temperature, pressure, volume, and heat, and it builds a few simple laws on top of them. Because it does not depend on any particular model of matter, nothing that we will learn about atoms and molecules later will ever force us to change it.
Before we can use these laws, we need a few tools. In this chapter, we will introduce them: a gentle version of calculus, which is the language thermodynamics is written in; the idea of a thermodynamic system, which is the piece of the universe we decide to study; and the variables that describe it, with the important distinction between state and path variables. None of these tools is difficult on its own, but we will use all of them in every chapter that follows, so it is worth taking the time to get comfortable with them now.
Calculus is a powerful mathematical tool that helps us understand and analyze change. At its core, calculus involves two main procedures: differentiation and integration. These concepts are fundamental to the study of thermodynamics, as they enable us to examine how physical systems change. Undergraduate students often find calculus intimidating due to its rigorous presentation in mathematical courses. However, a strong mathematical foundation, while beneficial, is not always mandatory to study thermodynamics effectively.
If you are a student who lacks confidence in mathematics, I encourage you not to be deterred by the presence of calculus in this physical chemistry textbook. If you break this initial wall of fear for calculus, you might find this textbook quite rewarding. After all, we will finally explain where all those unmemorable formulas that you’ve been presented in introductory general chemistry courses are coming from. To facilitate your task, we will present in this chapter a simplified view of calculus. The starting point will be a basic question: how do we measure things in science? To answer this question, we will use calculus to measure the length of an object. At a first glance, this approach might seem pedantic. Why do we need to use calculus, with all of its mathematical complications, when we can just grab a ruler and stack it against our object to measure its length? However, we need to remind ourselves that our ultimate goal is physical chemistry, and calculus is the language of this field. By focusing on the straightforward task of measuring a simple length, we aim to make calculus more accessible and less daunting.1 From this simple starting point, we will expand our horizon to introduce the central topic of this textbook: Thermodynamics. Our main focus will be on the relationship between chemistry and thermodynamics, but since this is an advanced undergraduate textbook, we will need to do that from a rigorous perspective. If we want to see it in simple terms, we either deal with the approach of not explaining where things are coming from that is abundantly used in freshman chemistry courses, or we make the effort of learning a bit of calculus so we can use it to understand the world.

title: 1  Introduction to Thermodynamics
text:
1.1.1 Differentiation: Infinite Slicing
Differentiation can be thought of as “slicing an object into infinitely thin pieces” to understand how it changes at a specific point. Imagine you have a long stick and you want to measure how its length changes along a specific direction. To do this, you would cut the stick into infinitely thin slices. Each slice is so thin that its change in length is practically infinitesimal. By examining each of these tiny slices and how they change, you can understand the rate at which the stick’s length changes at any given point. This process of infinite slicing is called differentiation, and it is the most powerful tool to understand things that change, that is, most of the things we are interested in science.
How so? Let’s look at a simple example. If we start from a stick of length \(L\), we can infinitely slice it into infinitesimally small pieces of length \(dL\). These incredibly tiny pieces are called differentials of the original quantity, in this particular case, the length of our stick. The beauty of these differentials, \(dL\), is that they don’t really depend on how long our object initially was: they will always be infinitesimally small. Imagine, for example, that you start with an object whose length is \(1\, \text{m}\). After you slice it an infinite amount of times, each differential could be pictured as a length of \(0.000[...]0001\, \text{m}\), where we have replaced an infinite amount of zeros with the notation \([...]\). If we start instead with a second object whose length is \(1\,\text{km}\), we end up with differentials that are just as infinitesimally small. This picture with infinitely many zeros is only a way to visualize the idea: a differential is smaller than any number that we could write down, no matter how many zeros we use.
Now, through some mathematical magic, these strange numbers with an infinite amount of zeros, are essentially the closest thing you can get to \(0\), without practically being \(0\). For this reason, they can be used much more effectively than something that purely doesn’t exist.2 The key word here is essentially, because the differentials are as close to zero as we want, but they still contain some fundamental information related to the original objects. In the first place, they still have the dimension (and the units) of the original quantity: \(dL\) is an infinitesimal length, measured in meters, and it cannot be compared with, say, an infinitesimal time. Additionally, the differentials will also contain information on the rate of change (the “slope”) of the length in the original objects. The question that remains is: How are we going to access this apparently hidden information? In other words, how are we going to reconstruct the length of the original object from the differentials? The answer is surprisingly simple: By comparing different differentials to each other. More specifically, despite their zero-ness, we are allowed to calculate the ratio between differentials, such as \(\frac{dL}{dx}\). In this specific case, we are calculating the ratio between the differential of the length of our stick, and the position, \(x\), along an axis that is oriented the same way as our stick.3 This special ratio is called the derivative, and it is fundamental to compare one differential to another. In simple terms, the derivative tells us how one quantity (the one at the top) changes, when we purposely change another (the one at the bottom). Going back to our simple example, the derivative \(\frac{dL}{dx}\) tells us how the length of our stick changes when we change the position on the axis. For this case, the derivative is a simple number \(\frac{dL}{dx}=1\), but more complicated cases are possible. So, how can we use this information to measure the length of our stick? A second calculus procedure, integration, comes to our rescue.


1.1.2 Integration: Gluing Together Differentials
Integration is the procedure that glues infinitely tiny slices back together to reconstruct the initial object. In simple terms, if you start with the infinitely thin slices of length that you cut earlier, you can add them all up to find the total length of the stick. Integration takes all these infinitesimally small pieces and combines them into a whole, helping you determine the accumulated total from the infinitesimal changes. Obviously this procedure is very complicated, and it involves gluing (summing over) an infinite amount of infinitesimally small things. If you can’t wrap your head around this, that’s OK, this concept puzzled humanity for thousands of years. The ancient Greeks were very concerned by this, but they failed to find a solution.4 It took two 17th century geniuses, Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, to figure out how to do so.
The solution came by first defining the mathematical operation that “undoes” the slicing:
\[
L = \int dL.
\tag{1.1}\]
This operation is called an integral, and is represented by the symbol \(\int\). The integral is the inverse of \(d\), as it reconstructs the original object by gluing together an infinite amount of infinitesimally small differentials. This operation is, in practice, just a sanity check for the differentiation procedure introduced in the previous section. What eq. 1.1 is telling us, is nothing other than: if you start from an object, \(L\), and apply a certain operation to it (\(d\)), then there has to be another operation (\(\int\)) that undoes what the first operation did. This inverse procedure becomes really useful when we want to measure things in the real world. How so? Because we can compare differentials of an unknown quantity to differentials of known ones, and then use the latter to reconstruct the former. In our simple example, we can use the derivative, \(\frac{dL}{dx}=1\), to compare the length of the object (unknown) to the position along our axis (known, because we can manipulate it). This is the mathematical counterpart of taking an object with unknown length, and comparing it to the length of a standard stick (a meter, a kilometer, a mile, …). The formula that describes this operation is:
\[
L=\int dL = \int_{i}^{f} 1 dx = x_f-x_i =\Delta x,
\tag{1.2}\]
where the length (\(L\)) of the original object is reconstructed by fixing the initial piece at position \(x_i\) on the \(x\) axis, the final piece at position \(x_f\), and then by gluing together the differentials \(dx\) in between these points, using the integral procedure. Switching from \(dL\) to \(dx\) has the noticeable advantage of going from something that we initially don’t know anything about (the length of the stick) to something that we can manipulate as much as we want, because we specifically built it for this task (the position along the axis, \(x\)). This concept, of course, is not limited to length. If we differentiate an area, or a volume, or a pressure, or a temperature using eq. 1.1, we obtain the corresponding differentials. By comparing these differentials to specifically built ones that we are able to manipulate to our will, we can reconstruct the original quantity via integration, using eq. 1.2. Every differential will retain the dimension of the original quantity (\(dT\) still retains the dimension of a temperature, a.k.a. it is a temperature, despite the fact that it has a value of essentially zero). In addition, every differential will retain hidden information about the initial object, which we can reconstruct by comparing to something we know, and then by applying integration to the latter. Notice that it is the operation in eq. 1.2 that turns the infinitesimal pieces back into a finite, measurable quantity, by comparing an unknown differential to a known one. This is effectively the “measuring” procedure, written in mathematical terms.
When we wrote eq. 1.2, we glanced over the fact that \(\int_{i}^{f} 1 dx = x_f-x_i\). Where did that come from? And most importantly, how are we going to manage more complicated cases? At this point, you’ll have to go fetch a mathematics textbook, as you need to know how to perform some of those integrals. For all intents and purposes, we can use those formulas as recipes that mathematicians have written in the past. Granted, we are well aware of the fact that if we want to understand where the formulas are coming from, it is possible to do so with a little effort.5 Mathematicians have clear rules on how to compute many of these objects, and one of such rules tells us that \(\int_{i}^{f} dx = x_f-x_i\). Other common integration rules that we’ll need in this course are, for example: \(\int_{i}^{f} x^{n}\,dx=\left.\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\right| _i^f  =\frac{1}{n+1}\left(x_f^{n+1}-x_i^{n+1}\right)\) for \(n\neq -1\), and \(\int_{i}^{f} x^{-1} dx=\ln \left|x_f\right|-\ln \left|x_i\right|=\ln \left|\frac{x_f}{x_i}\right|.\)
This is indeed a good point to go fetch that old math textbook and refresh some of the simplest integration rules, as well as some of the simplest differentiation ones. Not that we will use all of them, but we might indeed use a few ones.


1.1.3 Calculus for Thermodynamics
Now comes the interesting question: How are we going to practically perform these two important operations of differentiation and integration in thermodynamics? Well, imagine we need to study the behavior of a machine that prints out a number on a display. The first thing we need to do if we want to study this machine is to find something that makes the number change. Let’s represent this something with a knob. We can then turn the knob voluntarily one way or another, and register how the number changes on the display. This is how you apply calculus in thermodynamics (and in most science, for that matter). Our machine might be the length of an object \(L\), while our knob might be the position along an axis \(x\). We can voluntarily change the position on the axis, and observe how the length changes on the display. Does that sound familiar? Can we use eq. 1.2 to do so? I believe so…
Now, obviously the example of length and position is the simplest we could imagine, and doesn’t really pertain to physical chemistry. A more relevant example is that of a gas, whose pressure changes when we change the temperature at constant volume. In this case, the pressure, \(P\), is the machine, and the temperature, \(T\), is the knob. To understand the machine, we will need to know the derivative \(\frac{dP}{dT}\). In many cases the derivative between our machine and our knob(s) might not be as simple as 1. In some of such cases, the derivative might be a different number, while in others it might be as complicated as a function itself. Some of the machines we will encounter might have more than just one knob, each with their own specific derivative, and each as complicated as it might be. In all cases, however, our analysis follows the same procedure: First, we identify all the knobs that affect the machine. Second, we use calculus to voluntarily change the position of the knobs and to register how the machine behaves. In mathematical terms, this procedure is to define and study the total differential:
\[
\begin{aligned}
d\mathcal{M} &= \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{M}}{\partial a} \right) da + \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{M}}{\partial b} \right) db + \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{M}}{\partial c} \right) dc + \cdots ,\\
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.3}\]
where \(\mathcal{M}\) is our machine, \(d\mathcal{M}\) is its total differential, \(\left\{a,b,c,\cdots\right\}\) are the variables that affect the machine’s behavior (i.e. the knobs), and \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{M}}{\partial a}\) represents a partial derivative of the machine \(\mathcal{M}\) with respect to the variable \(a\) obtained by keeping all other variables constant. Notice that the number of variables is left unidentified, as it is our goal to identify all of the variables that a machine depends on, and there are as many as necessary.






Figure 1.1: A machine \(\mathcal{M}\) with three knobs, \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\). Turning each knob by an infinitesimal amount (\(da\), \(db\), \(dc\)) changes the number on the display. The total change, \(d\mathcal{M}\), is the sum of the three contributions in eq. 1.3, each obtained by multiplying how sensitive the machine is to that knob (the partial derivative) by how much we turned it.



The final piece of the puzzle we need to apply calculus to thermodynamics is to know whether or not we can apply these two procedures to any quantity that enters the picture. The answer to this question, unfortunately, is a resounding no. Differentiation and integration can be applied to many variables that are “well-behaved.” Such variables are called state variables in thermodynamics. Unfortunately though, there are also a few variables that are not well-behaved at all. These are called path variables in thermodynamics. It turns out that some of the quantities that thermodynamics is mostly concerned about, such as heat and work, belong to this “ill-behaved” category. Before we delve deeper into state and path variables, however, we need to define what variables are in thermodynamics. And before we can do that, we need to take a whole step back and define what thermodynamics is concerned about, that is the thermodynamic system.

title: 1  Introduction to Thermodynamics
text:
1.2 Thermodynamic Systems
A thermodynamic system—or just simply a system—is a portion of space with defined boundaries that separate it from its surroundings (see also the title picture of this book). The surroundings may include other thermodynamic systems or physical systems that are not thermodynamic systems. A boundary may be a real physical barrier or a purely notional one. Defining a system this way is itself a deliberate simplification that is common in science. This procedure is often jokingly referred to as the “spherical cow” analogy,6 where a complex real-world object (a cow) is treated as a simple sphere to make the math tractable. Typical examples of systems are reported in Figure 1.2 below.






Figure 1.2: Examples of Thermodynamic Systems and Their Boundaries. The Liquid in a Flask and the Gas in a Balloon Have Physical Boundaries, while the Boundaries of a Cloud and of a Flame (Dashed Red Lines) Are Defined by a Condition that We Choose.



In the first case, a liquid is contained in a typical Erlenmeyer flask. The boundaries of the system are the glass walls of the flask (and the surface of the liquid, which separates it from the air above). The second system is represented by the gas contained in a balloon. The boundary is a physical barrier also in this case, being the plastic of the balloon. The third case is that of a thundercloud. The boundary is not a well-defined physical barrier, but rather some condition of pressure and chemical composition at the interface between the cloud and the atmosphere. Finally, the fourth case is the case of an open flame. In this case, the boundary is again non-physical, and possibly even harder to define than for a cloud. For example, we can choose to define the flame based on some temperature threshold, color criterion, or even some chemical one. Despite the lack of physical boundaries, the cloud and the flame—as portions of space containing matter—can be defined as a thermodynamic system.
A system can exchange exclusively mass, exclusively energy, or both mass and energy with its surroundings. Depending on the boundaries’ ability to transfer these quantities, a system is defined as open, closed, or isolated. An open system exchanges both mass and energy. A closed system exchanges only energy, but not mass. Finally, an isolated system exchanges neither mass nor energy.
When a system exchanges mass or energy with its surroundings, some of its parameters (variables) change. For example, if a system loses mass to the surroundings, the number of molecules (or moles) in the system will decrease. Similarly, if a system absorbs some energy, one or more of its variables (such as its temperature) increase. Mass and energy can flow into the system or out of the system. Let’s consider mass exchange only. If some molecules of a substance leave the system, and then the same amount of molecules flow back into the system, the system will not be modified. We can count, for example, 100 molecules leaving a system and assign them the value of –100 in an outgoing process, and then observe the same 100 molecules going back into the system and assign them a value of +100. Regardless of the number of molecules present in the system in the first place, the overall balance will be –100 (from the outgoing process) +100 (from the ingoing process) = 0, which brings the system to its initial situation (mass has not changed). However, from a mathematical standpoint, we could have equally assigned the label +100 to the outgoing process and –100 to the ingoing one, and the overall total would have stayed the same: +100–100 = 0. Which of the two labels is best? For this case, it seems natural to define a mass going out of the system as negative (the system is losing it), and a mass going into the system as positive (the system is gaining it), but is it as straightforward for energy?

Here is another example. Let’s consider a system that is composed of your body. When you exercise, you lose mass in the form of water (sweat) and CO2 (from respiration). This mass loss can be easily measured by stepping on a scale before and after exercise. The number you observe on the scale will go down. Hence you have lost weight. After exercise, you will reintegrate the lost mass by drinking and eating. If you have reinstated the same amount you have lost, your weight will be the same as before the exercise (no weight loss). Nevertheless, which label do you attach to the amounts that you have lost and gained? Let’s say that you are running a 5 km race without drinking or eating, and you measure your weight dropping 2 kg after the race. After the race, you drink 1.5 kg of water and eat a 500 g energy bar. Overall you did not lose any weight, and it would seem reasonable to label the 2 kg that you’ve lost as negative (–2) and the 1.5 kg of water that you drank and the 500 g bar that you ate as positive (+1.5 +0.5 = +2). But is it the only way? After all, you didn’t gain nor lose any weight, so why not calling the 2 kg due to exercise +2 and the 2 that you’ve ingested as –2? It might seem silly, but mathematically it would not make any difference, the total would still be zero. Now, let’s consider energy instead of mass. To run the 5 km race, you have spent 500 kcal, which then you reintegrate precisely by eating the energy bar. Which sign would you put in front of the kilocalories that you “burned” during the race? In principle, you’ve lost them, so if you want to be consistent, you should use a negative sign. But if you think about it, you’ve put quite an effort to “lose” those kilocalories, so it might not feel bad to assign them a positive sign instead. After all, it’s perfectly OK to say, “I’ve done a 500 kcal run today”, while it might sound quite awkward to say, “I’ve done a –500 kcal run today.” Our previous exercise with mass demonstrates that it doesn’t really matter which sign you put in front of the quantities. As long as you are consistent throughout the process, the signs will cancel out. If you’ve done a +500 kcal run, you’ve eaten a bar for –500 kcal, resulting in a total zero loss/gain. Alternatively, if you’ve done a –500 kcal run, you would have eaten a +500 kcal bar, for a total of again zero loss/gain.

These simple examples demonstrate that the sign that we assign to quantities that flow through a boundary is arbitrary (i.e., we can define it any way we want, as long as we are always consistent with ourselves). There is no best way to assign those signs. If you ask two different people, you might obtain two different answers. But we are scientists, and we must make sure to be rigorous. For this reason, chemists have established a convention for the signs that we will follow throughout this course. If we are consistent in following the convention, we are guaranteed to never make any mistake with the signs.

Definition 1.1 The chemistry convention of the sign is system-centric:7

If something (energy or mass) goes into the system it has a positive sign (the system is gaining)
If something (energy or mass) goes out of the system it has a negative sign (the system is losing)


If you want a trick to remember the convention, use the weight loss/gain during the exercise example above. You are the system, if you lose weight, the kilograms will be negative (–2 kg), while if you gain weight, they will be positive (+2 kg). Similarly, if you eat an energy bar, you are the system, and you will have increased your energy by +500 kcal (positive). In contrast, if you burned energy during exercise, you are the system, and you will have lost energy, hence –500 kcal (negative). If the system is a balloon filled with gas, and the balloon is losing mass, you are the balloon, and you are losing weight; hence the mass will be negative. If the balloon is absorbing heat (likely increasing its temperature and increasing its volume), you are the system, and you are gaining heat; hence heat will be positive.

title: 1  Introduction to Thermodynamics
text:
1.3 Thermodynamic Variables
The system is defined and studied using parameters that are called variables. These variables are quantities that we can measure, such as pressure and temperature. However, don’t be surprised if, on some occasions, you encounter variables that are a little harder to measure directly, such as entropy. If we know the values of all the “relevant variables” of a system, we know the state of the system. The relationships between all possible variables and the state of the system are called “state functions”. Imagine state functions as the “machines” that we described in the previous section. The relevant variables are called natural variables, and you should imagine them as the “knobs” of the machines that we want to study. When we need to study a specific aspect of the system, then we need to know the total differential of the state function that is relevant for that aspect.
What are the “relevant variables” of a system? The answer to this question depends on the system, and it is not always straightforward. The simplest case is the case of an ideal gas, for which the natural variables are those that enter the ideal gas law and the corresponding equation:
\[
PV=nRT
\tag{1.4}\]
Therefore, the natural variables for an ideal gas are the pressure \(P\), the volume \(V\), the number of moles \(n\), and the temperature \(T\), with \(R\) being the ideal gas constant. Recalling from the general chemistry courses, \(R\) is a universal dimensional constant which has the value of \(R = 8.31 \,\text{J}\, \text{mol}^{-1}\, \text{K}^{-1}\) in SI units. We will use the ideal gas equation and its variables as an example to discuss variables and functions in this chapter. We will analyze more complicated cases in the next chapters. Variables can be classified according to numerous criteria, each with its advantages and disadvantages. A typical classification is:

Physical variables (\(P\), \(V\), \(T\) in the ideal gas law): independent of the chemical composition of the system.
Chemical variables (\(n\) in the ideal gas law): dependent on the chemical composition of the system.

Alternatively, another useful classification is:

Intensive variables (\(P\), \(T\) in the ideal gas law): independent of the physical size (extension) of the system.
Extensive variables (\(V\), \(n\) in the ideal gas law): dependent on the physical size (extension) of the system.

When we deal with thermodynamic systems, it is more convenient to work with intensive variables. Luckily, it is relatively easy to convert extensive variables into intensive ones by just taking the ratio between the two of them. For an ideal gas, by taking the ratio between \(V\) and \(n\), we obtain the intensive variable called molar volume:
\[
\overline{V}=\frac{V}{n}.
\tag{1.5}\]
We can then recast eq. 1.4 as:
\[
P\overline{V}=RT,
\tag{1.6}\]
which is the preferred equation that we will use for the remainder of this course. The ideal gas equation connects the 3 variables pressure, molar volume, and temperature, reducing the number of independent variables to just 2. In other words, once 2 of the 3 variables are known, the other one can be easily obtained using these simple relations:
\[
P(T,\overline{V})=\frac{RT}{\overline{V}},
\tag{1.7}\]
\[
\overline{V}(T,P)=\frac{RT}{P},
\tag{1.8}\]
\[
T(P,\overline{V})=\frac{P\overline{V}}{R}.
\tag{1.9}\]
These equations define three state functions, each one expressed in terms of two independent natural variables. For example, eq. 1.7 defines the state function called “pressure”, expressed as a function of temperature and molar volume. Similarly, eq. 1.8 defines the “molar volume” as a function of temperature and pressure, and eq. 1.9 defines the “temperature” as a function of pressure and molar volume. As we mentioned above, when we know the natural variables that define a state function, we can express the function using its total differential, for example for the pressure \(P(T, \overline{V})\), using the definition of total differential in eq. 1.3, we get:
\[
dP=\left( \frac{\partial P}{\partial T} \right)dT + \left( \frac{\partial P}{\partial \overline{V}} \right)d\overline{V}
\tag{1.10}\]
Recalling Schwarz’s theorem, the mixed partial second derivatives that can be obtained from eq. 1.10 are the same:
\[
\frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial T \partial \overline{V}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial \overline{V}}\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}=\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\frac{\partial P}{\partial \overline{V}}=\frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial \overline{V} \partial T}
\tag{1.11}\]
Which can be easily verified considering that:
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \overline{V}} \frac{\partial P}{\partial T}  = \frac{\partial}{\partial \overline{V}} \left(\frac{R}{\overline{V}}\right) = -\frac{R}{\overline{V}^2}
\tag{1.12}\]
and
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial T} \frac{\partial P}{\partial \overline{V}}  = \frac{\partial}{\partial T} \left(\frac{-RT}{\overline{V}^2}\right) = -\frac{R}{\overline{V}^2}
\tag{1.13}\]
While for the ideal gas law, all the variables are “well-behaved” and always satisfy Schwarz’s theorem, we will encounter some variables for which Schwarz’s theorem does not hold.

1.3.1 State and Path Variables
Mathematically, if Schwarz’s theorem is violated (i.e., if the mixed second derivatives are not equal), then the corresponding function cannot be integrated. These ill-behaved variables are called path variables (or path functions) because they depend on the path, rather than the state of the system. In contrast to these ill-behaved variables, well-behaved variables that can be used to define the state of the system are called state variables (or state functions).
Since path functions violate Schwarz’s theorem, their differential cannot be defined exactly, therefore eq. 1.2 does not exist. The most typical examples of path functions that we will encounter in the next chapters are heat (\(Q\)) and work (\(W\)). For these functions, we can attempt to infinitely slice the initial variable by using the same calculus procedure introduced in section 1.1.1 and defined in eq. 1.1. The resulting infinitely small pieces, however, are different than regular “exact” differentials, and are called inexact differentials. To differentiate between exact and inexact differentials, we use the letter \(d\) for the former, and the letter \(đ\) for the latter. It is important to remember that inexact differentials are defined using eq. 1.1, but the procedure in eq. 1.2 does not exist for them. Summarizing for a case that we will use often in thermodynamics, we can define the following quantity for heat (\(Q\)):
\[
Q = \int đQ.
\tag{1.14}\]
However, we cannot use the familiar formula given by eq. 1.2 to calculate it:
\[
\int_{i}^{f} đQ \neq Q_f - Q_i,
\tag{1.15}\]
as the left hand side of this equation is not defined.8 Work also behaves similarly.

We will return to exact and inexact differentials when we discuss heat and work, but for this chapter, it is crucial to notice the difference between a state function and a path function. A typical example to understand the difference between state and path function is to consider the distance between two geographical locations. Let’s, for example, consider the distance between New York City and Los Angeles. If we fly straight from one city to the other, there are roughly 4,000 km between them. This “air distance” depends exclusively on the geographical location of the two cities. It stays constant regardless of the method of transportation that I have access to travel between them. Since the cities’ positions depend uniquely on their latitudes and longitudes, the “air distance” is a state function, i.e., it is uniquely defined from a simple relationship between measurable variables. However, the “air distance” is not the distance that I will practically have to drive when I go from NYC to LA. Such “travel distance” depends on the method of transportation that I decide to take (airplane vs. car vs. train vs. boat vs. …). It will depend on a plentiful amount of other factors such as the choice of the road to be traveled (if going by car), the atmospheric conditions (if flying), and so on. A typical “travel distance” by car is, for example, about 4,500 km, which is about 12% more than the “air distance.” Indeed, we could even design a very inefficient road trip that avoids all highways and will result in a “travel distance” of 8,000 km or even more (200% of the “air distance”). The “travel distance” is a clear example of a path function because it depends on the specific path that I decide to travel to go from NYC to LA. See Figure 1.3.







Figure 1.3: State Functions vs. Path Functions.

title: 1  Introduction to Thermodynamics
text:
1.4 Chapter Review

1.4.1 Key Ideas

Calculus is slicing and gluing. A differential, such as \(dL\), is an infinitesimally small piece of a quantity; differentiation slices, and integration glues the pieces back together.
The total differential of a function of several variables adds up the effect of each variable: \(d\mathcal{M} = \left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{M}}{\partial a}\right) da + \left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{M}}{\partial b}\right) db + \cdots\).
A system is the part of the universe we choose to study. Open systems exchange mass and energy, closed systems only energy, and isolated systems neither.
Sign convention: in chemistry, energy that enters the system (heat absorbed, work done on it) is positive, and energy that leaves it is negative.
Variables are intensive or extensive. Intensive ones (such as \(T\) and \(P\)) do not depend on the size of the system; extensive ones (such as \(V\) and \(n\)) do.
State and path variables. State variables depend only on the current state and have exact differentials; heat and work are path variables, with inexact differentials, \(đQ\) and \(đW\).



1.4.2 Study Questions
1. What is a differential, such as \(dL\)?

The derivative of \(L\) with respect to position.
A small but finite change in \(L\), such as 1 mm.
An infinitesimally small piece of \(L\) that keeps the dimension of a length.
The total length \(L\) of the object.
A pure number with no dimension.


2. What does integration do, in the language of this chapter?

It glues together infinitely many infinitesimal pieces to reconstruct the whole quantity.
It slices a quantity into infinitesimal pieces.
It calculates the slope of a function at a point.
It converts a quantity from one unit to another.
It removes the dimension from a quantity.


3. Which of the following does an isolated system exchange with its surroundings?

Mass only.
Energy only.
Both mass and energy.
Neither mass nor energy.
Heat, but not work.


4. According to the chemistry sign convention, what is the sign of the heat released by a system to its surroundings?

Positive, since heat is energy.
Negative, since the system is losing energy.
Zero, since energy is conserved.
Positive if the process is fast, negative if it is slow.
It depends on the temperature of the surroundings.


5. Which of the following is an intensive variable?

Volume.
Number of moles.
Mass.
Temperature.
Total energy.


6. What is the total differential of the pressure of an ideal gas, \(P(T,\overline{V})\)?

\(dP = \frac{dT}{d\overline{V}}\).
\(dP = PdT + Pd\overline{V}\).
\(dP = \frac{\partial P}{\partial T} + \frac{\partial P}{\partial \overline{V}}\).
\(dP = \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\right)dT + \left(\frac{\partial \overline{V}}{\partial P}\right)d\overline{V}\).
\(dP = \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)dT + \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial \overline{V}}\right)d\overline{V}\).


7. What does Schwarz’s theorem state for a state function?

The mixed second partial derivatives are equal, regardless of the order of differentiation.
The first derivatives are always zero.
The function cannot be integrated.
The function depends on the path.
The second derivatives are always positive.


8. Which of the following is a path function?

Pressure.
Temperature.
Work.
Molar volume.
Internal energy.


9. What does the symbol \(đ\) indicate, as in \(đQ\)?

An exact differential.
An inexact differential, whose integral depends on the path.
A partial derivative.
A state function.
A very large change.


10. In the example of the trip from New York to Los Angeles, why is the air distance a state function?

Because it depends on the means of transportation.
Because it changes with the weather.
Because it depends only on the positions of the two cities, not on the route.
Because it is always longer than the travel distance.
Because it is measured in kilometers.








TipAnswers





1.c, 2.a, 3.d, 4.b, 5.d, 6.e, 7.a, 8.c, 9.b, 10.c

title: 2  Temperature, Heat, and Work
text:
2.1 What Is Thermodynamics?
In chapter 1, we introduced the tools that we need to study thermodynamics: a bit of calculus, the definition of a system, and the distinction between state and path functions. In this chapter, we will define the two ways in which a system can exchange energy with its surroundings, heat and work, and we will learn how to calculate them. Before we do that, however, we need a solid definition of temperature, which comes from the zeroth law of thermodynamics.
Thermodynamics is the branch of science that deals with heat and work, and their relation to energy. These are the two ways in which energy can be transferred between a system and its surroundings:
As we saw in chapter 1, heat and work are not “well-behaved” quantities because they are path functions. While it might be simple to measure the amount of heat and/or work experimentally, these measured quantities cannot be used to define the state of a system. Since heat and work are path functions, their values depend directly on the methods used to transfer them (their paths). Understanding and quantifying these energy transfers is the reason why thermodynamics was developed in the first place. The origins of thermodynamics date back to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, when steam engines started to be used to convert heat into work for technological applications. These early scientists needed a mathematical tool to understand how heat and work were related to each other, and how they were related to the other variables that they were able to measure, such as temperature and volume.
Before we even discuss the definition of energy and how it relates to heat and work, it is crucial to introduce the essential concept of temperature. Temperature is an intuitive concept that has a surprisingly complex definition at the microscopic level.1 However, for all our purposes, it is not essential to have a microscopic definition of temperature, as long as we have the guarantee that this quantity can be measured unambiguously. In other words, we only need a mathematical definition of temperature that agrees with the physical existence of thermometers.

title: 2  Temperature, Heat, and Work
text:
Work is exchanged when the system changes one of its external, macroscopic parameters against a force. The typical example in chemistry is a gas that changes its volume by pushing a piston against an external pressure.
Heat is exchanged because of a temperature difference between the system and its surroundings, without any change in the external parameters. Heat flows through the random collisions between the molecules at the boundary, from the hotter side to the colder one.

title: 2  Temperature, Heat, and Work
text:
2.2 The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
We all know from experience that if we put a hot object in contact with a cold one, after some time they reach the same temperature, and heat stops flowing between them. When this happens, we say that the two objects are in thermal equilibrium. The zeroth law of thermodynamics states that if two thermodynamic systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third one, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. The law might appear trivial and possibly redundant, but it is exactly what makes thermometers possible: the thermometer is the third system, and if it reads the same temperature when in contact with two different objects, we can conclude that the two objects are in thermal equilibrium with each other, even if they have never touched. For this reason, the zeroth law is a fundamental requirement for the mathematical formulation of thermodynamics, and it needs to be stated. The zeroth law can be summarized by the following simple mathematical relation:

Definition 2.1 Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics: If \(T_A = T_B\), and \(T_B = T_C\), then \(T_A = T_C\).

Notice that when we state the zeroth law, it appears intuitive. However, this is not necessarily the case. Let’s, for example, consider a pot of boiling water at \(P=1\;\mathrm{bar}\). Its temperature, \(T_{H_2O}\), is about 373 K. Let’s now submerge in this water a coin made of wood and another coin made of metal. After some sufficient time, the wood coin will be in thermal equilibrium with the water, and its temperature \(T_W = T_{H_2O}\). Similarly, the metal coin will also be in thermal equilibrium with the water, hence \(T_M = T_{H_2O}\). According to the zeroth law, the temperature of the wood coin and that of the metal coin are precisely the same \(T_W = T_M = 373\;\mathrm{K}\), even if they are not in direct contact with each other. Now here’s the catch: since wood and metal transmit heat in different manners, if I take the coins out of the water and put them immediately in your hands, one of them will feel just warm, but the other will burn you. If you had to guess the temperature of the two coins without a thermometer, and without knowing that they were immersed in boiling water, would you suppose that they have the same temperature? Probably not.
The zeroth law tells us that temperature can be measured, but not which numbers to assign to it. The Celsius scale uses two arbitrary reference points, the freezing and boiling points of water, at \(0\) and \(100\;°\text{C}\). A more natural choice comes from gases: at constant pressure, the volume of a gas decreases linearly as it cools, and, if we extrapolate, every gas reaches zero volume at the same temperature, \(-273.15\;°\text{C}\). Since a negative volume makes no sense, this temperature is the lowest possible one, called absolute zero. The Kelvin scale, which we use throughout this book, starts from it: \(T\,[\text{K}] = t\,[°\text{C}] + 273.15\), and absolute temperatures are never negative. We will see in chapter 4 that the second law gives this zero a meaning that does not depend on gases at all, in chapter 6 that it can never be reached, and in chapter 11 why gases behave this way.

title: 2  Temperature, Heat, and Work
section: 2.3 Equilibrium, Stationary States, and Quasi-Static Processes
text:
2.3 Equilibrium, Stationary States, and Quasi-Static Processes
In the rest of this chapter, we will compare processes that happen “fast” with processes that happen “slowly.” These words are vague on their own: is one second fast or slow? A second is an eternity for a molecule, and an instant for a geologist. To use them with precision, we need to compare the speed of a process with something that belongs to the system itself. That something is how quickly the system can return to equilibrium. Let’s start by defining exactly what we mean by equilibrium.

Definition 2.2 Equilibrium state: A state in which the macroscopic variables of the system (such as \(T\), \(P\), \(V\), and the composition) do not change with time, and there are no net flows of energy or matter, neither inside the system nor between the system and its surroundings.

The second part of the definition is important. A system can have variables that do not change with time, and still not be at equilibrium. Consider a metal rod with one end on a hot plate and the other end in a bucket of ice. After a while, the temperature at each point of the rod stops changing: it is high near the plate and low near the ice. Heat, however, flows continuously through the rod, from the plate to the ice. A state like this is called a stationary state (or steady state):

Definition 2.3 Stationary state: A state in which the macroscopic variables of the system do not change with time, but which is maintained by a continuous flow of energy or matter through the system.

The rod in a stationary state does not have a temperature: it has a different temperature at every point. Only at equilibrium are the intensive variables, such as \(T\) and \(P\), uniform throughout the system, so that a single value describes the whole system. This is why the thermodynamics in this book deals with equilibrium states: they are the only states that we can describe with a handful of variables, and the only ones that we can represent as points in a diagram such as the \(PV\) plots in this chapter. Stationary states are just as important in nature (a living cell is a stationary state, not an equilibrium one), but they are the subject of non-equilibrium thermodynamics, which is beyond the scope of this course.
When we disturb a system at equilibrium, for example by suddenly moving a piston, the system goes through a series of states that are not at equilibrium: for a short while, the gas near the piston has a different pressure than the gas far from it, and pressure waves bounce around the container. Eventually, these differences die out, and the system reaches a new equilibrium state. The time this takes has a name:

Definition 2.4 Relaxation time: The time, \(\tau\), that a system needs to return to equilibrium after a disturbance.

The relaxation time depends on the system and on the variable that is relaxing. Pressure differences in a gas travel at the speed of sound, so in a container that is a few centimeters wide, the pressure becomes uniform in a fraction of a millisecond. Temperature differences, instead, are smoothed out by heat conduction, which is much slower: a cold glass of water in a warm room takes tens of minutes to reach the temperature of the room. Some chemical reactions have relaxation times longer than the age of the universe: diamond is not at equilibrium with graphite, but nobody has ever seen a diamond turn into graphite at room temperature.
We now have the yardstick that we were looking for. A process is fast if the conditions of the system change on a time scale that is shorter than, or comparable to, its relaxation time, so that the system has no time to adjust and is driven away from equilibrium. A process is slow if the conditions change on a time scale much longer than the relaxation time, so that the system has always enough time to re-equilibrate. Notice that the same process can be slow for one variable and fast for another. Pushing a piston in one second is slow for the pressure of the gas, which equalizes in less than a millisecond, but it is fast for the exchange of heat through the walls of the container, which takes minutes. In the limit of a process that is slow compared to all the relevant relaxation times, we have:

Definition 2.5 Quasi-static process: A process that happens slowly enough, compared to the relaxation time of the system, that the system passes through a continuous sequence of equilibrium states.

A few things to notice about this definition:

A quasi-static process can be drawn as a line. Since every intermediate state is an equilibrium state, it has well-defined values of \(P\), \(V\), and \(T\), and the whole process is a continuous line in a \(PV\) diagram. A process that is not quasi-static, instead, has well-defined initial and final states only: in between, the gas does not have a single pressure, and the process cannot be drawn as a line. We will see an example of this in the one-step expansion below.
A quasi-static process is an idealization. Any real process takes a finite time, so it is never perfectly quasi-static. However, many real processes are slow enough to be treated as quasi-static to an excellent approximation, and, as we will see in this chapter, we can approach the quasi-static limit as closely as we want by splitting a process into more and more smaller steps.
Quasi-static does not mean “at equilibrium with the surroundings.” The system is at equilibrium internally at every moment, but it may still exchange energy with the surroundings. In chapter 3, we will see that when the system is also balanced with its surroundings at every moment, the process becomes reversible.

title: 2  Temperature, Heat, and Work
text:
2.4 Calculation of Heat
Heat (\(Q\)) is a property that gets transferred between substances. Similarly to work, the amount of heat that flows through a boundary can be measured, but its mathematical treatment is complicated because heat is a path function. As you probably recall from general chemistry, the ability of a substance to absorb heat is given by a coefficient called the heat capacity, which is measured in SI in \(\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol K}}\). However, since heat is a path function, these coefficients are not unique, and we have different ones depending on how the heat transfer happens.

2.4.1 Processes at Constant Volume (Isochoric)
The heat capacity at constant volume measures the ability of a substance to absorb heat at constant volume. Recalling from general chemistry, the molar heat capacity at constant volume has the following formal definition:

The molar heat capacity at constant volume is the amount of heat required to increase the temperature of 1 mol of a substance by 1 K at constant volume.

This is a procedural definition that defines how we can measure \(C_V\) in practice. While this procedure is useful in laboratory settings and in introductory chemistry courses, we need to go beyond it to understand its origin and its meaning. Have you ever wondered why you need to increase the temperature by 1 K? What if you want to increase it by 2? Or 1/2, or 1/1000? Also, the definition is highly imprecise, as there certainly has to be a difference when we increase the temperature of a substance from 1 K to 2 K, to when we increase it from 1001 K to 1002 K. Those situations certainly cannot lead to the same results. How are we going to circumvent this poor definition? We need to apply calculus to remove those arbitrary units and arbitrary increments (remember that differentials are all the same size, and unitless):
\[
C_V = \frac{đ Q_V}{n dT} \Rightarrow đ Q_V = n C_V dT.
\tag{2.1}\]
This new differential definition of \(C_V\) is independent of the unit we use to measure it, and does not require a procedural definition. Given a known value of \(C_V\), the amount of heat that gets transferred can be easily calculated by measuring the changes in temperature, after integration of eq. 2.1:
\[
đ Q_V = n C_V dT \rightarrow \int đ Q_V = n \int_{T_i}^{T_f}C_V dT \rightarrow Q_V = n C_V \int_{T_i}^{T_f}dT,
\tag{2.2}\]
which, assuming \(C_V\) independent of temperature, simply becomes:
\[
Q_V \cong n C_V \Delta T.
\tag{2.3}\]


2.4.2 Processes at Constant Pressure (Isobaric)
Similarly to the previous case, the heat capacity at constant pressure measures the ability of a substance to absorb heat at constant pressure. Recalling again from general chemistry:

The molar heat capacity at constant pressure is the amount of heat required to increase the temperature of 1 mol of a substance by 1 K at constant pressure.

And once again, applying calculus to obtain a differential definition of \(C_P\), we get:
\[
C_P = \frac{đ Q_P}{n dT} \Rightarrow đ Q_P = n C_P dT \rightarrow \int đ Q_P = n \int_{T_i}^{T_f}C_P dT,
\tag{2.4}\]
which results in the simple formula:
\[
Q_P \cong n C_P \Delta T.
\tag{2.5}\]

title: 2  Temperature, Heat, and Work
text:
2.5 Calculation of Work
In thermodynamics, work (\(W\)) is the ability of a system to transfer energy by exerting a force on its surroundings. Work can be measured simply by evaluating its effects, such as displacing a massive object by some amount of space. The mathematical treatment of work, however, is complicated because work is a path function. In the following sections, we will analyze how work is calculated in some prototypical situations commonly encountered in the thermodynamical treatment of systems.






Figure 2.1: Isothermal Expansion of an Ideal Gas Against a Constant External Pressure.



Let’s consider the situation in Figure 2.1, where a special beaker with a piston that is free to move is filled with an ideal gas. The beaker sits on a desk, so the piston is not subject to any external forces other than the external pressure, \(P_{\text{ext}}\), and the internal pressure of the gas, \(P\).2 The piston is initially compressed to a position that is not in equilibrium \((i)\). After the process, the piston reaches a final equilibrium position \((f)\). How do we calculate the work (\(W\)) performed by the system?
From basic physics, we recall that the infinitesimal amount of work associated with an object moving in space is given by the force acting on the object (\(F\)) multiplied by the infinitesimal amount it gets displaced (\(d h\)):
\[
đ W = - Fdh,
\tag{2.6}\]
where the negative sign comes from the chemistry sign convention, Definition 1.1, since the work in Figure 2.1 is performed by the system (expansion). Which force should we use? When the gas expands, the work it performs is the energy needed to push back the surroundings, so the relevant force is the one that the surroundings exert on the piston. Relying upon another definition from physics, the pressure is the ratio between the force (\(F\)) and the area (\(A\)) that such force acts upon, so the force exerted by the surroundings is related to the external pressure, \(P_{\text{ext}}\), by:
\[
P_{\text{ext}} = F/A.
\tag{2.7}\]
Obtaining \(F\) from eq. 2.7 and replacing it in eq. 2.6, we obtain:
\[
đ W = - P_{\text{ext}} \underbrace{Adh}_{dV},
\tag{2.8}\]
and considering that \(Adh\) (area times infinitesimal height) is the definition of an infinitesimal volume \(dV\), we obtain:
\[
đ W = - P_{\text{ext}}dV.
\tag{2.9}\]
The external pressure is not necessarily the same as the pressure of the gas, \(P\). In an expansion that is fast compared to the relaxation time of the gas, the gas inside the beaker does not even have a single pressure, and the part near the piston can be at a very different pressure than the surroundings. However, if the expansion is quasi-static (definition 2.5) and the piston is always balanced, \(P_{\text{ext}}=P\) at every moment, and the work can be written using the pressure of the gas:
\[
đ W = - PdV \qquad \text{(when } P_{\text{ext}}=P\text{)}.
\tag{2.10}\]
If we want to calculate the amount of work performed by a system, \(W\), from eq. 2.9, we need to recall that \(đ W\) is an inexact differential. As such, we cannot integrate it from initial to final as for the (exact) differential of a state function, because:
\[
\int_{i}^{f}đ W \neq W_f - W_i,
\tag{2.11}\]
but rather:
\[
\int_{\text{path}} đ W = W,
\tag{2.12}\]
where the integration is performed along the path. Using eq. 2.12, we can integrate eq. 2.9 as:
\[
\int đ W = W = - \int_{i}^{f} P_{\text{ext}}dV,
\tag{2.13}\]
where the integral on the left-hand side is taken along the path,3 while the integral on the right-hand side can be taken between the initial and final states, since \(V\) is a state function. How do we solve the integral in eq. 2.13? It turns out that there are many different ways to solve this integral (perhaps not surprisingly, since the left-hand side depends on the path), which we will explore in the next section.

2.5.1 \(| W_{\text{max}} |\) and \(| W_{\text{min}} |\) in Processes at Constant Temperature (Isothermal)
At constant temperature, the piston in Figure 2.1 moves along the isotherm in figure 2.2, obtained for 1 mol of an ideal gas at \(T=298\) K.






Figure 2.2: Isotherm of 1 mol of an ideal gas at 298 K, with the initial (i) and final (f) states of an expansion.



An expansion of the gas will happen between \(P_i\) and \(P_f\). If the expansion happens in one step, for example by suddenly releasing the piston against the external atmospheric pressure, the process is not quasi-static: only the initial and final states are equilibrium states, and the gas in between has no single pressure. The external pressure, however, is well defined and constant, and we can use it (for example \(P_f=P_{\text{ext}} =1\;\mathrm{bar}\)), and solve the integral as:
\[
W_{\text{1-step}} = - \int_{i}^{f} P_{\text{ext}}dV = -P_{\text{ext}} \int_{i}^{f} dV = -P_{\text{ext}} (V_f-V_i).
\tag{2.14}\]
Notice how the work is negative, since during an expansion the work is performed by the system (recall the chemistry sign convention). The absolute value of the work4 represents the red area in figure 2.3:






Figure 2.3: Work for a one-step expansion against a constant external pressure: the red rectangle under the final pressure.



\[
\left| W_{\text{1-step}} \right| = P_{\text{ext}} (V_f-V_i)
\tag{2.15}\]
If the process happens in two steps by pausing at an intermediate position (1) until equilibrium is reached, then we should calculate the work by dividing it into two separate processes, \(A\) and \(B\), and solve each one as we did in the previous case. The first process is an expansion between \(P_i\) and \(P_1\), with \(P_1\) constant. The absolute value of the work, \(W_A\), is represented by the blue area in figure 2.4:






Figure 2.4: Work for the first step of a two-step expansion: the blue rectangle under the intermediate pressure.



\[
\left| W_A \right| = P_1 (V_1-V_i)
\tag{2.16}\]
The second process is an expansion between \(P_1\) and \(P_f\), with \(P_f=P_{\text{ext}}\) constant. The absolute value of the work for this second process is represented by the green area in figure 2.5:






Figure 2.5: Work for the second step of a two-step expansion: the green rectangle under the final pressure.



\[
\left| W_B \right| = P_f (V_f-V_1)
\tag{2.17}\]
The total absolute value of the work for the 2-step process is given by the sum of the two areas, as in figure 2.6:






Figure 2.6: Total work for the two-step expansion: the sum of the blue and green rectangles.



\[
\left| W_{\text{2-step}} \right| = \left| W_A \right| + \left| W_B \right| = P_1 (V_1-V_i)+P_f (V_f-V_1).
\tag{2.18}\]
As can be easily verified by comparing the shaded areas in the plots, \(\left| W_{\text{2-step}} \right| > \left| W_{\text{1-step}} \right|\).
We can easily extend this procedure to consider processes that happen in 3, 4, 5, …, \(n\) steps. What is the limit of this procedure? In other words, what happens when \(n \rightarrow \infty\)? A simple answer is given by figure 2.7, which clearly demonstrates that the maximum value of the area underneath the curve \(\left| W_{\text{max}}\right|\) is achieved in an \(\infty\)-step process. In this limit, each step is infinitesimally small, the external pressure is always equal to the pressure of the gas, and we can use eq. 2.10 to calculate the work as:
\[
\left| W_{\infty \text{-step}} \right| = \left| W_{\text{max}} \right| = \sum_{n}^{\infty} P_n(V_n-V_{n-1}) = \int_{i}^{f} PdV.
\tag{2.19}\]






Figure 2.7: Maximum work for the isothermal expansion: the whole area under the isotherm, which is the limit of an expansion performed in more and more steps (6 steps in orange, 30 steps in green, \(\infty\) steps in gray).



The integral on the right hand side of eq. 2.19 can be solved for an ideal gas by calculating the pressure using the ideal gas law \(P=\frac{nRT}{V}\), and solving the integral since \(n\), \(R\), and \(T\) are constant:
\[
\left| W_{\text{max}} \right| = nRT \int_{i}^{f} \frac{dV}{V} = nRT \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i}.
\tag{2.20}\]
This example demonstrates why work is a path function. If we perform the expansion in a single step, which is not quasi-static, the system performs an amount of work that is much smaller than the amount of work it can perform if the expansion between the same points happens in an \(\infty\)-step process. Each step of the \(\infty\)-step process is infinitesimally small, so the gas is always at equilibrium: the \(\infty\)-step process is quasi-static, and it is the only one that follows the isotherm as a line.
The same considerations that we made up to this point for expansion processes apply in reverse to compression ones. The only difference is that the work associated with compressions will have a positive sign since it must be performed onto the system. As such, the amount of work for a transformation that happens in a finite number of steps will be an upper bound to the minimum amount of work required to compress the system.5 \(\left| W_{\text{min}} \right|\) for compressions is calculated as the area underneath the \(PV\) curve, exactly as \(\left| W_{\text{max}} \right|\) for expansions in eq. 2.19.

title: 2  Temperature, Heat, and Work
text:
2.6 Chapter Review

2.6.1 Key Ideas

The zeroth law: two systems in thermal equilibrium with a third one are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This is what makes thermometers possible.
Heat is exchanged because of a temperature difference. At constant volume or pressure, it is calculated from the heat capacities: \(Q_V = n\int C_V\,dT\) and \(Q_P = n\int C_P\,dT\).
Work of expansion is \(W=-\int P_{\text{ext}}\,dV\), negative for an expansion (the system does work) and positive for a compression.
Equilibrium vs. stationary states: at equilibrium, the variables do not change and nothing flows; a stationary state has constant variables maintained by a steady flow. “Fast” and “slow” are measured against the relaxation time, \(\tau\), and a quasi-static process is slow enough to pass only through equilibrium states.
Work depends on the path. Between the same two states, a one-step, a two-step, and an infinitely-many-step expansion give different amounts of work.
Maximum work: for an isothermal ideal gas expansion, the most work is extracted in infinitely many steps, \(|W_{\max}| = nRT\ln\frac{V_f}{V_i}\), and the least work is needed for a compression performed in the same way.



2.6.2 Study Questions
1. What does the zeroth law of thermodynamics state?

If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third one, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
The energy of the universe is conserved.
The entropy of the universe increases.
Heat always flows from hot to cold objects.
The entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at 0 K.


2. What is a quasi-static process?

A process that happens in less than one second.
A process in which the system is always in a stationary state, with a steady flow of heat through it.
A process in which the temperature of the system does not change.
A process slow enough, compared to the relaxation time of the system, that the system passes only through equilibrium states.
A process in which no work is exchanged.


3. What is the differential definition of the molar heat capacity at constant volume?

\(C_V = \frac{Q_V}{\Delta T}\).
\(C_V = \frac{đQ_V}{n\,dT}\).
\(C_V = n\,đQ_V\,dT\).
\(C_V = \frac{dT}{đQ_V}\).
\(C_V = \frac{đQ_P}{n\,dT}\).


4. How is the heat exchanged at constant pressure calculated, assuming \(C_P\) independent of temperature?

\(Q_P = n C_V \Delta T\).
\(Q_P = P \Delta V\).
\(Q_P = nRT \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i}\).
\(Q_P = 0\).
\(Q_P = n C_P \Delta T\).


5. Why is the work of an expansion negative in the chemistry sign convention?

Because the volume decreases.
Because the pressure is negative.
Because the work is performed by the system, which loses energy.
Because the temperature decreases.
Because work is a path function.


6. What is the work for a one-step expansion against a constant external pressure?

\(W = -P_{\text{ext}}(V_f-V_i)\).
\(W = P_{\text{ext}}(V_f-V_i)\).
\(W = -nRT \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i}\).
\(W = 0\).
\(W = n C_V \Delta T\).


7. A gas expands isothermally between the same initial and final states in one step, in two steps, or in infinitely many steps. In which case is the absolute value of the work the largest?

One step.
Two steps.
It is the same in all cases.
Infinitely many steps.
It depends on the gas.


8. What is the absolute value of the maximum work for the isothermal expansion of an ideal gas?

\(\left|W_{\text{max}}\right| = P_{\text{ext}}\Delta V\).
\(\left|W_{\text{max}}\right| = nRT \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i}\).
\(\left|W_{\text{max}}\right| = nR\Delta T\).
\(\left|W_{\text{max}}\right| = n C_V \Delta T\).
\(\left|W_{\text{max}}\right| = nRT\frac{V_f}{V_i}\).


9. What do the one-step, two-step, and infinitely-many-step expansions demonstrate?

That work is a state function.
That the temperature changes during an isothermal process.
That heat and work are the same thing.
That the ideal gas law is not valid.
That work depends on how the process is carried out between the same initial and final states.


10. How must a compression be performed to require the minimum amount of work?

As fast as possible, in one step.
In two steps.
Quasi-statically, in infinitely many steps.
At constant volume.
Against zero external pressure.








TipAnswers





1.a, 2.d, 3.b, 4.e, 5.c, 6.a, 7.d, 8.b, 9.e, 10.c

title: 3  First Law of Thermodynamics
text:
3.1 Calculation of Internal Energy Changes
In chapter 2, we learned how to calculate heat and work, and we saw that both of them are path functions: their values depend on how a process is carried out. In this chapter, we will connect heat and work to a state function, the internal energy, and we will see how this connection becomes one of the most fundamental laws of nature, the first law of thermodynamics. Along the way, we will introduce a second state function, the enthalpy, which will become the protagonist when we study the heat of chemical reactions in chapter 7.
Energy is a property of a system that can be either transferred or converted. The internal energy (\(U\)) of a system is a thermodynamic state function defined as:
In the absence of chemical transformations, heat and work are the only two forms of energy that thermodynamics is concerned with. Keeping in mind Definition 1.1, which gives the convention for the signs of heat and work, the change in internal energy of a system can be written as:
\[
\Delta U = Q + W,
\tag{3.1}\]
which we can write in differential form by considering that the internal energy is a state function, as: \[
dU = đ Q + đ W,
\tag{3.2}\]
which, for processes where the pressure of the system equals the external pressure (as in the quasi-static processes with a balanced piston that we discussed in section 2.5, and in processes at constant pressure, where the system is in mechanical equilibrium with the atmosphere), using eq. 2.10 becomes:
\[
dU = đ Q - PdV.
\tag{3.3}\]
