title: 3  First Law of Thermodynamics
text:
Definition 3.1 Internal Energy: The energy contained within the system, excluding kinetic energy and potential energy of motion and position of the system as a whole.







3.1.1 Internal Energy in Isothermal Processes
To study the behavior of the internal energy in a process at constant temperature (\(dT=0\)), James Prescott Joule (1818–1889) created the apparatus depicted in Figure 3.1.






Figure 3.1: The Joule Expansion Experiment.



The left side of the Joule apparatus’s inner chamber is filled with an ideal gas, while a vacuum is created in the right chamber. Both chambers are immersed in a water bath, whose temperature is monitored with a thermometer: if the gas absorbed or released any heat during the experiment, the temperature of the water would change. When the valve between the chambers is opened, the gas expands into the empty chamber and equilibrates. The work associated with the transformation is:
\[
đ W=-P_{\text{ext}}dV = 0,
\tag{3.4}\]
since the gas expands into a vacuum, there is nothing for it to push against, and \(P_{\text{ext}}=0\). Thus, any change in internal energy must be due to heat, which can be detected by monitoring the temperature at the beginning, \(T_i\), and at the end of the experiment, \(T_f\). Joule observed that, for a gas behaving ideally, the temperature does not change, \(T_i = T_f\). Since the temperature doesn’t change, no heat is exchanged, and therefore the internal energy stays constant:
\[
dU = đ Q = 0.
\tag{3.5}\]

Notice that Joule’s conclusion is valid only for an ideal gas. If we expand a real gas, we do notice a change in temperature associated with the expansion. A typical example of this behavior is when you use a pressurized spray bottle and release its content for an extended time in the air. The container will typically get colder. We will discuss this behavior in chapter 11 when we will study non-ideal gases.

From this simple experiment, we can conclude that the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature.


3.1.2 Internal Energy in Adiabatic Processes
An adiabatic process is defined as a process that happens without the exchange of heat. As such, \(đ Q=0\), and the work associated with an adiabatic process is equal to the change in internal energy:
\[
dU=đ W=-PdV,
\tag{3.6}\]
which can then be calculated using the formulas that we derived in section 2.5. Notice that the work is still a path function: in general, its value depends on the path. However, along adiabatic paths, the work is fixed by the change of a state function, so all adiabatic paths connecting the same two states require the same amount of work. Notice also that isothermal and adiabatic are two very different processes. While an adiabatic process happens without the exchange of heat across the system’s boundaries, this does not mean that the system’s temperature does not change. Isothermal processes are usually associated with a heat transfer across the boundaries to maintain the temperature of the system constant. For adiabatic processes, it is quite the opposite since they are usually associated with a change in temperature.


3.1.3 Internal Energy in Isochoric Processes
An isochoric process is a process in which the volume does not change. Therefore, \(đ W=0\), and \(dU = đ Q_V\), which using eq. 2.1, becomes:
\[
dU = đ Q_V = n C_V dT.
\tag{3.7}\]
Since no work is performed at these conditions, the heat exchanged is equal to the change of a state function, \(\Delta U\). Once again, heat is still a path function in general, but along constant-volume paths its value is fixed by the initial and final states only. Eq. 3.7 also gives a mathematical justification of the concept of heat capacity at constant volume. \(C_V\) can now be interpreted as the partial derivative (a coefficient) of a state function (the internal energy):
\[
C_V = \left( \frac{\partial U} {\partial T} \right)_{V,n=1},
\tag{3.8}\]
where we have replaced the total derivative \(d\) with a partial one \(\partial\), and we have specified that the differentiation happens at constant volume and number of moles. Eq. 3.8 brings a rigorous definition of heat capacity at constant volume for 1 mol of substance:

Definition 3.2 The heat capacity of a substance, \(C_V\), represents its ability to absorb energy at constant volume.



3.1.4 Internal Energy in Isobaric Processes
In an isobaric process, the pressure does not change, hence \(dP=0\). Unfortunately, eq. 3.2 for this case does not simplify further, as happened in the two previous cases. However, in section 2.4.2, we have introduced the useful concept of heat capacity at constant \(P\). \(C_P\) was used in an isobaric process in the same manner as \(C_V\) was used in the isochoric case. That is, as a coefficient to measure the amount of heat absorbed at constant pressure. Eq. 3.8 gave a mathematical definition of \(C_V\) as the partial derivative of a state function (the internal energy). But if heat capacities are coefficients, and coefficients are partial derivatives of state functions, how do we explain \(C_P\)? In order to do so, we can introduce a new state function, called the enthalpy (\(H\)), as:
\[
H = U + PV,
\tag{3.9}\]
and its differential, calculated as:
\[
dH = dU + d(PV) = dU + PdV + \overbrace{VdP}^{0},
\tag{3.10}\]
which can be rearranged as:
\[
dU = dH -PdV.
\tag{3.11}\]
Replacing eq. 3.11 into eq. 3.3:
\[
dH -PdV = đ Q_P - PdV,
\tag{3.12}\]
which simplifies to:
\[
dH = đ Q_P = n C_P dT.
\tag{3.13}\]
Eq. 3.13 establishes that the heat exchanged at constant pressure is equal to a new state function called the enthalpy, defined by eq. 3.9. It also establishes a mathematical justification of the concept of heat capacity at constant pressure. Similarly to \(C_V\), \(C_P\) can now be interpreted as the partial derivative (a coefficient) of the new state function (the enthalpy):
\[
C_P = \left( \frac{\partial H} {\partial T} \right)_{P,n=1},
\tag{3.14}\]
Eq. 3.14 brings also a rigorous definition of heat capacity at constant pressure for 1 mol of substance:

Definition 3.3 The heat capacity of a substance, \(C_P\), represents its ability to absorb enthalpy at constant pressure.

title: 3  First Law of Thermodynamics
text:
3.2 The First Law of Thermodynamics
We finally come to a working definition of the first law. If we take an isolated system—i.e., a system that exchanges neither energy nor mass with its surroundings—its internal energy is conserved. If the internal energy is conserved, \(dU=0\). Therefore, for an isolated system:
\[
đ Q = -đ W,
\tag{3.15}\]
and heat and work can be easily calculated using any of the appropriate formulas introduced in either section 2.5 or section 2.4.
The first law is a conservation law. It is intuitive since it comes directly from Lavoisier’s principle of “nothing is lost, nothing is created, everything is transformed.” Considering that the only system that is truly isolated is the universe, we can condense the first law in one simple sentence:

Definition 3.4 First Law of Thermodynamics: The energy of the universe is conserved.

title: 3  First Law of Thermodynamics
text:
3.3 Reversible and Irreversible Processes
Let’s now consider the cycle in Figure 3.2. The process in this case starts from state 1 (system at \(P_1V_1\)), expands to state 2 (system at \(P_2V_2\)), and compresses back to state 1 (system back to \(P_1V_1\)).






Figure 3.2: Expansion/Compression Cycle of an Ideal Gas.



Since the process starts and finishes at the same state, the value of the internal energy at the end of the process will be the same as its value at the beginning, regardless of the path:1
\[
\oint dU=0,
\tag{3.16}\]
where the symbol \(\oint\) indicates an integral around a cycle. Considering the work associated with the cycle, however, the situation is radically different because it depends on the path that the system is taking, and in general \[
\oint_{\text{path}} đW \neq 0.
\tag{3.17}\]
For instance, if we perform the expansion in one step, the work associated with it will be (using eq. 2.14):2
\[
W^{\text{expansion}}_{\text{1-step}}=-P_2(\underbrace{V_2-V_1}_{>0})<0,
\tag{3.18}\]
and if we also perform the compression in 1-step:3
\[
W^{\text{compression}}_{\text{1-step}}=-P_1(\underbrace{V_1-V_2}_{<0})>0.
\tag{3.19}\]
With a little bit of math, it is easy to prove that the total work for the entire cycle is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
W^{\text{cycle}}_{\text{1-step}} {} & =  W^{\text{expansion}}_{\text{1-step}}+W^{\text{compression}}_{\text{1-step}} \\
& = -P_2(V_2-V_1)-P_1(V_1-V_2) \\
& = -P_2(V_2-V_1)+P_1(V_2-V_1) \\
& = (\underbrace{V_2-V_1}_{>0})(\underbrace{P_1-P_2}_{>0}) > 0,
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.20}\]
or, in other words, the surroundings have to put more work into the compression than they get back from the expansion. Since the gas returns to its initial state, \(\oint dU=0\), and this extra work must leave the system as heat. The energy is not destroyed, but part of the work has been degraded into heat.

In practice, if we want to manually perform this cycle by pushing on the piston by hand, we will notice that it requires more energy to push down than the amount it gives back when we release it, and it moves back up.

In contrast, if both the expansion and the compression happen in a quasi-static \(\infty\)-step manner, the work associated with them will be \(W_{\text{max}}\) and \(W_{\text{min}}\), respectively, which are calculated using eq. 2.20. The total work related to the cycle will be in this case:
\[
\begin{aligned}
W^{\text{cycle}}_{\infty\text{-step}} {} & = W^{\text{expansion}}_{\text{max}}+W^{\text{compression}}_{\text{min}} \\
& = -nRT \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i}-nRT \ln \frac{V_i}{V_f} \\
& = -nRT \underbrace{\left( \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i} - \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i} \right) }_{=0}  = 0,
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.21}\]
which means that, in this case, the work obtained from the expansion is exactly the work needed for the compression, and no work is degraded into heat.

In practice, if we were able to perform this cycle manually by pushing the piston down by hand, we would notice that it requires the same amount of energy to push down as the amount it gives back when it moves up.

This process can happen both ways without losses, and is called reversible:

Definition 3.5 Reversible process: A process whose direction can be inverted at any moment by an infinitesimally small change in the conditions of the surroundings (for example, an infinitesimally small increase of the external pressure), so that the system goes back through exactly the same states.4

What does Definition 3.5 imply in practice? Three things:

A reversible process is quasi-static, and more. It happens in an infinite number of infinitesimal steps, so the system passes through equilibrium states only (definition 2.5). In addition, at each step the system is balanced with its surroundings (for example, \(P=P_{\text{ext}}\) at every moment), and there is no friction or other dissipation. Every reversible process is quasi-static, but a quasi-static process is not necessarily reversible: a piston that moves very slowly but with friction converts part of the work into heat at every step, and the process cannot be undone without leaving a trace. We will see a second example, a slow flow of heat between two bodies at different temperatures, in section 5.3.
A reversible process is the most efficient one. A reversible expansion gives the maximum work, \(W_{\text{max}}\), and a reversible compression requires the minimum work, \(W_{\text{min}}\). Running a reversible process forward and then backward leaves no trace, neither in the system nor in the surroundings.
All real processes are irreversible. Reversible processes are idealizations, like the ideal gas. We can approach them by carrying out a process slowly compared to the relaxation time of the system, and with as little friction as possible, but never reach them. Despite this, they are extremely useful, since they set the limits that real processes can only approach.

title: 3  First Law of Thermodynamics
text:
3.4 Chapter Review

3.4.1 Key Ideas

Internal energy, \(U\), is a state function: the energy contained in the system.
The first law: energy is conserved, \(dU = đQ + đW\). Heat and work are path functions, but their sum is not.
Ideal gas: \(U\) depends only on the temperature (Joule’s experiment), so \(\Delta U = 0\) for any isothermal process.
Special processes: \(\Delta U = W\) in an adiabatic process, and \(\Delta U = Q_V\) in an isochoric one, with \(C_V = \frac{1}{n}\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V\).
Enthalpy, \(H = U + PV\), is the state function whose change equals the heat at constant pressure, \(\Delta H = Q_P\).
Reversible processes happen in infinitely many steps, always at equilibrium; an expansion followed by the reverse compression leaves no net work only if both are reversible.



3.4.2 Study Questions
1. What is the internal energy of a system?

The kinetic energy of the system as a whole.
The energy contained within the system, excluding the kinetic and potential energy of the system as a whole.
The heat stored in the system.
The work that the system can perform.
The potential energy of the system in a gravitational field.


2. What is the first law of thermodynamics in differential form for a closed system?

\(dU = đQ + đW\).
\(dU = đQ - đW\).
\(dU = TdS\).
\(dU = 0\) always.
\(dU = PdV\).


3. What did Joule conclude from the expansion of an ideal gas into a vacuum?

The gas cools down during the expansion.
The gas performs work on the surroundings.
Heat flows into the gas.
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature.
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends on its volume.


4. What characterizes an adiabatic process?

The temperature is constant.
The volume is constant.
The pressure is constant.
The internal energy is constant.
No heat is exchanged, so \(dU = đW\).


5. How does the internal energy change in an isochoric process?

\(dU = -PdV\).
\(dU = 0\).
\(dU = n C_V dT\).
\(dU = n C_P dT\).
\(dU = đW\).


6. How can the heat capacity at constant volume be written as a derivative of a state function?

\(C_V = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V\) (for 1 mol).
\(C_V = \left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_P\) (for 1 mol).
\(C_V = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T\).
\(C_V = \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial U}\right)_V\).
\(C_V = \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V\).


7. What is the definition of enthalpy?

\(H = U - PV\).
\(H = U + TS\).
\(H = Q + W\).
\(H = U + PV\).
\(H = U - TS\).


8. To which quantity is the heat exchanged at constant pressure equal?

The change in internal energy, \(\Delta U\).
The change in enthalpy, \(\Delta H\).
The work, \(W\).
Zero.
The change in temperature, \(\Delta T\).


9. An ideal gas is expanded in one step and then compressed back in one step. What is the total work of this cycle?

Zero, since the gas returns to its initial state.
Negative, since net work is performed by the gas.
It is equal to the change in internal energy.
It cannot be calculated.
Positive, since more work is spent compressing the gas than is obtained from the expansion.


10. What is the total work of an expansion–compression cycle of an ideal gas performed reversibly, in infinitely many steps, at constant temperature?

Positive.
Negative.
Zero.
Infinite.
Equal to \(nRT\).








TipAnswers





1.b, 2.a, 3.d, 4.e, 5.c, 6.a, 7.d, 8.b, 9.e, 10.c

title: 4  Thermodynamic Cycles
text:
4.1 Carnot Cycle
The first law of thermodynamics places no restrictions on the conversion of energy from one form to another. For example, let’s consider once again the Joule experiment (Figure 3.1). If we design a cycle that goes from the gas on the left chamber only to the gas equilibrated in both chambers and backward, as in Figure 4.1, there are no restrictions imposed on this hypothetical cycle by the first law.
As we saw in section 3.1.1, states 1 and 2 have exactly the same energy at constant temperature. Restricting the analysis to the information contained in the first law, the ideal gas could hypothetically go from state 1 (all gas in the left chamber) to state 2 (gas in both chambers), as well as spontaneously close the cycle back from state 2 to state 1, without external intervention. While the transformation from 1 \(\rightarrow\) 2 is intuitively spontaneous (it’s the same transformation that we considered in section 3.1.1), the backward transformation from 2 \(\rightarrow\) 1 is clearly not as intuitive. In this case, the gas should spontaneously compress back to the left side, leaving a vacuum on the right chamber, without interventions from the outside. This transformation is clearly never observed. A gas just does not spontaneously concentrate on one side of a room, leaving a vacuum on the other side. In fact, when we need to create a vacuum, a lot of energy must be spent. Suppose we use exclusively information contained in the first law. In this case, there is nothing that might suggest a system’s preference to perform the transformation 1 \(\rightarrow\) 2, while preventing the 2 \(\rightarrow\) 1 from happening spontaneously. Both states have the same energy, and
\[
\oint dU=0.
\tag{4.1}\]
James Joule himself was indeed convinced that this must be the case and that we don’t observe the backward transformation in practice only because we cannot build ideal machines.1 Another scientist of that era was not convinced. William Thomson, the 1st Baron Kelvin (1824–1907), was unsure about this idea, and invested substantial resources to try to prove Joule wrong.2
The key to resolving the controversy, in favor of Kelvin, came from an unexpected source: the theoretical work of the French military engineer Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot (1796–1832), published years before Joule and Kelvin started working on this problem, and largely forgotten until Kelvin and Rudolf Clausius built on it in the late 1840s and 1850s.3 At that time, the importance of steam engines was growing for industrial applications, but a theoretical perspective was lacking. Carnot was convinced that a scientific understanding of heat engines was necessary to improve their efficiency.
The main contribution of Carnot to thermodynamics is his abstraction of the steam engine’s essential features into a more general and idealized heat engine. The definition of Carnot’s idealized cycle is as follows:
A Carnot cycle connects two “heat reservoirs” at temperatures \(T_h\) (hot) and \(T_l\) (low), respectively. The reservoirs have a large thermal capacity so that their temperatures are unaffected by the cycle. The system is composed exclusively of the ideal gas, which is the only substance that changes temperature throughout the cycle. If we report the four transformations of a Carnot cycle on a \(PV\) diagram, we obtain the following plot:

title: 4  Thermodynamic Cycles
text:
Definition 4.1 A Carnot cycle is an idealized process composed of two isothermal and two adiabatic transformations. Each transformation is either an expansion or a compression of an ideal gas. All transformations are assumed to be reversible, and no energy is lost to mechanical friction.








Figure 4.2: PV-Diagram of a Carnot Cycle (computed for 1 mol of a monatomic ideal gas between \(T_h=600\;\text{K}\) and \(T_l=300\;\text{K}\)).




4.1.1 Stage 1: Isothermal Expansion \(A \rightarrow B\)






Figure 4.3: Stage 1 of a Carnot cycle: isothermal expansion. The cylinder is in contact with the hot reservoir, from which the gas absorbs the heat \(|Q_h|\).



Starting the analysis of the cycle from point \(A\) in Figure 4.2, (figure 4.3)(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnot_cycle), and have been generated and distributed by Author BlyumJ under CC-BY-SA license.] the first transformation we encounter is an isothermal expansion at \(T_h\). Since the transformation is isothermal:
\[
\Delta U_1 = \overbrace{W_1}^{<0} + \overbrace{Q_1}^{>0} = 0 \Rightarrow Q_1 = -W_1,
\tag{4.2}\]
and heat and work can be calculated for this stage using eq. 2.20:
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_1 & = \left| Q_h \right|  = nRT_h \overbrace{\ln \frac{V_B}{V_A}}^{>0 \text{ since } V_B>V_A} > 0, \\
W_1 & = -Q_1 = - nRT_h \ln \frac{V_B}{V_A} < 0,
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.3}\]
where we denoted \(\left| Q_h \right|\) the absolute value of the heat that gets into the system from the hot reservoir.


4.1.2 Stage 2: Adiabatic Expansion \(B \rightarrow C\)






Figure 4.4: Stage 2 of a Carnot cycle: adiabatic expansion. The cylinder is insulated, no heat is exchanged, and the gas cools down while it keeps expanding.



The second transformation is an adiabatic expansion between \(T_h\) and \(T_l\). Since we are at adiabatic conditions:
\[
Q_2 = 0 \Rightarrow \Delta U_2 = W_2,
\tag{4.4}\]
and the negative energy (expansion work) can be calculated using:
\[
\Delta U_2 = W_2 = n \underbrace{\int_{T_h}^{T_l} C_V dT}_{<0 \text{ since } T_\mathrm{l}<T_\mathrm{h}} < 0.
\tag{4.5}\]


4.1.3 Stage 3: Isothermal Compression \(C \rightarrow D\)






Figure 4.5: Stage 3 of a Carnot cycle: isothermal compression. The cylinder is in contact with the cold reservoir, to which the gas releases the heat \(|Q_l|\).



The third transformation is an isothermal compression at \(T_l\). The formulas are the same as those used for stage 1, but they will result in heat and work with reversed signs (since this is a compression):
\[
\Delta U_3 = \overbrace{W_3}^{>0} + \overbrace{Q_3}^{<0} = 0 \Rightarrow Q_3 = -W_3,
\tag{4.6}\]
and:
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_3 & = -\left| Q_l \right|  = nRT_l \overbrace{\ln \frac{V_D}{V_C}}^{<0 \text{ since } V_D<V_C} < 0 , \\
W_3 & = -Q_3 = - nRT_l \ln \frac{V_D}{V_C} > 0,
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.7}\]
where \(\left| Q_l \right|\) is the absolute value of the heat that gets out of the system to the cold reservoir (\(Q_3 = -\left| Q_l \right|\) being the heat entering the system).


4.1.4 Stage 4: Adiabatic Compression \(D \rightarrow A\)






Figure 4.6: Stage 4 of a Carnot cycle: adiabatic compression. The cylinder is insulated again, and the compression warms the gas back to its initial temperature.



The fourth and final transformation is an adiabatic compression that restores the system to point \(A\), bringing it from \(T_l\) to \(T_h\). Similarly to stage 2:
\[
Q_4 = 0 \Rightarrow \Delta U_4 = W_4,
\tag{4.8}\]
since we are at adiabatic conditions. The energy associated with this process is now positive (compression work), and can be calculated using:
\[
\Delta U_4 = W_4 = n \underbrace{\int_{T_l}^{T_h} C_V dT}_{>0 \text{ since } T_\mathrm{h}>T_\mathrm{l}} > 0.
\tag{4.9}\]
Notice how \(\Delta U_4 = - \Delta U_2\) because \(\int_x^y=-\int_y^x\).

title: 4  Thermodynamic Cycles
section: 4.2 Energy, Heat, and Work in the Carnot Cycle
text:
4.2 Energy, Heat, and Work in the Carnot Cycle
Summarizing the results of the previous sections, the total amount of energy for a Carnot cycle is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \Delta U_{\text{TOT}} & = \Delta U_1+\Delta U_2+\Delta U_3+\Delta U_4 \\
                 & = 0 + n \int_{T_h}^{T_l} C_V dT + 0 + n \int_{T_l}^{T_h} C_V dT  \\
                 & = n \int_{T_h}^{T_l} C_V dT - n \int_{T_h}^{T_l} C_V dT = 0 \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.10}\]
which is zero, as it must be for any cycle, since \(\oint dU=0\). Notice how the result comes about: the two isothermal stages do not change the energy of an ideal gas, while the energy lost by the gas in the adiabatic expansion (from \(T_h\) to \(T_l\)) is exactly regained in the adiabatic compression (from \(T_l\) back to \(T_h\)). The amounts of work and heat, however, are not zero, since \(Q\) and \(W\) are path functions. Adding up the work of the four stages, the two adiabatic terms cancel out for the same reason, and we obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  W_{TOT} & = W_1+W_2+W_3+W_4 \\
                 & = - nRT_h \ln \frac{V_B}{V_A} + n \int_{T_h}^{T_l} C_V dT - nRT_l \ln \frac{V_D}{V_C} + n \int_{T_l}^{T_h} C_V dT \\
                 & = - nRT_h \ln \frac{V_B}{V_A} - nRT_l \ln \frac{V_D}{V_C}, \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.11}\]
The two volume ratios are not independent. Since the two adiabats connect the same two temperatures, it can be shown that \(V_C/V_D=V_B/V_A\).4 Therefore, \(\ln\frac{V_D}{V_C}=-\ln\frac{V_B}{V_A}\), and eq. 4.11 reduces to:
\[
W_{TOT} = - nR \left( T_h-T_l \right) \ln \frac{V_B}{V_A} < 0,
\tag{4.12}\]
which is negative, because \(T_h>T_l\) and \(V_B>V_A\). Negative work means that the work is done by the system. In other words, the system is performing \(PV\)-work by transferring heat from a hot reservoir to a cold one via a Carnot cycle. On the other hand, for the heat:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  Q_{\text{TOT}} & = Q_1+Q_2+Q_3+Q_4 \\
                 & = \left| Q_h \right| + 0 - \left| Q_l \right| + 0    \\
                 & = nRT_h \ln \frac{V_B}{V_A} + nRT_l \ln \frac{V_D}{V_C} \\
                 & = nR \left( T_h-T_l \right) \ln \frac{V_B}{V_A} = -W_{TOT},
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.13}\]
which is exactly what we should expect from the first law: since \(\Delta U_{\text{TOT}}=0\), all the net heat absorbed by the gas in a cycle must leave it as work. Since the heat is exchanged only in the two isothermal stages, this can be written as:
\[
W_{TOT}=-(Q_1+Q_3),
\tag{4.14}\]
and, replacing \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) with the absolute values of the heats drawn from the hot and cold reservoirs, \(\left| Q_h \right|\), and \(\left| Q_l \right|\) respectively:
\[
\left| W_{TOT} \right| = \left| Q_h \right| - \left| Q_l \right|,
\tag{4.15}\]
or, in other words, more heat is extracted from the hot reservoir than it is put into the cold one. The difference between the absolute value of these amounts of heat gives the total work of the cycle. This process is depicted in Figure 4.7.






Figure 4.7: Carnot Cycle Diagram.




Example 4.1 (A Carnot Cycle Run in Reverse) Up to this point, we have discussed Carnot cycles working in the hot \(\rightarrow\) cold direction (\(A\) \(\rightarrow\) \(B\) \(\rightarrow\) \(C\) \(\rightarrow\) \(D\) \(\rightarrow\) \(A\)), since this is the primary mode of operation of heat engines that produce work. However, a heat engine could also—in principle—work in the reversed cold \(\rightarrow\) hot direction (\(A\) \(\rightarrow\) \(D\) \(\rightarrow\) \(C\) \(\rightarrow\) \(B\) \(\rightarrow\) \(A\)). Write the equations for heat, work, and energy of each stage of a Carnot cycle going the opposite direction than the one discussed in section 4.1 and section 4.2.
Solution: When the heat engine works in reverse order, the formulas remain the same, but all the signs in front of \(Q\), \(W\), and \(U\) will be reversed. In this case, the total work would get into the system, and heat would be transferred from the cold reservoir to the hot one. Figure 4.7 would be modified as in figure 4.8.






Figure 4.8: A Carnot cycle run in reverse works as a refrigerator: the work \(|W_{TOT}|\) is used to move the heat \(|Q_l|\) from the cold reservoir to the hot one.




This reversed mode of operation is the basic principle behind refrigerators and air conditioning.

title: 4  Thermodynamic Cycles
text:
4.3 Efficiency of a Carnot Cycle
The efficiency (\(\varepsilon\)) of a cycle is defined as the ratio between the absolute value of the work extracted from the cycle (\(\left| W_{TOT} \right|\)) and the heat that gets into the system (\(\left| Q_h \right|\)):
\[
\varepsilon = \frac{\left| W_{TOT} \right|}{\left| Q_h \right|} =\frac{-W_{TOT}}{Q_1}
\tag{4.16}\]
where the minus sign in front of the work is necessary because the efficiency is defined as a positive number. Replacing eq. 4.14 into eq. 4.16, we obtain:
\[
\varepsilon = \frac{Q_3+Q_1}{Q_1} = 1+\frac{Q_3}{Q_1}.
\tag{4.17}\]
If we go back to eq. 4.16 and we replace eq. 4.12 for \(W_{TOT}\) and eq. 4.3 for \(Q_1\), we obtain:
\[
\varepsilon = \frac{nR \left( T_h - T_l \right) \ln V_B/V_A}{nRT_h \ln V_B/V_A} = \frac{T_h-T_l}{T_h}=1-\frac{T_l}{T_h }<1,
\tag{4.18}\]
which proves that the efficiency of a Carnot cycle is strictly smaller than 1.5 In other words, no cycle can convert 100% of the heat into work it extracts from a hot reservoir. Eq. 4.18 also has a deeper meaning. Since the efficiency of a Carnot cycle does not depend on the substance inside it, the ratio \(\frac{\left| Q_l \right|}{\left| Q_h \right|} = \frac{T_l}{T_h}\) defines temperature without any reference to a particular thermometer. This is the thermodynamic temperature scale, introduced by Kelvin in 1848, and it coincides with the scale of the gas thermometer of chapter 2. In this scale, absolute zero is the temperature of a cold reservoir that would receive no heat at all, so that the engine could turn all the heat into work, which is exactly what the second law forbids. This finding had remarkable consequences on the entire thermodynamics field and set the foundation for the introduction of entropy. We will use eq. 4.16 and eq. 4.18 for this purpose in the next chapter, but we conclude the discussion on Carnot cycles by returning to Lord Kelvin. In 1851 he used this finding to formulate his statement “It is impossible for a self-acting machine, unaided by any external agency, to convey heat from one body to another at a higher temperature. It is impossible, by means of inanimate material agency, to derive mechanical effect from any portion of matter by cooling it below the temperature of the coldest of the surrounding objects.”6 This statement conclusively disproved Joule’s original theories and demonstrated that there is some fundamental principle to govern the flow of heat beyond the first law of thermodynamics.

4.3.1 Refrigerators and Heat Pumps
For a cycle run in reverse, as in figure 4.8, the efficiency is replaced by the coefficient of performance (COP), the ratio between what we want and the work that we pay for it. A refrigerator is meant to extract the heat \(\left| Q_l \right|\) from the cold reservoir (the inside of the fridge), while a heat pump is meant to deliver the heat \(\left| Q_h \right|\) to the hot reservoir (the inside of a house in winter). Following the same steps as for eq. 4.18, for a Carnot cycle:
\[
\text{COP}_{\text{refrigerator}} = \frac{\left| Q_l \right|}{\left| W_{TOT} \right|} = \frac{T_l}{T_h-T_l}, \qquad \qquad
\text{COP}_{\text{heat pump}} = \frac{\left| Q_h \right|}{\left| W_{TOT} \right|} = \frac{T_h}{T_h-T_l}.
\tag{4.19}\]
Unlike the efficiency, the COP can be (and usually is) larger than 1, since the work is used only to move heat, not to create it. For example, a heat pump that keeps a house at \(20\;°\text{C}\) (\(293\;\text{K}\)) when it is \(0\;°\text{C}\) outside (\(273\;\text{K}\)) has a Carnot COP of \(\frac{293}{20} \approx 15\): in the ideal case, every joule of electricity delivers 15 joules of heat to the house. Real heat pumps reach COPs of about 3–4, which still makes them much more efficient than electric heaters, whose COP is 1. The COP decreases as the temperature difference grows, which is why heat pumps work less well in very cold climates.

title: 4  Thermodynamic Cycles
text:
4.4 Chapter Review

4.4.1 Key Ideas

The first law is not enough: it allows processes that never happen, such as a gas spontaneously compressing into half of its container.
The Carnot cycle is made of two reversible isotherms and two reversible adiabats, between a hot reservoir at \(T_h\) and a cold one at \(T_l\).
Over a full cycle, \(\Delta U = 0\), so the total work equals minus the total heat exchanged.
Efficiency is the work produced divided by the heat absorbed from the hot reservoir. For a Carnot cycle, \(\varepsilon = 1 - \frac{T_l}{T_h} < 1\).
No engine converts all of its heat into work, because some heat must always be released to the cold reservoir.
Refrigerators and heat pumps are reversed cycles, rated by their coefficient of performance: \(\frac{T_l}{T_h-T_l}\) and \(\frac{T_h}{T_h-T_l}\) for Carnot cycles. The COP is usually larger than 1.
Run in reverse, a Carnot cycle uses work to move heat from the cold to the hot reservoir: it works as a refrigerator.



4.4.2 Study Questions
1. What does the first law of thermodynamics say about a gas that spontaneously compresses back into one side of the Joule apparatus?

It forbids it, since energy would not be conserved.
It requires work to be done on the gas.
It requires heat to flow out of the gas.
Nothing: the process would conserve energy, so the first law does not forbid it.
It shows that the process is spontaneous.


2. What transformations make up a Carnot cycle?

Two isochoric and two isobaric transformations.
Two isothermal and two adiabatic reversible transformations.
Four isothermal transformations.
Four adiabatic transformations.
One isothermal, one adiabatic, one isochoric, and one isobaric transformation.


3. What happens during the isothermal expansion at \(T_h\) in a Carnot cycle?

\(\Delta U = 0\), heat is absorbed from the hot reservoir, and the same amount of energy leaves as work.
No heat is exchanged.
The temperature drops from \(T_h\) to \(T_l\).
Heat is released to the cold reservoir.
Work is done on the gas.


4. What happens during the adiabatic expansion in a Carnot cycle?

Heat is absorbed from the hot reservoir.
The internal energy stays constant.
Heat is released to the cold reservoir.
The volume decreases.
No heat is exchanged, the gas performs work, and its temperature drops from \(T_h\) to \(T_l\).


5. What is the total change in internal energy for a complete Carnot cycle?

\(nR(T_h-T_l)\ln\frac{V_B}{V_A}\).
\(nC_V(T_h-T_l)\).
Zero, since the internal energy is a state function.
Equal to the total work.
Equal to the heat absorbed from the hot reservoir.


6. What is the total work of a Carnot cycle?

\(W_{TOT} = nR(T_h-T_l)\ln\frac{V_B}{V_A}\).
\(W_{TOT} = -nR(T_h-T_l)\ln\frac{V_B}{V_A}\).
\(W_{TOT} = 0\).
\(W_{TOT} = nRT_h\ln\frac{V_B}{V_A}\).
\(W_{TOT} = nC_V(T_h-T_l)\).


7. How is the efficiency of a heat engine defined?

\(\varepsilon = \frac{|Q_h|}{|W_{TOT}|}\).
\(\varepsilon = \frac{|Q_l|}{|Q_h|}\).
\(\varepsilon = \frac{|W_{TOT}|}{|Q_l|}\).
\(\varepsilon = \frac{|W_{TOT}|}{|Q_h|}\).
\(\varepsilon = \frac{T_h}{T_l}\).


8. What is the efficiency of a Carnot cycle in terms of the reservoir temperatures?

\(\varepsilon = 1-\frac{T_l}{T_h}\).
\(\varepsilon = 1-\frac{T_h}{T_l}\).
\(\varepsilon = \frac{T_h}{T_l}\).
\(\varepsilon = \frac{T_h-T_l}{T_l}\).
\(\varepsilon = 1\).


9. Why is the efficiency of a Carnot cycle always smaller than 1?

Because of friction in the engine.
Because the gas is not ideal.
Because heat is a state function.
Because the cycle is irreversible.
Because it would be 1 only if \(T_l=0\;\text{K}\) or \(T_h=\infty\), which are impossible.


10. What happens when a Carnot cycle is run in reverse?

It produces more work than the forward cycle.
It reaches 100% efficiency.
Work is put into the system, and heat is moved from the cold reservoir to the hot one, as in a refrigerator.
Heat flows from the hot reservoir to the cold one without work.
It violates the first law.








TipAnswers





1.d, 2.b, 3.a, 4.e, 5.c, 6.b, 7.d, 8.a, 9.e, 10.c

title: 5  Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
text:
5.1 Entropy
In chapter 4, we used heat engines to understand why some processes are spontaneous while others are not, and we found that no engine can convert all the heat it absorbs into work. Carnot’s findings did not just inspire Lord Kelvin on this subject, but they also motivated Rudolf Clausius (1822–1888) to introduce a new state function, the entropy. In this chapter, we will follow Clausius’ reasoning to define the entropy, we will use it to write the second law of thermodynamics, and we will then look at the same quantity from the microscopic point of view of Boltzmann, to understand what entropy really measures.
Let’s return to the efficiency of a Carnot cycle, and bring together the two expressions that we found in eq. 4.17 and eq. 4.18:
\[
\varepsilon = 1+\frac{Q_3}{Q_1} = 1-\frac{T_l}{T_h}.
\tag{5.1}\]
Subtracting 1 from both sides, we obtain \(\frac{Q_3}{Q_1}=-\frac{T_l}{T_h}\). We can then multiply both sides by \(\frac{Q_1}{T_l}\), which separates the quantities related to the cold reservoir from the ones related to the hot reservoir:
\[
\frac{Q_3}{T_l} = -\frac{Q_1}{T_h},
\tag{5.2}\]
or, moving everything to the left-hand side:
\[
\frac{Q_3}{T_l} + \frac{Q_1}{T_h} = 0.
\tag{5.3}\]
The left-hand side of eq. 5.3 is a sum of two terms, one for each isothermal stage of the Carnot cycle. Each term is the heat exchanged during that stage, divided by the temperature at which it is exchanged. Since, according to Definition 4.1, each transformation in a Carnot cycle is reversible, these are heats exchanged at reversible conditions, \(Q_{\mathrm{REV}}\). The two adiabatic stages do not contribute, since no heat is exchanged during them.
Is this result special to the Carnot cycle? To find out, let’s look at the heat exchanged by an ideal gas along any reversible path, not just along isotherms and adiabats. From the first law, the reversible heat is \(đQ_{\mathrm{REV}} = dU - đW_{\mathrm{REV}}\). Since the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature (section 3.1.1), \(dU = nC_V\,dT\) for any process, and the reversible work is \(đW_{\mathrm{REV}} = -P\,dV = -\frac{nRT}{V}dV\). Therefore:
\[
đQ_{\mathrm{REV}} = nC_V\,dT + \frac{nRT}{V}\,dV.
\tag{5.4}\]
This looks like a total differential, eq. 1.3, but it is not one. If we apply the Schwarz test of chapter 1 to the two coefficients, the derivative of \(nC_V\) with respect to \(V\) is zero, while the derivative of \(\frac{nRT}{V}\) with respect to \(T\) is \(\frac{nR}{V}\). The two mixed derivatives are different, as we expect for the heat, which is a path function. Now let’s divide both sides of eq. 5.4 by the temperature:
\[
\frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T} = \frac{nC_V}{T}\,dT + \frac{nR}{V}\,dV.
\tag{5.5}\]
This time, the derivative of \(\frac{nC_V}{T}\) with respect to \(V\) is zero, and the derivative of \(\frac{nR}{V}\) with respect to \(T\) is also zero. The test is passed: eq. 5.5 is an exact differential.1 Dividing by \(T\) removed the \(T\) from the coefficient of \(dV\), which was the only thing that made the heat path-dependent. And since the integral of an exact differential around a closed path is always zero, for any reversible cycle of an ideal gas we have:
\[
\oint \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T} = 0.
\tag{5.6}\]
The Carnot result, eq. 5.3, is just a special case: along the two isotherms we add \(\frac{Q}{T}\), and along the two adiabats we add nothing.
We have proved eq. 5.6 only for the ideal gas, but the result is general. Carnot showed that every reversible engine working between the same two temperatures has the same efficiency, whatever substance it contains (otherwise, coupling two different engines would let us move heat from a cold body to a hot one with no other effect, which, as we will see in this chapter, never happens). Since the efficiency fixes \(\frac{Q_3}{Q_1}\), eq. 5.3 holds for the Carnot cycles of every substance, and from there one can show that eq. 5.6 holds for any reversible cycle of any substance. We will not go through this general proof, which requires more work than it is worth here; the ideal-gas calculation already shows the essential point.
Eq. 5.6 is a remarkable result. The heat, \(đQ\), is a path function, and its integral around a cycle is in general not zero. However, if we take the heat exchanged reversibly and divide it by the temperature, we obtain a quantity whose integral around any reversible cycle is zero. As we saw for the energy in eq. 3.16, this is precisely the property that defines a state function: when we go back to the starting point, we always find the same value. Clausius realized this in 1865, and he decided to call the new state function entropy, and to indicate it with the letter \(S\):
For a transformation between an initial and a final state, the change in entropy is obtained by integration along any reversible path that connects the two states:
\[
\Delta S = S_f - S_i = \int_i^f \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T}.
\tag{5.8}\]
Let’s unpack Definition 5.1:

title: 5  Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
text:
Definition 5.1 Entropy: The state function \(S\) whose infinitesimal change is equal to the heat exchanged at reversible conditions, divided by the temperature at which it is exchanged: \[
dS = \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T}.
\tag{5.7}\]





Dividing by \(T\) turns a path function into a state function. In chapter 1, we introduced inexact differentials, such as \(đQ\), which cannot be integrated as differences between final and initial values. Eq. 5.7 tells us that, for reversible processes, dividing \(đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}\) by the temperature turns it into the exact differential of a state function, \(dS\). Mathematicians call \(1/T\) an integrating factor.
Only the reversible heat works. The heat exchanged along an irreversible path is different, and dividing it by \(T\) does not give \(dS\). To calculate the entropy change of an irreversible process, we must find a reversible path between the same initial and final states and calculate \(\Delta S\) along that path. Since the entropy is a state function, the result is valid for the irreversible process as well.
The same heat matters more at low temperature. The entropy change produced by a given amount of heat is larger when the heat is exchanged at a low temperature than at a high temperature. Intuitively, giving 1 kJ of heat to a cold object changes it more than giving the same 1 kJ to a hot one.
The units of entropy are energy divided by temperature, \(\text{J/K}\) in SI. The entropy is an extensive property, and its molar version, \(\overline{S}\), is measured in \(\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\).
Only changes in entropy are defined, for now. Eq. 5.8 gives us differences in entropy, but not absolute values. We will see in chapter 6 that the third law of thermodynamics fixes the zero of the entropy scale.

5  Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics

title: 5  Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
text:
5.2 Irreversible Cycles
Up to this point, we have discussed reversible cycles only. What happens when the cycle is irreversible? In chapter 4, we saw that the efficiency of a Carnot cycle, eq. 4.18, is the maximum efficiency that any cycle working between two temperatures can reach. Any real (irreversible) cycle loses some energy along the way, for example to friction, and its efficiency is always smaller than the Carnot one. Therefore, eq. 5.1 does not hold anymore for an irreversible cycle, and it must be replaced by an inequality:
\[
\overbrace{1+\frac{Q^{\mathrm{IRR}}_3}{Q^{\mathrm{IRR}}_1}}^{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{IRR}}} < \overbrace{1-\frac{T_l}{T_h}}^{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{REV}}}.
\tag{5.9}\]
Following exactly the same steps used in section 5.1 (subtracting 1 from both sides and multiplying by \(\frac{Q^{\mathrm{IRR}}_1}{T_l}\), which is positive, so the direction of the inequality does not change), we obtain:
\[
\frac{Q^{\mathrm{IRR}}_3}{Q^{\mathrm{IRR}}_1} < - \frac{T_l}{T_h} \longrightarrow \frac{Q^{\mathrm{IRR}}_3}{T_l} + \frac{Q^{\mathrm{IRR}}_1}{T_h} < 0 \longrightarrow \sum_i \frac{Q_{\mathrm{IRR},i}}{T_i} < 0,
\tag{5.10}\]
which, using the same calculus procedure as before, becomes:
\[
\oint \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{IRR}}}{T} < 0.
\tag{5.11}\]
Putting eq. 5.6 and eq. 5.11 together, we obtain:
\[
\oint \frac{đQ}{T} \leq 0,
\tag{5.12}\]
where the equal sign holds for reversible cycles exclusively, while the inequality sign holds for irreversible ones. Eq. 5.12 is known as the Clausius inequality. In words, it tells us that around an irreversible cycle, the system always gives away more “heat divided by temperature” than it absorbs. This is the mathematical version of the fact that some of the energy that goes through a real engine is always wasted.

5  Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics

title: 5  Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
text:
5.3 The Second Law of Thermodynamics
We are now ready to use the Clausius inequality to understand spontaneity. Let’s consider an isolated system that undergoes an irreversible transformation from state 1 to state 2, and then let’s bring it back from state 2 to state 1 along a reversible path, as in Figure 5.1.






Figure 5.1: Spontaneous and Non-Spontaneous Transformations in a Cycle.



This cycle is similar to the one in Figure 4.1 for the Joule expansion experiment: the gas expands spontaneously into the vacuum (1 \(\rightarrow\) 2), but it never goes back on its own (2 \(\rightarrow\) 1). To bring it back, we must compress it from the outside.2 Since the cycle contains an irreversible step, it is irreversible overall, and the Clausius inequality, eq. 5.12, gives:
\[
\int_1^2 \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{IRR}}}{T} + \int_2^1 \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T} < 0.
\tag{5.13}\]
The second integral is taken along a reversible path, so, according to eq. 5.8, it is the entropy change from state 2 to state 1, which is \(-\Delta S\), where \(\Delta S=S_2-S_1\) is the entropy change of the forward process. Moving it to the right-hand side, we obtain:
\[
\underbrace{\int_1^2 \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T}}_{\Delta S} > \underbrace{\int_1^2 \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{IRR}}}{T}}_{=0},
\tag{5.14}\]
where the right-hand side is zero because the system is isolated during the forward process, and therefore \(đQ_{\mathrm{IRR}}=0\). Eq. 5.14 simply becomes:
\[
\Delta S > 0.
\tag{5.15}\]
What does eq. 5.15 tell us?

In an isolated system, spontaneous processes increase the entropy. Every irreversible process that happens on its own in an isolated system has \(\Delta S > 0\). Spontaneous processes are always irreversible, since reversible processes are idealizations that require infinitely slow, controlled changes.
The entropy changes even if no heat is exchanged. In the Joule expansion, \(Q=0\), and yet \(\Delta S>0\). This is not a contradiction: the entropy change must be calculated along a reversible path between the same states, and along that path heat is exchanged. We will calculate this value in chapter 6.
The reverse process would decrease the entropy, and it never happens on its own in an isolated system. This is why the gas never goes back to one side of the box.

Since the only system that is truly isolated is the universe, we can write a concise statement for a new fundamental law of thermodynamics:

Definition 5.2 Second Law of Thermodynamics: For any spontaneous process, the entropy of the universe increases.

Historically, the second law was first stated in terms of heat and engines, in two classical forms that we can now derive from the entropy:

Clausius statement: heat cannot flow spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter one. If the heat \(Q>0\) moved on its own from a reservoir at \(T_l\) to one at \(T_h > T_l\), the entropy of the universe would change by \(-\frac{Q}{T_l}+\frac{Q}{T_h} < 0\).
Kelvin statement: no cyclic process can absorb heat from a single reservoir and convert it entirely into work. After a full cycle, the entropy of the engine is unchanged, while the reservoir loses the entropy \(\frac{Q}{T}\), so the entropy of the universe would decrease.

The two statements are equivalent: a device that violated one of them could be combined with an ordinary engine or refrigerator to violate the other. Both are contained in Kelvin’s 1851 words that we quoted at the end of chapter 4.
The entropy also lets us complete the distinction between quasi-static and reversible processes that we started in chapter 3. Consider two large reservoirs, at \(T_h\) and \(T_l\), connected by a thin rod that conducts heat very poorly. Heat flows so slowly that both reservoirs pass only through equilibrium states, and the process is quasi-static. Yet, when the heat \(Q\) moves from the hot reservoir to the cold one, the entropy of the universe changes by \(\frac{Q}{T_l}-\frac{Q}{T_h}>0\), and the process is irreversible: the heat will never flow back on its own. A slow process is reversible only if, in addition, there are no finite differences of temperature (or pressure) between the system and its surroundings, and no friction.

title: 5  Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
text:
5.4 Boltzmann Entropy
Up to this point, we have treated entropy as a macroscopic quantity, defined through heat and temperature. This definition is powerful, but it does not tell us what entropy is at the level of molecules, which is where chemistry happens. The microscopic meaning of entropy was found by Ludwig Eduard Boltzmann (1844–1906), who connected it to the number of ways in which the molecules of a system can be arranged.
To understand Boltzmann’s idea, we need to distinguish between two ways of describing a system:

A macrostate is described by the macroscopic variables that we can measure, such as pressure, volume, and temperature.
A microstate is a complete specification of where every single molecule is and how it moves.3

Many different microstates correspond to the same macrostate, since we can swap molecules around without changing the pressure or the temperature. The number of microstates that correspond to a given macrostate is called its multiplicity, and is indicated with \(\Omega\).

5.4.1 Counting Microstates
Let’s see how this works with a simple example. Consider a box divided into two halves, left and right, containing just four molecules, which we label \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), and \(d\). Each molecule can be in either half, and we consider as a macrostate the number of molecules in the left half. The microstates are all the possible ways of assigning each molecule to one of the two halves:



Table 5.1: Microstates of four molecules in a box divided into two halves.










Molecules on the left
Microstates (molecules on the left)
\(\Omega\)




4
\(abcd\)
1


3
\(abc\), \(abd\), \(acd\), \(bcd\)
4


2
\(ab\), \(ac\), \(ad\), \(bc\), \(bd\), \(cd\)
6


1
\(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(d\)
4


0
none
1






There are \(2^4=16\) microstates in total. If the molecules move around randomly, each microstate is equally likely, and the probability of each macrostate is proportional to its multiplicity. Notice three things in table 5.1:

The evenly distributed macrostate is the most probable. Two molecules on each side has \(\Omega=6\), which corresponds to a probability of \(6/16\), almost 40%.
The macrostate with all molecules on one side is the least probable. It has \(\Omega=1\), so its probability is only \(1/16\).
The effect becomes overwhelming for many molecules. With \(N\) molecules, the probability of finding all of them on the left is \(1/2^N\). For \(N=100\) molecules, this is about \(10^{-30}\). For a mole of gas, with \(N\approx 6\times 10^{23}\), it is so small that it will never be observed. This is why the gas in the Joule experiment never goes back to one side of the box: not because it is forbidden, but because it is overwhelmingly improbable.



5.4.2 The Boltzmann Equation
Boltzmann connected the multiplicity to the thermodynamic entropy through the formula that became famous as the Boltzmann equation:
\[
S = k_B \ln \Omega,
\tag{5.16}\]
where \(k_B\) is the Boltzmann constant, \(k_B = R/N_A = 1.380649 \times 10^{-23} \, \text{J/K}\), with \(R\) being the ideal gas constant and \(N_A\) Avogadro’s constant. The Boltzmann constant is the ideal gas constant “per molecule”, and it is the conversion factor between the microscopic counting of \(\Omega\) and the macroscopic entropy measured in \(\text{J/K}\).
Why the logarithm? If we put together two independent systems, the number of microstates of the combined system is the product of the two multiplicities, \(\Omega=\Omega_1\Omega_2\), since every microstate of the first can be combined with every microstate of the second. However, the entropy is extensive, so the entropy of the combined system must be the sum of the two entropies. The logarithm is the function that turns products into sums: \(k_B\ln(\Omega_1\Omega_2)=k_B\ln\Omega_1+k_B\ln\Omega_2\).
Let’s now check that Boltzmann’s entropy agrees with Clausius’ one, using the expansion of an ideal gas into twice its initial volume. Each molecule now has twice as many positions available, so, for each microstate of the initial state, there are \(2^N\) microstates of the final state, where \(N\) is the number of molecules. Using eq. 5.16:
\[
\Delta S = k_B \ln \Omega_f - k_B \ln \Omega_i = k_B \ln \frac{\Omega_f}{\Omega_i} = k_B \ln 2^N = N k_B \ln 2 = nR \ln 2,
\tag{5.17}\]
where in the last step we used \(N k_B = n N_A \frac{R}{N_A} = nR\). In chapter 6, we will calculate the same entropy change from Clausius’ definition, obtaining \(\Delta S = nR \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i}\), which for \(V_f=2V_i\) is exactly the same result. The two definitions of entropy describe the same quantity.


5.4.3 Why “Disorder” Can Be Misleading
Entropy is often described as a measure of “disorder.” This description is not completely wrong, but it can be misleading. A more accurate description is that the entropy measures the number of microscopic arrangements compatible with what we observe macroscopically. For example, when ice melts, the entropy increases because the water molecules in the liquid can move around and take many more positions and orientations than in the rigid crystal. Calling the liquid “more disordered” is a shortcut for “has many more microstates,” and it is the number of microstates that we should keep in mind.
The shortcut becomes a misconception when we apply it to everyday objects. A messy room does not have a higher thermodynamic entropy than a tidy one. The thermodynamic entropy counts the arrangements of about \(10^{23}\) molecules, and the arrangement of a few dozen books and socks does not contribute to it in any measurable way. Moreover, a messy room and a tidy room are each just one specific arrangement of the objects. If we really want to count arrangements of objects, we need many identical copies of the same room.4

title: 5  Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
text:
5.5 Chapter Review

5.5.1 Key Ideas

Clausius entropy: \(dS = \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T}\). The entropy is a state function, measured in \(\text{J/K}\).
Why dividing by \(T\) works: for an ideal gas, \(đQ_{\mathrm{REV}} = nC_V\,dT + \frac{nRT}{V}dV\) fails the Schwarz test, but \(\frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T}\) passes it. Its integral around any reversible cycle is zero, which makes \(S\) a state function (\(1/T\) is an integrating factor).
Irreversible processes: to calculate \(\Delta S\), we use a reversible path between the same two states, since \(S\) is a state function.
Clausius inequality: \(\oint \frac{đQ}{T} \leq 0\) around any cycle, with the equal sign only for reversible cycles.
The second law: the entropy of the universe increases in every spontaneous process, and stays constant only in reversible ones.
Classical statements: heat does not flow spontaneously from cold to hot (Clausius), and no cycle turns the heat of a single reservoir entirely into work (Kelvin). Both follow from the increase of the entropy of the universe.
Boltzmann entropy: \(S = k_B \ln \Omega\), where \(\Omega\) counts the microstates compatible with the macroscopic state. Spontaneous processes move toward the macrostates with the most microstates.



5.5.2 Study Questions
1. Which quantity has a sum (or integral) equal to zero around any reversible cycle?

The heat, \(Q_{\mathrm{REV}}\).
The heat divided by the temperature, \(\frac{Q_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T}\).
The work, \(W\).
The temperature, \(T\).
The heat multiplied by the temperature, \(Q_{\mathrm{REV}}T\).


2. Which formula defines the entropy according to Clausius?

\(dS = \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T}\).
\(dS = \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{IRR}}}{T}\).
\(dS = đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}\,T\).
\(S = \frac{T}{Q}\).
\(dS = \frac{đW}{T}\).


3. How can we calculate the entropy change of an irreversible process?

By integrating the irreversible heat divided by the temperature.
It cannot be calculated.
By using the work instead of the heat.
By calculating it along a reversible path between the same initial and final states.
By assuming it is always zero.


4. What are the units of entropy in the SI?

\(\text{J}\).
\(\text{K/J}\).
\(\text{J}\cdot\text{K}\).
\(\text{J/mol}\).
\(\text{J/K}\).


5. What is the Clausius inequality?

\(\oint \frac{đQ}{T} \geq 0\).
\(\oint \frac{đQ}{T} = 0\) always.
\(\oint \frac{đQ}{T} \leq 0\).
\(\oint đQ \leq 0\).
\(\oint dS > 0\).


6. How does the efficiency of an irreversible cycle compare with that of a Carnot cycle between the same temperatures?

It is smaller.
It is larger.
It is the same.
It is always zero.
It can be larger than 1.


7. What does the second law of thermodynamics state?

The energy of the universe is conserved.
The entropy of the universe is constant.
The entropy of a system always increases.
For any spontaneous process, the entropy of the universe increases.
Heat can be completely converted into work.


8. A gas expands into a vacuum inside an insulated container (the Joule expansion). What are the heat exchanged and the entropy change of the gas?

\(Q>0\) and \(\Delta S>0\).
\(Q=0\) and \(\Delta S>0\).
\(Q=0\) and \(\Delta S=0\).
\(Q<0\) and \(\Delta S<0\).
\(Q=0\) and \(\Delta S<0\).


9. Which formula is the Boltzmann equation for the entropy?

\(S = k_B\,\Omega\).
\(S = R \ln T\).
\(S = \frac{\Omega}{k_B}\).
\(S = k_B T\).
\(S = k_B \ln \Omega\).


10. Four molecules move randomly in a box divided into two halves. Which macrostate is the most probable?

All four molecules on the left.
Three molecules on the left and one on the right.
Two molecules on each side.
All four molecules on the right.
All macrostates are equally probable.








TipAnswers





1.b, 2.a, 3.d, 4.e, 5.c, 6.a, 7.d, 8.b, 9.e, 10.c

text:
In fact, we can integrate it directly: if \(C_V\) is constant, \(\frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T} = d\left(nC_V \ln T + nR \ln V\right)\).↩︎
Strictly speaking, during the reversible compression the system cannot be isolated, since a reversible return to state 1 requires exchanging heat and work with the surroundings. This does not affect our argument: we use the reversible path only as a tool to calculate the entropy change between states 1 and 2, and since the entropy is a state function, the result does not depend on how we actually bring the system back. This is therefore a plausibility argument rather than a rigorous proof, but it leads to the correct result.↩︎
Positions and velocities are continuous quantities, so to count microstates we have to divide space into small cells, and only ask which cell each molecule is in. Quantum mechanics, which we will study in P-Chem 2, makes this counting exact, since the energy levels of molecules are discrete.↩︎
A better version of the analogy is that of a hotel with many identical rooms containing the same objects. The collection of all the unmade rooms in the morning has a higher entropy than the collection of the same rooms after the housekeepers have arranged all the objects in every room in exactly the same way.↩︎

title: 6  Calculation of Entropy and the Third Law of Thermodynamics
text:
6.1 Calculation of \(\Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}}\)
In chapter 5, we defined the entropy as a state function, and we found that the entropy of the universe increases in every spontaneous process. A definition, however, is not very useful until we know how to calculate it. In this chapter, we will learn how to calculate the entropy changes of the most common transformations: heating and cooling, expansions and compressions, and phase changes. We will then see how to account for the surroundings, and we will introduce the third law of thermodynamics, which fixes the zero of the entropy scale and allows us to tabulate absolute entropies. Finally, we will define the standard state, the common reference for all thermodynamic tables, and we will use it to look at our first chemical reaction.
The Second Law can be used to infer the spontaneity of a process, as long as the entropy of the universe is considered. To do so, we need to remind ourselves that the universe can be divided into a system and its surroundings (environment). When we calculate the entropy of the universe as an indicator of the spontaneity of a process, we need to always consider changes in entropy in both the system (sys) and its surroundings (surr):
\[
\Delta S^{\mathrm{universe}} = \Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}} + \Delta S^{\mathrm{surr}},
\tag{6.1}\]
or, in differential form:
\[
d S^{\mathrm{universe}} = d S^{\mathrm{sys}} + d S^{\mathrm{surr}}.
\tag{6.2}\]
In general \(\Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}}\) can be calculated from its definition, definition 5.1, integrated along a reversible path, eq. 5.8. In practice, it is always convenient to keep in mind that entropy is a state function, and as such it does not depend on the path. For this reason, we can break every transformation into elementary steps, and calculate the entropy on any path that goes from the initial state to the final state, such as, for example:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_i, T_i & \quad \xrightarrow{ \Delta_{\text{TOT}} S^{\text{sys}} } \quad P_f, T_f \\
  \scriptstyle{\Delta_1 S^{\text{sys}}} & \searrow \qquad  \qquad \nearrow \; \scriptstyle{\Delta_2 S^{\text{sys}}} \\
& \qquad P_i, T_f \\
\\
\Delta_{\text{TOT}} S^{\text{sys}} & = \Delta_1 S^{\text{sys}} + \Delta_2 S^{\text{sys}},
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.3}\]
with \(\Delta_1 S^{\text{sys}}\) calculated at constant \(P\), and \(\Delta_2 S^{\text{sys}}\) at constant \(T\). The most important elementary steps from which we can calculate the entropy resemble the prototypical processes for which we calculated the energy in section 3.1.

6  Calculation of Entropy and the Third Law of Thermodynamics

title: 6  Calculation of Entropy and the Third Law of Thermodynamics
text:
6.1.1 Entropy in Isothermal Processes

For an ideal gas at constant temperature \(\Delta U =0\), and \(Q_{\mathrm{REV}} = -W_{\mathrm{REV}}\). Using the formula for \(W_{\mathrm{REV}}\) in eq. 2.19 (or its analogue for \(P\)), we obtain: \[
\Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}} = \int_i^f \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T} = \frac{-W_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T} = \frac{nRT \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i}}{T} = nR \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i},
\tag{6.4}\] or, similarly: \[
\Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}} = nR \ln \frac{P_i}{P_f}.
\tag{6.5}\]
A phase change is a particular case of an isothermal process that does not follow the formulas introduced above since an ideal gas never liquefies. The entropy associated with a phase change at constant pressure can be calculated from its definition, remembering that \(Q_{\mathrm{REV}}= \Delta H\). For example for vaporizations:

\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{vap}} S = \frac{\Delta_{\mathrm{vap}}H}{T_B},
\tag{6.6}\]
with \(\Delta_{\mathrm{vap}}H\) being the enthalpy of vaporization of a substance, and \(T_B\) its boiling temperature.
It is experimentally observed that the entropies of vaporization of many liquids have almost the same value of:
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{vap}} S \approx 10.5 R,
\tag{6.7}\]
which corresponds in SI to the range of about 85–88 J/(mol K). This simple rule is named Trouton’s rule, after the Irish physicist who discovered it, Frederick Thomas Trouton (1863–1922).

Example 6.1 (Entropy of vaporization of water) Calculate the standard entropy of vaporization of water knowing \(\Delta_{\mathrm{vap}} H_{\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}}^\standardstate = 44 \  \text{kJ/mol}\).1
Solution: Using eq. 6.6—and knowing that at standard conditions of \(P^\standardstate = 1 \  \text{bar}\) the boiling temperature of water is 373 K—we calculate:
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{vap}} S_{\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}}^\standardstate = \frac{44 \times 10^3 \text{J/mol}}{373 \ \text{K}} = 118 \  \text{J} \, \text{mol}^{-1} \, \text{K}^{-1}.
\tag{6.8}\]
The entropy of vaporization of water is far from Trouton’s rule range of 85–88 J/(mol K) because of the hydrogen bond interactions between its molecules. Other similar exceptions are ethanol, formic acid, and hydrogen fluoride.



6.1.2 Entropy in Adiabatic Processes
Since adiabatic processes happen without the exchange of heat, \(đQ=0\), it would be tempting to think that \(\Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}} = 0\) for every one of them. A transformation at constant entropy (isentropic) is always, in fact, a reversible adiabatic process. However, the opposite case is not always true, and an irreversible adiabatic transformation is usually associated with a change in entropy. To explain this fact, we need to recall that the definition of entropy includes the heat exchanged at reversible conditions only. Therefore, for irreversible adiabatic processes \(\Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}} \neq 0\). The calculation of the entropy change for an irreversible adiabatic transformation requires a substantial effort, and we will not cover it at this stage. The situation for adiabatic processes can be summarized as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{reversible:} \qquad & \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T} = 0 \longrightarrow \Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}} = 0 \quad \text{(isentropic),}\\
\text{irreversible:} \qquad & \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{IRR}}}{T}  = 0 \longrightarrow \Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}} \neq 0. \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.9}\]


6.1.3 Entropy in Isochoric Processes
We can calculate the heat exchanged in a process that happens at constant volume, \(Q_V\), using eq. 2.2. Since the heat exchanged at those conditions equals the energy (eq. 3.7), and the energy is a state function, we can use \(Q_V\) regardless of the path (reversible or irreversible). The entropy associated with the process will then be:
\[
\Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}} = \int_i^f \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T} = \int_i^f nC_V \frac{dT}{T},
\tag{6.10}\]
which, assuming \(C_V\) independent of temperature and solving the integral on the right-hand side, becomes:
\[
\Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}} \approx n C_V \ln \frac{T_f}{T_i}.
\tag{6.11}\]


6.1.4 Entropy in Isobaric Processes
Similarly to the constant volume case, we can calculate the heat exchanged in a process that happens at constant pressure, \(Q_P\), using eq. 2.4. Again, similarly to the previous case, \(Q_P\) equals a state function (the enthalpy), and we can use it regardless of the path to calculate the entropy as:
\[
\Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}} = \int_i^f \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T} = \int_i^f nC_P \frac{dT}{T},
\tag{6.12}\]
which, assuming \(C_P\) independent of temperature and solving the integral on the right-hand side, becomes:
\[
\Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}} \approx n C_P \ln \frac{T_f}{T_i}.
\tag{6.13}\]

title: 6  Calculation of Entropy and the Third Law of Thermodynamics
text:
6.2 Calculation of \(\Delta S^{\mathrm{surr}}\)
While the entropy of the system can be broken down into simple cases and calculated using the formulas introduced above, the entropy of the surroundings does not require such a complicated treatment, and it can always be calculated as:
\[
\Delta S^{\mathrm{surr}} = \frac{Q_{\text{surr}}}{T_{\text{surr}}}=\frac{-Q_{\text{sys}}}{T_{\text{surr}}},
\tag{6.14}\]
or, in differential form:
\[
d S^{\mathrm{surr}} = \frac{đQ_{\text{surr}}}{T_{\text{surr}}}=\frac{-đQ_{\text{sys}}}{T_{\text{surr}}},
\tag{6.15}\]
where the substitution \(Q_{\text{surr}}=-Q_{\text{sys}}\) can be performed regardless of whether the transformation is reversible or not. In other words, the surroundings always absorb heat reversibly. To justify this statement, we need to restrict the analysis of the interaction between the system and the surroundings to just the vicinity of the system itself. Outside of a generally restricted region, the rest of the universe is so vast that it remains untouched by anything happening inside the system.2 To facilitate our comprehension, we might consider a system composed of a beaker on a workbench. We can then consider the room that the beaker is in as the immediate surroundings. To all effects, the beaker+room combination behaves as a system isolated from the rest of the universe. The room is obviously much larger than the beaker itself, and therefore every energy production that happens in the system will have minimal effect on the parameters of the room. For example, an exothermic chemical reaction occurring in the beaker will not affect the overall temperature of the room substantially. When we study our reaction, \(T_{\text{surr}}\) will be constant, and the transfer of heat from the reaction to the surroundings will happen at reversible conditions.

Example 6.2 (Freezing of supercooled water) Calculate the changes in entropy of the universe for the process of 1 mol of supercooled water, freezing at –10°C, knowing the following data: \(\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}H = 6 \; \text{kJ/mol}\), \(C_P^{\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)}}=76 \; \text{J} \, \text{mol}^{-1} \, \text{K}^{-1}\), \(C_P^{\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(s)}}=38 \; \text{J} \, \text{mol}^{-1} \, \text{K}^{-1}\), and assuming both \(C_P\) to be independent of temperature.
Solution: \(\Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}}\) for the process under consideration can be calculated using the following cycle:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)} & \quad \xrightarrow{\quad \Delta S_{\text{sys}} \quad} \quad \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(s)} \qquad \quad T=263\;\text{K}\\
\scriptstyle{\Delta S_1} \; \bigg\downarrow \quad & \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \scriptstyle{\bigg\uparrow  \; \Delta S_3} \\
\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)} & \quad \xrightarrow{\quad \Delta S_2 \qquad} \quad \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(s)} \qquad \; T=273\;\text{K}\\
\\
\Delta S^{\text{sys}} & = \Delta S_1 + \Delta S_2 + \Delta S_3
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.16}\]
\(\Delta S_1\) and \(\Delta S_3\) are the isobaric heating and cooling processes of liquid and solid water, respectively, and can be calculated by filling the given data into eq. 6.12. \(\Delta S_2\) is a phase change (isothermal process) and can be calculated translating eq. 6.6 to the freezing transformation. Overall:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta S^{\text{sys}} & = \int_{263}^{273} \frac{C_P^{\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)}}}{T}dT+\frac{-\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}H}{273}+\int_{273}^{263} \frac{C_P^{\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(s)}}}{T}dT \\
& = 76 \ln \frac{273}{263} - \frac{6 \times 10^3}{273} + 38 \ln \frac{263}{273}= -20.6 \; \text{J/K}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.17}\]
Don’t be confused by the fact that \(\Delta S^{\text{sys}}\) is negative. This is not the entropy of the universe! Hence it tells nothing about spontaneity! We can now calculate \(\Delta S^{\text{surr}}\) from \(Q_{\text{sys}}\), noting that we can calculate the enthalpy around the same cycle in eq. 6.16. To do that, we already have \(\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}H\) from the given data, and we can calculate \(\Delta H_1\) and \(\Delta H_3\) using eq. 2.4.
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q^{\text{sys}} & = \Delta H = \int_{263}^{273} C_P^{\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)}} dT + (-\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}H) + \int_{273}^{263} C_P^{\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(s)}}dT \\
& = 76 \times 10^{-3} (273-263) - 6 + 38  \times 10^{-3} (263-273) \\ &= -5.6 \; \text{kJ}. \\
\\
\Delta S^{\text{surr}} & = \frac{-Q_{\text{sys}}}{T}=\frac{5.6 \times 10^3}{263} = + 21.3 \; \text{J/K}. \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.18}\]
Bringing eq. 6.16 and eq. 6.18 results together, we obtain:
\[
\Delta S^{\text{universe}}=\Delta S^{\text{sys}} + \Delta S^{\text{surr}} =  -20.6+21.3=+0.7 \; \text{J/K}.
\tag{6.19}\]
Since the entropy changes in the universe are positive, the process is spontaneous, as expected.

title: 6  Calculation of Entropy and the Third Law of Thermodynamics
text:
6.3 Clausius Theorem
By replacing eq. 6.15 into eq. 6.2 we can write the differential change in the entropy of the system as:
\[
d S^{\mathrm{sys}} = d S^{\mathrm{universe}} - d S^{\mathrm{surr}} = d S^{\mathrm{universe}} + \frac{đQ_{\text{sys}}}{T}.
\tag{6.20}\]
According to the second law, for any spontaneous process \(d S^{\mathrm{universe}}\geq0\), and therefore, replacing it into eq. 6.20:
\[
d S^{\mathrm{sys}} \geq \frac{đQ_{\text{sys}}}{T},
\tag{6.21}\]
which is the mathematical expression of the so-called Clausius theorem. Eq. 6.21 distinguishes between three conditions:
\[
\begin{aligned}
d S^{\mathrm{sys}} > \frac{đQ_{\text{sys}}}{T} \qquad &\text{spontaneous, irreversible transformation} \\
d S^{\mathrm{sys}} = \frac{đQ_{\text{sys}}}{T} \qquad &\text{reversible transformation} \\
d S^{\mathrm{sys}} < \frac{đQ_{\text{sys}}}{T} \qquad &\text{non-spontaneous, irreversible transformation}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.22}\]
Clausius theorem provides a useful criterion to infer the spontaneity of a process, especially in cases where it’s hard to calculate \(\Delta S^{\mathrm{universe}}\). Eq. 6.21 requires knowledge of quantities that are dependent on the system exclusively, such as the difference in entropy, the amount of heat that crosses the boundaries, and the temperature at which the process happens.3 If a process produces more entropy than the amount of heat that crosses the boundaries divided by the absolute temperature, it will be spontaneous. Vice versa, if the entropy produced is smaller than the amount of heat crossing the boundaries divided by the absolute temperature, the process will be non-spontaneous. The equality holds for systems in equilibrium with their surroundings, or for reversible processes since they happen through a series of equilibrium states. Measuring or calculating these quantities might not always be the simplest of calculations. We will return to the Clausius theorem in chapter 8, when we seek more convenient indicators of spontaneity.
