title: 6  Calculation of Entropy and the Third Law of Thermodynamics
text:
6.4 The Third Law of Thermodynamics
So far, we have calculated only changes of the entropy, \(\Delta S\), in the same way that we calculated only changes of the internal energy and of the enthalpy in chapter 3. Thermodynamics, in general, gives us only differences, and we never need, nor know, the absolute value of the energy of a system. For the entropy, however, nature gives us a zero that is not arbitrary at all, thanks to the third law of thermodynamics.
The third law has an interesting history. At the beginning of the twentieth century, Walther Hermann Nernst (1864–1941) was measuring \(\Delta G\) and \(\Delta H\) of reactions between solids at lower and lower temperatures.4 He noticed that the two quantities became closer and closer as the temperature decreased, and that their curves approached each other with the same slope. Since \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\), this meant that \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}S \rightarrow 0\) as \(T \rightarrow 0\). In 1906, he proposed that this is always true, and the statement became known as Nernst’s heat theorem: the entropy change of any reaction between pure crystalline solids goes to zero at absolute zero. If all reactions have \(\Delta S = 0\) at \(T=0\), then all substances must have the same entropy at \(T=0\), and we can choose this common value as the zero of the scale. A few years later, Max Planck (1858–1947) made this choice explicit, and the statement took the form that we use today:

Definition 6.1 Third Law of Thermodynamics: The entropy of a perfectly ordered, pure, crystalline substance is zero at \(T=0 \; \text{K}\).

Why zero, and why only for a perfect crystal? The Boltzmann equation, eq. 5.16, gives us the answer. In a perfect crystal at absolute zero, every atom is at its place in the lattice, and the crystal is in its lowest energy state. There is only one way to arrange it, so \(\Omega=1\) and \(S = k_B \ln 1 = 0\).
If a crystal can freeze in more than one arrangement with the same energy, it keeps some entropy even at \(0\;\text{K}\), which is called residual entropy. A classic example is carbon monoxide. The \(\mathrm{CO}\) molecule is almost symmetric, so in the crystal each molecule can point either way, \(\mathrm{CO}\) or \(\mathrm{OC}\), with almost the same energy. If each of the \(N_A\) molecules in one mole has 2 orientations, \(\Omega = 2^{N_A}\), and:
\[
S_{\text{residual}} = k_B \ln 2^{N_A} = N_A k_B \ln 2 = R\ln 2 = 5.76\;\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol K}},
\tag{6.23}\]
which is close to the residual entropy measured for solid carbon monoxide. Ice has a residual entropy too, because the hydrogen atoms in the crystal can be arranged in many equivalent ways. This is why the definition specifies a perfectly ordered crystal: the residual entropy could be removed, at least in principle, by forcing the substance into a single perfect arrangement, a procedure that in practice can be extremely difficult.
The third law sets an unambiguous zero of the entropy scale, similar to what happens with absolute zero in the temperature scale (chapter 2 and chapter 4). The absolute value of the entropy of every substance can then be calculated in reference to this zero, and absolute entropies are always positive. This is in stark contrast to the internal energy and the enthalpy, for which we cannot measure absolute values, and we must always resort to differences.
How are absolute entropies measured? Putting together the third law with the entropy changes that we calculated in section 6.1, we can follow the absolute entropy of a substance from \(0\;\text{K}\) up to any temperature, as in figure 6.1 for water. The entropy starts from zero, increases smoothly while the substance is heated, as \(\int \frac{C_P}{T}dT\), and jumps up at each phase transition, by \(\frac{\Delta H}{T}\). The jump at boiling is by far the largest, since the gas has much more room for its molecules than the liquid. In the lab, the absolute entropy is obtained exactly this way, by measuring the heat capacity from temperatures as low as possible, together with the enthalpies of the phase transitions.






Figure 6.1: Absolute Entropy of Water at 1 bar as a Function of Temperature, Computed from Approximate Heat Capacities of Ice, Liquid Water, and Vapor, and from the Enthalpies of Fusion and Vaporization.



The third law has two important consequences at low temperatures:

Heat capacities vanish at absolute zero. The entropy at temperature \(T\) is \(S(T) = \int_0^T \frac{C_P}{T}\,dT\) (plus the jumps at the phase transitions). For this integral to give a finite value, \(C_P\) must go to zero as \(T \rightarrow 0\); otherwise, the \(\frac{1}{T}\) in the integrand would make it infinite. Experiments confirm this: the heat capacity of crystals drops to zero at low temperatures, typically as \(T^3\), as you can see from the way the curve of ice starts in figure 6.1.5 This is very different from the ideal gas, whose \(C_V = \frac{3}{2}R\) does not depend on temperature. The ideal gas, however, is not a good model near absolute zero, where every substance is a solid.
Absolute zero cannot be reached. This consequence, also due to Nernst, is often called the unattainability principle. Let’s see why it follows from the third law.

How do we cool something to very low temperatures? Many cooling methods work by alternating two steps, as in figure 6.2. First, at constant temperature, we change a parameter \(X\) that affects the entropy of the substance, such as the pressure of a gas or the magnetic field applied to a magnetic salt, and we let the heat flow out into a cold reservoir. This lowers the entropy of the substance from the blue curve to the red curve. Then, we isolate the substance and change the parameter back adiabatically, so that the entropy stays constant. To keep the same entropy on the blue curve, the substance must move to a lower temperature. Repeating the two steps, we go down a staircase toward absolute zero.






Figure 6.2: Cooling by Alternating Isothermal and Adiabatic Steps Between Two Values of a Parameter \(X\) (Schematic). Since the Third Law Requires Both Entropy Curves to Reach \(S=0\) at \(T=0\), Each Step Is Smaller than the Previous One, and Absolute Zero Is Approached but Never Reached.



Here is where the third law comes in. Since both curves must reach \(S=0\) at \(T=0\), they get closer and closer to each other as the temperature decreases. Each isothermal step lowers the entropy by less, and each adiabatic step lowers the temperature by less. The staircase gets finer and finer, and it would take an infinite number of steps to reach \(T=0\). If the two curves ended at different entropies at \(T=0\), a single adiabatic step from the lower curve could bring the substance all the way to absolute zero. The third law forbids this.
This is a true limit of nature, not of our technology. Physicists have cooled small samples to below a billionth of a kelvin, but never to absolute zero, and the third law tells us that they never will. Notice the parallel with the second law: the second law says that no engine can convert all its heat into work, and the third law says that no refrigerator can extract all the heat from a system.

section: 6.5 Standard States and a First Chemical Reaction
text:
6.5 Standard States and a First Chemical Reaction
Since we can measure the absolute entropy of every substance, we can collect the values in tables and use them for any process that we like. To make such tables useful, however, everybody must agree on the conditions at which the values are reported. The entropy of a substance depends on its temperature, as in figure 6.1, and, for a gas, it also depends strongly on the pressure, as we saw in eq. 6.5. For this reason, thermodynamic tables report the properties of each substance in a common reference state, called the standard state:

Definition 6.2 Standard State: The standard state of a substance is its pure form at the standard pressure, \(P^{\standardstate} = 1\;\text{bar}\). For a gas, it is the pure gas, behaving ideally, at \(P^{\standardstate}\). For a liquid or a solid, it is the pure liquid or the pure solid at \(P^{\standardstate}\).

Quantities that refer to the standard state are marked with the symbol \(^\standardstate\), as in \(S^\standardstate\). The standard pressure is \(P^{\standardstate} = 100\;\text{kPa} = 1\;\text{bar}\).6 Notice that the definition does not include a temperature. A standard state can be defined at any temperature, but most tables report their values at room temperature, \(T = 298.15\;\text{K}\), which we will often round to \(298\;\text{K}\). Do not confuse the standard state with the “standard temperature and pressure” (STP, \(0\;°\text{C}\) and \(1\;\text{atm}\)) that you might have used for gases in general chemistry. For example, the standard molar entropy of liquid water at \(298\;\text{K}\) is \(S^\standardstate_{\mathrm{H_2O}_{(l)}} = 70.0\;\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol K}}\), close to the value that we can read on the curve in figure 6.1 at that temperature. A comprehensive list of standard entropies of inorganic and organic compounds is reported in Appendix A.
We now have everything that we need to look at our first chemical reaction. A chemical reaction transforms some substances, the reactants, into other substances, the products. We can write a general reaction as:
\[ a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B} \rightarrow c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D},  \tag{6.24}\]
where \(a,b,c,d\) are the stoichiometric coefficients of species \(\mathrm{A,B,C,D}\). The change of a state function during a reaction is the value for the products minus the value for the reactants, each multiplied by its stoichiometric coefficient. To write this in a compact form, we give a sign to each coefficient, and we call the result the stoichiometric number, \(\nu_i\):

Definition 6.3 Signs of the stoichiometric numbers:

\(\nu_i\) is positive if \(i\) is a product.
\(\nu_i\) is negative if \(i\) is a reactant.


For the general reaction in eq. 6.24, \(\nu_{\mathrm{A}}=-a\), \(\nu_{\mathrm{B}}=-b\), \(\nu_{\mathrm{C}}=+c\), and \(\nu_{\mathrm{D}}=+d\). With this convention, the standard entropy of a reaction is calculated from the tabulated standard entropies as:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} S^\standardstate = \sum_i \nu_i S_i^\standardstate = \underbrace{\left( cS^\standardstate_{\mathrm{C}}+dS^\standardstate_{\mathrm{D}} \right) }_{\text{products}} - \underbrace{\left( aS^\standardstate_{\mathrm{A}}+bS^\standardstate_{\mathrm{B}}\right)}_{\text{reactants}},
\tag{6.25}\]
where the sum runs over all reactants and products.

Example 6.3 (Entropy of the synthesis of ammonia) Calculate the standard entropy of reaction at \(298\;\text{K}\) for the synthesis of ammonia:
\[
\mathrm{N}_{2(g)} + 3\mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH}_{3(g)},
\]
knowing the following standard entropies: \(S^\standardstate_{\mathrm{N}_{2(g)}} = 191.6\;\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol K}}\), \(S^\standardstate_{\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}} = 130.7\;\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol K}}\), and \(S^\standardstate_{\mathrm{NH}_{3(g)}} = 192.8\;\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol K}}\).
Solution: The stoichiometric numbers are \(\nu_{\mathrm{N}_2}=-1\), \(\nu_{\mathrm{H}_2}=-3\), and \(\nu_{\mathrm{NH}_3}=+2\). Using eq. 6.25:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} S^\standardstate &= 2\,S^\standardstate_{\mathrm{NH}_{3(g)}} - S^\standardstate_{\mathrm{N}_{2(g)}} - 3\,S^\standardstate_{\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}} \\
&= 2(192.8) - 191.6 - 3(130.7) = -198.1\;\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol K}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The entropy of the system decreases. This makes sense, since four molecules of gas become two, and fewer molecules have fewer ways to arrange themselves in the same volume.

Does this negative result mean that nitrogen and hydrogen cannot form ammonia? Not at all. As we learned in section 6.2, and as we saw for supercooled water in example 6.2, the entropy of the system alone tells us nothing about spontaneity: we must also account for the surroundings. When the reaction happens at constant temperature and pressure, it exchanges heat with its surroundings, and their entropy changes by \(\Delta S^{\text{surr}} = -Q_{\text{sys}}/T\). To decide whether ammonia forms, we need to know how much heat the reaction releases or absorbs. Calculating the heat of chemical reactions is the job of thermochemistry, the topic of the next chapter, where we will finally apply the laws of thermodynamics to chemistry. And even then, thermodynamics will tell us only which way the reaction goes, not how fast. These are two separate questions, and we will need both to understand chemistry.

title: 6  Calculation of Entropy and the Third Law of Thermodynamics
text:
6.6 Chapter Review

6.6.1 Key Ideas

Spontaneity requires the entropy of the whole universe: \(\Delta S^{\mathrm{universe}} = \Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}} + \Delta S^{\mathrm{surr}}\).
System: \(\Delta S^{\mathrm{sys}} = nR\ln\frac{V_f}{V_i}\) (isothermal ideal gas), \(0\) (reversible adiabatic), \(nC_P\ln\frac{T_f}{T_i}\) (isobaric heating), and \(\frac{\Delta H}{T}\) (phase change at the transition temperature).
Surroundings: \(\Delta S^{\mathrm{surr}} = -\frac{Q_{\text{sys}}}{T_{\text{surr}}}\), since the surroundings behave as a large reservoir.
Trouton’s rule: many liquids have \(\Delta_{\text{vap}}S \approx 85\text{–}88\;\text{J/(mol K)}\); liquids with hydrogen bonds, such as water, have more.
A process can be spontaneous even if the entropy of the system decreases, as long as the surroundings gain more entropy (as when supercooled water freezes).
The third law: the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at \(0\;\text{K}\) (Nernst and Planck), since a perfect crystal has a single microstate. It allows us to tabulate absolute entropies, \(S^\standardstate\); crystals that freeze in many arrangements keep a residual entropy.
Consequences: heat capacities vanish as \(T \rightarrow 0\), and absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps.
Standard state: the pure substance at \(P^\standardstate = 1\;\text{bar}\) (an ideal gas, for gases), at any temperature, usually \(298.15\;\text{K}\). Thermodynamic tables report standard values, marked with \(^\standardstate\).
Reaction entropies: \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}S^\standardstate = \sum_i \nu_i S_i^\standardstate\), with stoichiometric numbers \(\nu_i\) positive for products and negative for reactants. A negative \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}S^\standardstate\), as for the synthesis of ammonia, does not mean that a reaction cannot happen: we also need the entropy of the surroundings.



6.6.2 Study Questions
1. How is the entropy change of the universe calculated?

\(\Delta S^{\text{universe}} = \Delta S^{\text{sys}} + \Delta S^{\text{surr}}\).
\(\Delta S^{\text{universe}} = \Delta S^{\text{sys}} - \Delta S^{\text{surr}}\).
\(\Delta S^{\text{universe}} = \Delta S^{\text{sys}}\).
\(\Delta S^{\text{universe}} = \Delta S^{\text{sys}} \cdot \Delta S^{\text{surr}}\).
\(\Delta S^{\text{universe}} = 0\) always.


2. What is the entropy change of an ideal gas in an isothermal expansion?

\(\Delta S = 0\).
\(\Delta S = nC_V \ln\frac{T_f}{T_i}\).
\(\Delta S = nR \ln\frac{V_f}{V_i}\).
\(\Delta S = nR(V_f-V_i)\).
\(\Delta S = \frac{W}{T}\).


3. How is the entropy of vaporization of a liquid calculated at its boiling point?

\(\Delta_{\text{vap}}S = \Delta_{\text{vap}}H \cdot T_B\).
\(\Delta_{\text{vap}}S = nR\ln T_B\).
\(\Delta_{\text{vap}}S = 0\).
\(\Delta_{\text{vap}}S = \Delta_{\text{vap}}H - T_B\).
\(\Delta_{\text{vap}}S = \frac{\Delta_{\text{vap}}H}{T_B}\).


4. Why does water deviate from Trouton’s rule?

Because it boils at 100 °C.
Because of the hydrogen bonds between its molecules.
Because its molar mass is small.
Because it is an ideal liquid.
Because its enthalpy of vaporization is negative.


5. What is the entropy change of the system in a reversible adiabatic process?

Always positive.
Always negative.
Equal to \(\frac{Q}{T}\) with \(Q>0\).
Zero, since the process is isentropic.
Infinite.


6. What is the standard state of a gas?

The pure gas, behaving ideally, at \(P^\standardstate = 1\;\text{bar}\), at any temperature.
The gas at \(0\;°\text{C}\) and \(1\;\text{atm}\).
The gas at \(0\;\text{K}\), where its entropy is zero.
The gas mixed with air at \(1\;\text{bar}\) and \(298.15\;\text{K}\).
The gas at the pressure where it liquefies.


7. How is the entropy change of the surroundings calculated?

\(\Delta S^{\text{surr}} = \frac{Q_{\text{sys}}}{T_{\text{sys}}}\).
\(\Delta S^{\text{surr}} = -\Delta S^{\text{sys}}\).
\(\Delta S^{\text{surr}} = \frac{-Q_{\text{sys}}}{T_{\text{surr}}}\).
\(\Delta S^{\text{surr}} = 0\).
\(\Delta S^{\text{surr}} = nR\ln\frac{V_f}{V_i}\).


8. Supercooled water freezes spontaneously at –10 °C, even though the entropy of the water decreases. How is this possible?

The entropy of the universe decreases, which is allowed for freezing.
The second law does not apply to phase changes.
The process is reversible.
The entropy of the water actually increases.
The heat released to the surroundings increases their entropy by more than the water loses.


9. What does the Clausius theorem state?

\(dS^{\text{sys}} = \frac{đQ}{T}\) always.
\(dS^{\text{sys}} \geq \frac{đQ}{T}\), with the equality for reversible processes.
\(dS^{\text{sys}} \leq \frac{đQ}{T}\) for spontaneous processes.
\(dS^{\text{sys}} = 0\) for all processes.
\(dS^{\text{universe}} < 0\) for spontaneous processes.


10. What does the third law of thermodynamics make possible for the entropy that is not possible for the enthalpy?

Calculating changes at constant pressure.
Measuring it with a calorimeter.
Using it for chemical reactions.
Tabulating absolute values, since it fixes the zero of the entropy scale.
Making it independent of temperature.








TipAnswers





1.a, 2.c, 3.e, 4.b, 5.d, 6.a, 7.c, 8.e, 9.b, 10.d

title: 7  Thermochemistry
text:
7.1 Reaction Enthalpies
With this chapter, we begin the second part of the book, where we apply the laws of thermodynamics to chemistry. So far, we have studied changes in energy and entropy in the absence of chemical reactions, with one exception: at the end of chapter 6, we found that the synthesis of ammonia decreases the entropy of the system (example 6.3), and we left open the question of whether the reaction happens at all. To answer it, we need to know the heat that the reaction exchanges with its surroundings. When a chemical reaction takes place, some bonds break and some new ones form. Breaking a bond always requires energy, while forming a bond always releases energy. The balance between the energy spent to break the bonds of the reactants and the energy released when the bonds of the products form determines whether the reaction, overall, absorbs or releases energy.1 For a proper thermodynamic treatment of the system, this extra energy must be included in the net balance. In this chapter, we will learn how to calculate it from tabulated data, and we will then use it to answer our question about ammonia.
Since most chemical reactions happen at constant atmospheric pressure (isobaric conditions) in the lab, we can use eq. 3.13 to replace the inexact differential of the heat with the exact differential of the state function called enthalpy. The advantage of this transformation is that it allows us to study the heat associated with chemical reactions at constant pressure independently of their path. Using the same notation that we introduced for reaction entropies in section 6.5, the heat associated with the reaction (rxn) is defined as:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H = H_{\text{products}}-H_{\text{reactants}} \; .
\tag{7.1}\]
For example, if we take a simple reaction of the form:
\[ \mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{D}, \]
the heat at constant pressure is equal to the enthalpy of reaction, which is calculated as:
\[
Q_P = \Delta_{\text{rxn}} H = \underbrace{ \left (H_{\mathrm{C}}+H_{\mathrm{D}} \right) }_{\text{products}} - \underbrace{\left( H_{\mathrm{A}}+H_{\mathrm{B}}\right)}_{\text{reactants}}.
\tag{7.2}\]
Using the chemistry sign convention, Definition 1.1, reactions are classified in terms of the sign of their reaction enthalpies as follows:
If we expand the sample reaction to account for its stoichiometry, as in the general reaction of eq. 6.24, eq. 7.2 can be rewritten as:
\[
Q_P = \Delta_{\text{rxn}} H = \underbrace{\left( cH_{\mathrm{C}}+dH_{\mathrm{D}} \right) }_{\text{products}} - \underbrace{ \left( aH_{\mathrm{A}}+bH_{\mathrm{B}} \right)}_{\text{reactants}},
\tag{7.3}\]
while for the most general case we can write it:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H = \sum_i \nu_i H_i,
\tag{7.4}\]
where \(\nu_i\) is the stoichiometric number of species \(i\), positive for products and negative for reactants, as in definition 6.3. Eq. 7.4 has exactly the same form as the one that we used for reaction entropies, eq. 6.25.
crumbs: The Live Textbook of Physical Chemistry 1

title: 7  Thermochemistry
text:
Definition 7.1 \(\;\)

\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H > 0 \Rightarrow\) Endothermic reaction (heat is gained by the system).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H < 0 \Rightarrow\) Exothermic reaction (heat is lost by the system).
crumbs: The Live Textbook of Physical Chemistry 1

title: 7  Thermochemistry
text:
7.2 Calorimetry
Reaction enthalpies are measured with a calorimeter, an insulated container in which the reaction takes place. Since the calorimeter does not exchange heat with the rest of the lab, the heat released or absorbed by the reaction stays inside it and changes its temperature. If the calorimeter (including everything inside it) has a total heat capacity \(C_{\text{cal}}\), a temperature change \(\Delta T\) corresponds to the heat of reaction:
\[
Q_{\text{rxn}} = -C_{\text{cal}}\,\Delta T,
\tag{7.5}\]
where the negative sign follows the chemistry sign convention: an exothermic reaction (\(Q_{\text{rxn}}<0\)) warms the calorimeter (\(\Delta T>0\)). The heat capacity of the calorimeter is determined beforehand by calibration, either with an electrical heater that supplies a known amount of energy, or with a reaction whose heat is accurately known, such as the combustion of benzoic acid.
There are two main kinds of calorimeters, and they measure two different state functions:

Constant-pressure calorimeters are open to the atmosphere. The simplest example is the “coffee-cup” calorimeter of general chemistry labs, used for reactions in solution. At constant pressure, eq. 3.13 tells us that the heat equals the enthalpy change, \(Q_P = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}H\).
Constant-volume (bomb) calorimeters are sealed steel containers, called bombs, immersed in a water bath. They are used for combustions, where the sample burns in an excess of oxygen under pressure. At constant volume, no work is done, and the heat equals the energy change, \(Q_V = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}U\), as in eq. 3.7.

Since tables report enthalpies, the energies measured in bomb calorimeters must be converted. Using the definition of enthalpy, eq. 3.9:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H = \Delta_{\text{rxn}} U + \Delta(PV).
\]
The volumes of liquids and solids are so small that their contribution to \(\Delta(PV)\) is negligible. For the gases, we can use the ideal gas law, \(PV = nRT\), and at constant temperature \(\Delta(PV) = \Delta n_{\text{gas}}RT\), which gives:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H = \Delta_{\text{rxn}} U + \Delta n_{\text{gas}} RT,
\tag{7.6}\]
where \(\Delta n_{\text{gas}}\) is the number of moles of gaseous products minus the number of moles of gaseous reactants, per mole of reaction. If the number of moles of gas does not change, or if no gases are involved, \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H \approx \Delta_{\text{rxn}} U\).

Example 7.1 (Combustion of methane in a bomb calorimeter) A sample of \(0.0200\;\text{mol}\) of methane is burned in a bomb calorimeter with \(C_{\text{cal}} = 10.00\;\text{kJ/K}\), and the temperature of the calorimeter increases by \(1.772\;\text{K}\). Calculate \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}U\) and \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H\) at \(298\;\text{K}\) for the reaction:
\[
\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)} + 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)} + 2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)}.
\]
Solution: Using eq. 7.5, the heat released by the sample is:
\[
Q_V = -C_{\text{cal}}\,\Delta T = -10.00 \times 1.772 = -17.72\;\text{kJ}.
\]
Since the bomb has a constant volume, this heat is the energy change of the reaction, and per mole of methane:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} U = \frac{Q_V}{n} = \frac{-17.72\;\text{kJ}}{0.0200\;\text{mol}} = -886\;\text{kJ/mol}.
\]
In the reaction, 3 moles of gas (1 of methane and 2 of oxygen) become 1 mole of gas (carbon dioxide), while water is liquid, so \(\Delta n_{\text{gas}} = 1 - 3 = -2\). Using eq. 7.6:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H = -886 + (-2)(8.314 \times 10^{-3})(298) = -886 - 5 = -891\;\text{kJ/mol}.
\]
The difference between \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H\) and \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}U\) is only about 0.5%. The reaction enthalpy is more negative than the energy because the gas contracts, and at constant pressure the atmosphere does work on the system as it shrinks. We will obtain the same value of \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H\) from tabulated data in example 7.2.

Experiments like this one, repeated for many substances, are the source of the tabulated enthalpies of formation that we introduce next.
crumbs: The Live Textbook of Physical Chemistry 1

title: 7  Thermochemistry
text:
7.3 Standard Enthalpies of Formation
In principle, we could use eq. 7.3 to calculate the reaction enthalpy associated with any reaction. However, to do so, the absolute enthalpies \(H_i\) of reactants and products would be required. Unfortunately, absolute enthalpies are not known—and theoretically unknowable, since this would require an absolute zero for the enthalpy scale, which does not exist. This is the key difference with the entropy, for which the third law provides a natural zero (section 6.4), so that we could use the absolute values \(S_i^\standardstate\) directly in eq. 6.25. For the enthalpy, we must instead choose a zero, and use enthalpies relative to this reference. The reference is defined as the constituent elements in their standard state, and the enthalpies of 1 mol of substance relative to this reference are called standard enthalpies of formation.

Definition 7.2 The standard enthalpy of formation of compound \(i\), \(\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H_i^\standardstate\), is the change of enthalpy during the formation of 1 mol of \(i\) from its constituent elements, with all substances in their standard states.

The standard states are the ones that we defined in definition 6.2, at the standard pressure \(P^{\standardstate} = 1 \; \mathrm{bar}\). As for the entropies, there is no standard temperature, but standard enthalpies of formation are usually reported at room temperature, \(T = 298.15 \; \mathrm{K}\). For the elements, the reference is the form in which each element is most stable at standard pressure (for example, for hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen the reference forms are \(\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}, \mathrm{C}_{(s,\text{graphite})}, \text{and }\mathrm{O}_{2(g)}\), respectively). Since forming an element from itself requires no change at all, the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its reference form is zero.2
For example, the standard enthalpies of formation of some common compounds at \(T = 298.15 \; \mathrm{K}\) are calculated from the following reactions:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \mathrm{C}_{(s,\text{graphite})}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)} \qquad & \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H_{\mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}}^\standardstate = -394 \; \text{kJ/mol} \\
   \mathrm{C}_{(s,\text{graphite})}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{4(g)} \qquad & \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H_{\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)}}^\standardstate = -75 \; \text{kJ/mol} \\
   \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)} \qquad & \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H_{\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)}}^\standardstate = -286 \; \text{kJ/mol}
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.7}\]
A comprehensive list of standard enthalpies of formation of inorganic and organic compounds is also reported in Appendix A.
crumbs: The Live Textbook of Physical Chemistry 1

title: 7  Thermochemistry
text:
7.4 Hess’s Law
The calculation of a standard reaction enthalpy can be performed using the following cycle:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{reactants} & \quad \xrightarrow{\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate} \quad \text{products} \\
\scriptstyle{-\Delta_{\text{f}} H_{\text{reactants}}^\standardstate} \quad \bigg\downarrow \quad & \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \scriptstyle{\bigg\uparrow  \; \Delta_{\text{f}} H_{\text{products}}^\standardstate} \\
\text{"elements in } & \text{their standard reference state"}
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.8}\]
This process is summarized by the simple formula:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate = \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H_{\text{products}}^\standardstate - \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H_{\text{reactants}}^\standardstate.
\tag{7.9}\]
Notice how there is a negative sign in front of the enthalpy of formation of the reactants because they are normally defined for the reactions that go from the elements to the reactants and not vice-versa. To close the cycle in eq. 7.8, however, we should go from the reactants to the elements, and therefore we must invert the sign in front of the formation enthalpies of the reactants. Eq. 7.9 can be generalized using the same technique used to derive eq. 7.4, resulting in:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate = \sum_i \nu_i \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H_i^\standardstate,
\tag{7.10}\]
which is a mathematical expression of the law that is known as Hess’s Law. Hess’s law is valid at constant pressure because, at those conditions, the heat of reaction—a path function—is equal to the enthalpy of reaction—a state function. Therefore, the enthalpy of a reaction depends exclusively on the initial and final state, and it can be obtained via the pathway that passes through the elements in their standard state (the formation pathway).

Example 7.2 (Combustion enthalpy of methane from Hess’s law) Calculate the standard enthalpy of combustion at 298 K of 1 mol of methane, using the data in eq. 7.7.
Solution: The reaction that is under consideration is: \[
\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)} + 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)} + 2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)} \qquad \Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate = ?
\]
Using Hess’s Law, eq. 7.10, the enthalpy of combustion of methane is:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate =  \Delta_{\text{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}} + 2 \Delta_{\text{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{H_2O}_{(l)}} - \Delta_{\text{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)}} - 2 \underbrace{\Delta_{\text{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{O}_{2(g)}}}_{=0}
\]
whose values are reported in eq. 7.7. Notice that the formation enthalpy of \(\mathrm{O}_{2(g)}\) is zero, since it is an element in its standard state. The final result is:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate =  \overbrace{-394}^{\Delta_{\text{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}}} +2 \overbrace{(-286)}^{\Delta_{\text{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{H_2O}_{(l)}}} - \overbrace{(-75)}^{\Delta_{\text{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)}}}  = -891 \; \mathrm{kJ/mol}.
\]
where the negative sign indicates that the reaction is exothermic (see definition 7.1), as we should expect. This is the same value that we obtained from the bomb calorimeter in example 7.1. The cycle that we used to solve this exercise can be summarized as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)} + & 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \quad \xrightarrow{\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate} \quad \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)} + 2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)} \\
  \scriptstyle{-\Delta_{\text{f}} H_{\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)},\mathrm{O}_{2(g)}}^\standardstate} & \searrow \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \nearrow \; \scriptstyle{\Delta_{\text{f}} H_{\text{CO}_{2(g)},\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{(l)}}^\standardstate}\\
  & \qquad \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}, \mathrm{C}_{(s,\text{graphite})}, \mathrm{O}_{2(g)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Notice that at standard pressure and \(T = 298 \; \mathrm{K}\) water is in liquid form. However, when we burn methane, the heat associated with the exothermic reaction immediately vaporizes the water. Substances in different states of matter have different formation enthalpies, and \(\Delta_{\text{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{H_2O}_{(g)}} =  -242 \  \mathrm{kJ/mol}\). The difference between the formation enthalpies of the same substance in different states represents the latent heat that separates them. For example, for water:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_{\text{vap}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{H_2O}} & = \Delta_{\text{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{H_2O}_{(g)}} - \Delta_{\text{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{H_2O}_{(l)}} \\
& = (-242) - (-286) = + 44 \; \text{kJ/mol}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is the latent heat of vaporization for water, \(\Delta_{\text{vap}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{H_2O}}\), the same value that we used in example 6.1. The latent heat is positive to indicate that the system absorbs energy in going from the liquid to the gaseous state (and it will release energy when going the opposite direction from gas to liquid).

The same cycle can be drawn as an enthalpy diagram, figure 7.1, where each species sits at its enthalpy relative to the elements. Since the enthalpy is a state function, the two paths from the reactants to the products, directly or through the elements, must give the same enthalpy change.






Figure 7.1: Enthalpy Diagram of the Hess Cycle for the Combustion of Methane at 298 K, with the Data of eq. 7.7. The Reaction Enthalpy (Purple) Is the Difference Between the Formation Enthalpies of the Products (Red) and of the Reactants (Blue).

title: 7  Thermochemistry
text:
7.5 Bond Enthalpies
When the formation enthalpies of a compound are not available, we can still estimate a reaction enthalpy from the bonds that break and form, as we described at the beginning of this chapter. The bond enthalpy is the enthalpy needed to break 1 mol of a given bond in the gas phase. Since the same bond has slightly different strengths in different molecules, tables report average values, such as those in table 7.1.



Table 7.1: Average Bond Enthalpies.

Breaking a bond always requires energy, and forming a bond always releases it, so:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H \approx \sum_{\text{broken}} \text{(bond enthalpies)} - \sum_{\text{formed}} \text{(bond enthalpies)}.
\tag{7.11}\]
Notice that the order is the opposite of Hess’s law: the bonds of the reactants come first, with a positive sign. For example, in the synthesis of ammonia we break one N≡N bond and three H–H bonds, and we form six N–H bonds:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H \approx \left[945 + 3(436)\right] - 6(391) = 2253 - 2346 = -93\;\text{kJ/mol},
\]
very close to the value of \(-91.8\;\text{kJ/mol}\) obtained from the formation enthalpies. The agreement is not always this good, since bond enthalpies are averages, and eq. 7.11 is valid only when all reactants and products are gases. Formation enthalpies, when available, should always be preferred.

title: 7  Thermochemistry
section: 7.6 Calculations of Enthalpies of Reaction at \(T \neq 298 \; \text{K}\)
text:
7.6 Calculations of Enthalpies of Reaction at \(T \neq 298 \; \text{K}\)
Standard enthalpies of formation are usually reported at room temperature (\(T\) = 298 K), but enthalpies of formation at any temperature \(T'\) can be calculated from the values at 298 K using eq. 2.4 and eq. 3.13:
\[
\begin{aligned}
dH = C_P dT \rightarrow & \int_{H_{298}^\standardstate}^{H_{T'}^\standardstate} dH =  \int_{298}^{T'} C_P dT \\
            & H_{T'}^\standardstate - H_{298}^\standardstate = \int_{298}^{T'} C_P dT \\
            & H_{T'}^\standardstate = H_{298}^\standardstate + \int_{298}^{T'} C_P dT,
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.12}\]
which, in conjunction with Hess’s Law, eq. 7.10, results in:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H_{T'}^\standardstate = \Delta_{\text{rxn}} H_{298}^\standardstate + \int_{298}^{T'} \Delta C_P dT,
\tag{7.13}\]
with \(\Delta C_P = \sum_i \nu_i C_{P,i}\). Eq. 7.13 is known as Kirchhoff’s law, after the German physicist Gustav Robert Kirchhoff (1824–1887).

Example 7.3 (Reaction enthalpy at 398 K) Calculate \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^\standardstate_{398}\) of the following reaction at 398 K, knowing that \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^\standardstate_{298}\) is -283.0 kJ/mol, and the following \(C_P\) values: \(\mathrm{CO}_{(g)}\) = 29 J/(mol K), \(\mathrm{O}_{2(g)}\) = 30 J/(mol K), \(\mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}\) = 38 J/(mol K):
\[
\mathrm{CO}_{(g)}+\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)},
\]
Solution: Using eq. 7.13 we obtain:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate_{398} = \overbrace{-283.0}^{\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^\standardstate_{298}} + \int_{298}^{398} ( \overbrace{38}^{C_P^{\mathrm{CO}_2}} -\overbrace{29}^{C_P^{\mathrm{CO}}} -\frac{1}{2}\overbrace{30}^{C_P^{\mathrm{O}_2}} ) \times 10^{-3} dT,
\]
which, assuming that the heat capacities do not depend on the temperature, becomes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate_{398} &= -283.0 + \left(38-29-\frac{1}{2}30 \right) \times 10^{-3} (398-298) \\ &= -283.6 \; \text{kJ/mol}.
\end{aligned}
\]
As we notice from this result, a difference in temperature of 100 K translates into a change in \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^\standardstate\) of this reaction of only 0.6 kJ/mol. This is a trend that is often observed, and values of \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H\) are very weakly dependent on changes in temperature for most chemical reactions. This numerical result can also be compared with the amount that is experimentally measured for \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^\standardstate_{398}\) of this reaction, which is –283.67 kJ/mol. This comparison strongly supports the assumption that we used to solve the integral in eq. 7.13, confirming that the heat capacities are mostly independent of temperature.

title: 7  Thermochemistry
text:
7.7 Spontaneity of Chemical Reactions
We can now go back to the question that we left open at the end of chapter 6: does the synthesis of ammonia happen? To decide whether a process is spontaneous, we need the entropy of the universe, eq. 6.1. For a reaction at constant temperature and pressure, both of its pieces come from tabulated data:

The entropy of the system is the reaction entropy, which we calculate from the standard entropies with eq. 6.25.
The entropy of the surroundings comes from the heat that the reaction exchanges with them, eq. 6.14. At constant pressure, this heat is the reaction enthalpy, \(Q_{\text{sys}} = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}H\), and therefore:

\[
\Delta S^{\text{surr}} = -\frac{\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H}{T}.
\tag{7.14}\]
An exothermic reaction releases heat and increases the entropy of the surroundings, while an endothermic reaction absorbs heat and decreases it.

Example 7.4 (Is the synthesis of ammonia spontaneous?) Using the result of example 6.3, \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} S^\standardstate = -198.1\;\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol K}}\), and knowing that \(\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{NH}_{3(g)}} = -45.9\;\text{kJ/mol}\), decide whether the synthesis of ammonia at standard conditions and \(298\;\text{K}\) is spontaneous:
\[
\mathrm{N}_{2(g)} + 3\mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH}_{3(g)}.
\]
Solution: Using Hess’s law, eq. 7.10, and remembering that the formation enthalpies of \(\mathrm{N}_{2(g)}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}\) are zero, since they are elements in their reference form:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate = 2 \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{NH}_{3(g)}} - \underbrace{\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{N}_{2(g)}}}_{=0} - 3\underbrace{\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}}}_{=0} = 2(-45.9) = -91.8\;\text{kJ/mol}.
\]
The reaction is exothermic, and the heat that it releases increases the entropy of the surroundings, eq. 7.14:
\[
\Delta S^{\text{surr}} = -\frac{\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate}{T} = -\frac{-91.8 \times 10^3}{298} = +308.1\;\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol K}}.
\]
The entropy of the universe is therefore:
\[
\Delta S^{\text{universe}} = \Delta_{\text{rxn}} S^\standardstate + \Delta S^{\text{surr}} = -198.1 + 308.1 = +110.0\;\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol K}},
\]
and the reaction is spontaneous. Just as for the freezing of supercooled water in example 6.2, the system loses entropy, but the heat that it releases increases the entropy of the surroundings by more.

This result should not make us think that a bottle of nitrogen and hydrogen turns into ammonia on its own. At room temperature, the reaction is so slow that nothing measurable happens, even over years. In industry, ammonia is produced with the Haber–Bosch process, which uses a catalyst and high temperatures to make the reaction fast enough. Thermodynamics tells us which way a reaction goes; how fast it goes is the subject of chemical kinetics, which we will study in chapter 14.
The calculation in example 7.4 works, but it requires two separate pieces, one for the system and one for the surroundings. We can combine them in a single expression by multiplying the entropy of the universe by \(-T\):
\[
-T\Delta S^{\text{universe}} = -T\Delta_{\text{rxn}} S + \Delta_{\text{rxn}} H = \Delta_{\text{rxn}} H - T\Delta_{\text{rxn}} S.
\tag{7.15}\]
Since \(T\) is positive, a reaction is spontaneous (\(\Delta S^{\text{universe}}>0\)) when the right-hand side of eq. 7.15 is negative. For the synthesis of ammonia, it is \(-91.8 - 298 \times (-0.1981) = -32.8\;\text{kJ/mol}\). Notice that the right-hand side contains only properties of the system, and no reference to the surroundings. This combination of enthalpy and entropy is so useful that it deserves its own name. In the next chapter, we will see that it is the change of a new state function, the Gibbs energy, and we will discover the general family of functions to which it belongs, called the thermodynamic potentials.

title: 7  Thermochemistry
text:
7.8 Chapter Review

7.8.1 Key Ideas

Reaction enthalpy is the heat exchanged by a reaction at constant pressure: negative for exothermic reactions, positive for endothermic ones.
Reaction enthalpies are calculated with the same stoichiometric numbers, \(\nu_i\), that we used for reaction entropies: negative for reactants and positive for products.
Calorimetry: \(Q_{\text{rxn}} = -C_{\text{cal}}\Delta T\). A constant-pressure calorimeter measures \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H\), a bomb calorimeter measures \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}U\), and the two are related by \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}U + \Delta n_{\text{gas}}RT\).
Standard enthalpies of formation, \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H^\standardstate\), refer to the standard state at \(P^\standardstate = 1\;\text{bar}\), and they are zero for elements in their most stable form. Unlike entropies, enthalpies have no natural zero, so only these relative values can be tabulated.
Hess’s law: since \(H\) is a state function, \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^\standardstate = \sum_i \nu_i \Delta_{\text{f}}H_i^\standardstate\), whatever the path of the reaction.
Bond enthalpies give quick estimates for gas-phase reactions: bonds broken minus bonds formed.
Other temperatures (Kirchhoff’s law): \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^\standardstate_{T'} = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^\standardstate_{298} + \int_{298}^{T'} \Delta C_P\,dT\), and the correction is usually small.
Spontaneity of a reaction: \(\Delta S^{\text{universe}} = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}S - \frac{\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H}{T}\). A reaction that lowers the entropy of the system, such as the synthesis of ammonia, can still be spontaneous if it releases enough heat. The combination \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H - T\Delta_{\text{rxn}}S = -T\Delta S^{\text{universe}}\) depends only on the system, and it is negative for spontaneous reactions.
Which way, not how fast: thermodynamics tells us whether a reaction is spontaneous, but not how fast it goes.



7.8.2 Study Questions
1. What characterizes an endothermic reaction?

\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H < 0\), and heat is released by the system.
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H = 0\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H > 0\), and heat is gained by the system.
The reaction is always spontaneous.
The reaction happens at constant volume.


2. What is the sign convention for the stoichiometric coefficients \(\nu_i\)?

Positive for products and negative for reactants.
Positive for reactants and negative for products.
Always positive.
Positive for gases and negative for liquids.
Positive for elements and negative for compounds.


3. What is the standard enthalpy of formation of a compound?

The enthalpy of the compound at 0 K.
The enthalpy change when 1 mol of the compound is decomposed into atoms.
The heat released when the compound burns in oxygen.
The absolute enthalpy of the compound at 298 K.
The enthalpy change when 1 mol of the compound is formed from its elements, with all substances in their standard states.


4. What is the standard pressure used in thermodynamic tables?

0 bar.
1 bar.
1 atm exactly.
10 bar.
It depends on the substance.


5. What is the standard enthalpy of formation of \(\mathrm{O}_{2(g)}\)?

\(-286\;\text{kJ/mol}\).
\(-394\;\text{kJ/mol}\).
\(+498\;\text{kJ/mol}\).
\(0\;\text{kJ/mol}\), since it is an element in its standard state.
It cannot be measured.


6. Which formula expresses Hess’s law?

\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^{\standardstate} = \sum_i \nu_i \Delta_{\text{f}}H_i^{\standardstate}\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^{\standardstate} = \sum_i \Delta_{\text{f}}H_i^{\standardstate}\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^{\standardstate} = \prod_i \nu_i \Delta_{\text{f}}H_i^{\standardstate}\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^{\standardstate} = Q_V\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^{\standardstate} = \sum_i \nu_i S_i^{\standardstate}\).


7. Why can Hess’s law be used to calculate reaction enthalpies?

Because all reactions are exothermic.
Because heat is a state function.
Because the enthalpy is a state function, so its change does not depend on the path.
Because all reactions happen at standard conditions.
Because enthalpies of formation are always negative.


8. What does the difference between the enthalpies of formation of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(g)}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(l)}\) represent?

The enthalpy of formation of water.
The heat capacity of water.
The enthalpy of combustion of hydrogen.
Zero, since they are the same substance.
The enthalpy (latent heat) of vaporization of water.


9. How can a reaction enthalpy at a temperature \(T'\) be calculated from its value at 298 K?

\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H_{T'} = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}H_{298} \cdot \frac{T'}{298}\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H_{T'} = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}H_{298} + \int_{298}^{T'} \Delta C_P\,dT\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H_{T'} = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}H_{298}\) always.
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H_{T'} = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}H_{298} - T'\Delta S\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H_{T'} = \int_{298}^{T'} C_P\,dT\).


10. The synthesis of ammonia has \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}S^\standardstate < 0\). Why is it spontaneous at 298 K?

Because the entropy of the system does not matter for spontaneity.
Because the reaction is endothermic.
Because every reaction between gases is spontaneous.
Because the heat that it releases increases the entropy of the surroundings by more than the system loses.
Because the reaction is fast at room temperature.


11. A bomb calorimeter measures the heat of a reaction at constant volume. Which quantity does it give?

\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}U\), which can be converted to \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H\) with \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}U + \Delta n_{\text{gas}}RT\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}S\).
The work done by the reaction.
The heat capacity of the products.


12. How is a reaction enthalpy estimated from bond enthalpies?

Bonds formed minus bonds broken.
Bonds broken plus bonds formed.
Bonds broken minus bonds formed.
The sum of the bond enthalpies of the products.
It cannot be estimated from bond enthalpies.








TipAnswers





1.c, 2.a, 3.e, 4.b, 5.d, 6.a, 7.c, 8.e, 9.b, 10.d, 11.b, 12.c

title: 7  Thermochemistry
text:
A common misconception is that energy is “stored” in chemical bonds and released when they break. It is the opposite: a bond is a more stable (lower-energy) arrangement than the separated atoms, so breaking it always costs energy. Fuels release energy when they burn because the bonds that form in the products (for example, in \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) are, overall, stronger than the ones broken in the reactants.↩︎
There are some exceptions, such as phosphorus, for which the most stable form at 1 bar is black phosphorus, but white phosphorus is chosen as the standard reference state for zero enthalpy of formation. For the purposes of this course, however, we can safely ignore them.↩︎

title: 8  Thermodynamic Potentials
text:
8.1 Fundamental Equation of Thermodynamics
In chapter 5 and chapter 6, we learned that the entropy of the universe tells us whether a process is spontaneous, and in section 7.7 we used it to show that the synthesis of ammonia is spontaneous. This criterion is general, but it is not very practical: to use it, we always need to calculate what happens to the surroundings, in addition to what happens to the system. Chemists would much rather have a criterion that depends only on the system, and that works at the conditions that we can easily control in a lab, such as constant temperature and constant pressure. At the end of chapter 7, we already found a hint: for a reaction at constant \(T\) and \(P\), the combination \(\Delta H - T\Delta S\) of the system alone tells us whether the reaction is spontaneous (eq. 7.15). In this chapter, we will build such criteria. We will start by combining the first and second laws into a single equation, and we will then use a simple mathematical trick to define new state functions, called thermodynamic potentials, each tailored to a specific set of experimental conditions. One of them, the Gibbs energy, will be the protagonist of the rest of this book.
Let’s summarize some of the results from the first and second law of thermodynamics that we have seen so far. For reversible processes in closed systems, the first law gives us the change in internal energy, and the definition of entropy gives us the reversible heat:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{From 1}^{\text{st}} \text{ Law:} \qquad \quad & dU = đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}-PdV \\
\text{From The Definition of Entropy:} \qquad \quad & dS = \frac{đQ_{\mathrm{REV}}}{T} \rightarrow đQ_{\mathrm{REV}} = TdS \\
\\
\Rightarrow \quad & dU = TdS - PdV.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.1}\]
Eq. 8.1 is called the fundamental equation of thermodynamics since it combines the first and the second laws. Even though we started the derivation above by restricting to reversible transformations only, if we look carefully at eq. 8.1, we notice that it exclusively involves state functions (\(U\), \(T\), \(S\), \(P\), and \(V\)). Since state functions do not care about the path, the relation between their changes must be the same for any path, and it applies to both reversible and irreversible processes. The fundamental equation, however, remains constrained to closed systems. This fact restricts its utility for chemistry, since when a chemical reaction happens, the amounts of the chemical species change.
At the end of the 19th century, Josiah Willard Gibbs (1839–1903) proposed an important addition to the fundamental equation to account for changes in composition. Gibbs was able to do so by introducing a new quantity that he called the chemical potential:
The chemical potential of species \(i\) is usually abbreviated as \(\mu_i\), and it enters the fundamental equation of thermodynamics as:
\[
dU = TdS-PdV+\sum_i\mu_i dn_i,
\tag{8.2}\]
where \(dn_i\) is the differential change in the number of moles of substance \(i\), and the summation extends over all chemical species in the system. In words, \(\mu_i\) tells us by how much the energy of the system changes when we add a tiny amount of species \(i\), while keeping everything else fixed. As we will see in the next chapters, it measures the “escaping tendency” of a species: matter spontaneously moves from where its chemical potential is high to where it is low, just like heat moves from high to low temperature.
According to the fundamental equation, the internal energy of a system is a function of the three variables entropy, \(S\), volume, \(V\), and the numbers of moles \(\{n_i\}\).1 To emphasize this connection, we can use the notation \(U(S,V,\{n_i\})\), and we call \(S\), \(V\), and \(\{n_i\}\) the natural variables of the energy. Using the language of chapter 1, the natural variables are the “knobs” that control the “machine” \(U\): if we know how to turn them, we know everything about how \(U\) changes.

text:
Definition 8.1 The chemical potential is the amount of energy absorbed or released due to a change of the particle number of a given chemical species.











Figure 8.1: The internal energy as a machine. Its natural variables, the knobs that control it, are the entropy \(S\), the volume \(V\), and the numbers of moles \(\{n_i\}\), as in eq. 8.2.

title: 8  Thermodynamic Potentials
text:
8.2 Thermodynamic Potentials
The natural variables of the internal energy have a practical problem. While the volume and the number of moles are easy to control, nobody has ever built an “entropy-meter,” and we have no knob to set the entropy of a system in the lab. The knobs that we can easily turn are the temperature (with a thermostat or a water bath) and the pressure (by leaving the beaker open to the atmosphere). We would like, therefore, to define new state functions whose natural variables include \(T\) and \(P\) instead of \(S\) and \(V\).
There is a simple trick to do this, called a Legendre transformation. Look at eq. 8.2: the variables appear in pairs, multiplied together, as \(T\) and \(S\) in \(TdS\), and \(-P\) and \(V\) in \(-PdV\). These pairs are called conjugate variables. In each pair, one variable is intensive (\(T\) and \(-P\)), the other one is extensive (\(S\) and \(V\)), and their product has the units of an energy.2 Now, let’s subtract the product \(TS\) from \(U\) and take the differential. Using the product rule, \(d(TS)=TdS+SdT\), and therefore:
\[
d(U-TS) = \underbrace{TdS-PdV+\sum_i\mu_i dn_i}_{dU} - TdS - SdT = -SdT-PdV+\sum_i\mu_i dn_i.
\tag{8.3}\]
The term \(TdS\) has disappeared, and it has been replaced by \(-SdT\). The new function, \(U-TS\), has \(T\) as a natural variable instead of \(S\): we have swapped a knob that we cannot turn for one that we can. This is all there is to a Legendre transformation: to replace a natural variable with its conjugate partner, we subtract the product of the two from the original function. In the language of our machines, a Legendre transformation swaps one knob for its partner, as summarized in figure 8.2. The new functions obtained this way are called thermodynamic potentials.3






Figure 8.2: The Legendre transformations as knob swaps. Starting from the internal energy, whose knobs are \(S\), \(V\), and \(\{n_i\}\), we obtain the enthalpy by swapping the volume knob for the pressure knob, the Helmholtz energy by swapping the entropy knob for the temperature knob, and the Gibbs energy by swapping both. The knob of each variable has the same color in all the figures of this chapter.



We have already used this trick, without saying it, when we defined the enthalpy in section 3.1.4. If we take the internal energy and subtract the product of the conjugate variables \(-P\) and \(V\), we obtain \(U-(-P)V=U+PV=H\), as in eq. 3.9. Taking the differential of this definition, we obtain:
\[
dH = dU +VdP +PdV,
\tag{8.4}\]
and using the fundamental equation, eq. 8.2, to replace \(dU\), we obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
dH & = TdS -PdV +\sum_i\mu_i dn_i +VdP +PdV  \\
   & = TdS +VdP +\sum_i\mu_i dn_i,
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.5}\]
which is the fundamental equation for enthalpy. The natural variables of the enthalpy are \(S\), \(P\), and \(\{n_i\}\). The Legendre transformation has allowed us to go from \(U(S,V,\{n_i\})\) to \(H(S,P,\{n_i\})\) by replacing the dependence on the extensive variable, \(V\), with an intensive one, \(P\).
The function that we have obtained in eq. 8.3, where we replaced the entropy with the temperature, is called the Helmholtz energy, \(A\):
\[
A = U -TS,
\tag{8.6}\]
and its fundamental equation is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
dA &= dU -SdT -TdS = TdS - PdV +\sum_i \mu_i dn_i -SdT -TdS  \\
   &= -SdT -PdV +\sum_i \mu_i dn_i.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.7}\]
The Helmholtz energy is named after Hermann Ludwig Ferdinand von Helmholtz (1821–1894), and its natural variables are temperature, volume, and the number of moles.
Finally, we can perform both Legendre transformations at once, to replace both the entropy and the volume with their intensive partners. In that case, we define a new function called the Gibbs energy, \(G\), as:
\[
G = U -TS +PV = H-TS,
\tag{8.8}\]
which, taking again the differential and using eq. 8.2 becomes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
dG &= dU -SdT -TdS +VdP +PdV = dH -SdT -TdS\\
   &= TdS - PdV +\sum_i\mu_i dn_i -SdT -TdS +VdP +PdV \\
   &= VdP -SdT +\sum_i\mu_i dn_i.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.9}\]
The Gibbs energy is named after Willard Gibbs himself, and its natural variables are temperature, pressure, and number of moles: exactly the knobs that we control when we run a reaction in an open beaker.
A summary of the four thermodynamic potentials is given in the following table.









Name
Symbol
Fundamental Equation
Natural Variables




Energy
\(U\)
\(dU=TdS-PdV+\sum_i\mu_i dn_i\)
\(S,V,\{n_i\}\)


Enthalpy
\(H\)
\(dH=TdS+VdP+\sum_i\mu_i dn_i\)
\(S,P,\{n_i\}\)


Helmholtz Energy
\(A\)
\(dA=-SdT-PdV+\sum_i\mu_i dn_i\)
\(T,V,\{n_i\}\)


Gibbs Energy
\(G\)
\(dG=VdP-SdT+\sum_i\mu_i dn_i\)
\(T,P,\{n_i\}\)



Let’s look at what this table tells us:

Each potential is suited to different conditions. We should use the potential whose natural variables are the ones that we keep constant in our experiment. The internal energy is natural for an isolated, rigid container. The enthalpy is natural for heat exchanged at constant pressure, as we saw in chapter 7. The Helmholtz energy is natural for processes at constant temperature and volume, such as reactions in a sealed rigid vessel. The Gibbs energy is natural for processes at constant temperature and pressure, which is the case for most chemical reactions in the lab and for all the processes in living organisms.
No information is lost. A Legendre transformation does not throw away anything: the four potentials contain exactly the same information, written in terms of different variables.
The thermodynamic potentials are the analog of the potential energy in classical mechanics. A ball rolls downhill, and it stops at the bottom, where its potential energy is at a minimum. As we will show in the next section, a system at constant \(T\) and \(V\) evolves spontaneously towards the minimum of \(A\), and a system at constant \(T\) and \(P\) evolves towards the minimum of \(G\).4

title: 8  Thermodynamic Potentials
text:
8.3 Gibbs and Helmholtz Energies
The Legendre transformation procedure translates all information contained in the original function to the new one. Therefore, \(H(S,P,\{n_i\})\), \(A(T,V,\{n_i\})\), and \(G(T,P,\{n_i\})\) all contain the same information that is in \(U(S,V,\{n_i\})\). However, the new functions depend on different natural variables, and they are useful at different conditions. For example, when we want to study chemical changes, we are interested in studying the term \(\sum_i\mu_i dn_i\) that appears in each thermodynamic potential. To do so, we need to isolate the chemical term by keeping all other natural variables constant. For example, changes in the chemical term will correspond to changes in the internal energy at constant \(S\) and constant \(V\):
\[
dU(S,V,\{n_i\}) = \sum_i\mu_i dn_i \quad \text{if} \quad dS=dV=0.
\tag{8.10}\]
Similarly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
dH(S,P,\{n_i\}) = \sum_i\mu_i dn_i \quad \text{if} \quad dS=dP=0, \\
dA(T,V,\{n_i\}) = \sum_i\mu_i dn_i \quad \text{if} \quad dT=dV=0, \\
dG(T,P,\{n_i\}) = \sum_i\mu_i dn_i \quad \text{if} \quad dT=dP=0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.11}\]
The latter two cases are particularly interesting, since most of chemistry happens at constant temperature and either constant volume,5 or constant pressure.6 Neither of them requires the entropy to be constant, which we could not control anyway. We will now show that \(A\) and \(G\) also give us what we were looking for at the beginning of this chapter: criteria for spontaneity that depend only on the system. The starting point is the Clausius theorem, eq. 6.21, which contains the second law written in terms of the system only:
\[
d S^{\mathrm{sys}} \geq \frac{đQ}{T_{\text{surr}}} \quad \longrightarrow \quad TdS \geq đQ,
\tag{8.12}\]
where in the second step we multiplied both sides by \(T\), the temperature of the system and of its surroundings, which we keep constant. We can now consider two cases, side by side: constant \(V\) (left), where no work is done and the heat is \(đQ_V=dU\), and constant \(P\) (right), where the heat is \(đQ_P=dH\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{constant} & \; V:           & \qquad \qquad & \qquad \qquad &     \text{constant} & \; P: \\
\\
TdS & \geq dU           & &   &     TdS & \geq dH \\
\\
TdS -dU & \geq 0         & &   &      TdS -dH & \geq 0 \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.13}\]
On the other hand, at constant temperature, \(SdT=0\), and the differentials of the definitions of \(A\) and \(G\), eq. 8.6 and eq. 8.8, simplify to:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{constant} & \; T,V:           & \qquad & \qquad &     \text{constant} & \; T,P: \\
\\
(dA)_{T,V} &= dU -TdS     & &   &       (dG)_{T,P} &= dH - TdS \\
\\
dU = (dA)_{T,V} &+TdS       & &   &       dH = (dG)_{T,P} &+TdS
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.14}\]
Replacing \(dU\) and \(dH\) from the last line of eq. 8.14 into eq. 8.13, the terms \(TdS\) cancel out, and we obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
TdS -(dA)_{T,V} &- TdS \geq 0 & \qquad & \qquad & TdS -(dG)_{T,P} &- TdS \geq 0 \\
\\
(dA)_{T,V} & \leq 0 & \qquad & \qquad & (dG)_{T,P} & \leq 0. \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.15}\]
These are the conditions on \(dA\) and \(dG\) for inferring the spontaneity of a process. Notice how they contain only properties of the system: the entropy change of the surroundings is hidden inside them, through the heat that the system exchanges. They can be summarized as follows:

Definition 8.2 \(\;\)

During a spontaneous process at constant temperature and volume, the Helmholtz energy will decrease \((dA<0)\), until it reaches a stationary point at which the system will be at equilibrium \((dA=0)\).
During a spontaneous process at constant temperature and pressure, the Gibbs energy will decrease \((dG<0)\), until it reaches a stationary point at which the system will be at equilibrium \((dG=0)\).








Figure 8.3: Behavior of Helmholtz (red) and Gibbs (blue) Energies for Spontaneous Processes at Constant \(T,V\) (left) and Constant \(T,P\) (right).

title: 8  Thermodynamic Potentials
text:
8.4 Maxwell Relations
Let’s consider the fundamental equations for the thermodynamic potentials that we have derived in section 8.2:
\[
\begin{aligned}
dU(S,V,\{n_i\}) &= \enspace T dS -P dV + \sum_i \mu_i dn_i \\
dH(S,P,\{n_i\}) &= \enspace T dS + V dP + \sum_i \mu_i dn_i \\
dA(T,V,\{n_i\}) &= -S dT -P dV + \sum_i \mu_i dn_i \\
dG(T,P,\{n_i\}) &= -S dT + V dP + \sum_i \mu_i dn_i\;.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.16}\]
Since we know the natural variables of each potential, we can also write the same differentials using the general formula for the total differential, eq. 1.3. Each coefficient in front of \(dS\), \(dV\), \(dT\), \(dP\), or \(dn_i\) is a partial derivative of the potential:
\[
\begin{aligned}
dU &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial S} \right)_{V,\{n_i\}}}_{T} dS + \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V} \right)_{S,\{n_i\}}}_{-P} dV + \sum_i \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial n_i} \right)_{S,V,\{n_{j \neq i}\}}}_{\mu_i} dn_i \\
dH &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial S} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}}}_{T} dS + \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial P} \right)_{S,\{n_i\}}}_{V} dP + \sum_i \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial n_i} \right)_{S,P,\{n_{j \neq i}\}}}_{\mu_i} dn_i \\
dA &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial A}{\partial T} \right)_{V,\{n_i\}}}_{-S} dT + \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial A}{\partial V} \right)_{T,\{n_i\}}}_{-P} dV + \sum_i \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial A}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,V,\{n_{j \neq i}\}}}_{\mu_i} dn_i \\
dG &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}}}_{-S} dT + \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P} \right)_{T,\{n_i\}}}_{V} dP + \sum_i \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,P,\{n_{j \neq i}\}}}_{\mu_i} dn_i\;,
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.17}\]
Comparing eq. 8.16 and eq. 8.17 term by term, we can read off what each partial derivative is equal to. For example, the coefficient of \(dS\) in \(dU\) is \(T\) in the first equation and \(\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial S}\right)_{V,\{n_i\}}\) in the second one, so these two quantities must be equal. In this way, we obtain the following new definitions:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T &= \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial S} \right)_{V,\{n_i\}} = \left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial S} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}}  \\
-P &= \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V} \right)_{S,\{n_i\}} = \left(\frac{\partial A}{\partial V} \right)_{T,\{n_i\}}  \\
V &= \left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial P} \right)_{S,\{n_i\}} = \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P} \right)_{T,\{n_i\}}  \\
-S &= \left(\frac{\partial A}{\partial T} \right)_{V,\{n_i\}} = \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}}  \\
\text{and:}
\\
\mu_i &=  \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial n_i} \right)_{S,V,\{n_{j \neq i}\}} =  \left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial n_i} \right)_{S,P,\{n_{j \neq i}\}} \\
       &= \left(\frac{\partial A}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,V,\{n_{j \neq i}\}} = \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,P,\{n_{j \neq i}\}}\;.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.18}\]
Since \(T\), \(P\), \(V\), and \(S\) are now defined as first partial derivatives of a thermodynamic potential, we can take a second partial derivative with respect to the other natural variable. As we saw in chapter 1, Schwarz’s theorem guarantees that, for a state function, the order in which we take the two derivatives does not matter. Therefore, the two mixed second derivatives of each potential must be equal, which gives the following relations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial^2 U }{\partial S \partial V} &=& +\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial V}\right)_{S,n_{i}} &=& -\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial S}\right)_{V,n_{i}}   \\
\frac{\partial^2 H }{\partial S \partial P} &=& +\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\right)_{S,n_{i}} &=& +\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\right)_{P,n_{i}}  \\
-\frac{\partial^2 A }{\partial T \partial V} &=& +\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_{T,n_{i}} &=& +\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_{V,n_{i}}  \\
\frac{\partial^2 G }{\partial T \partial P} &=& -\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_{T,n_{i}} &=& +\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{P,n_{i}}
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.19}\]
The relations in eq. 8.19 are called Maxwell relations,7 and are useful in experimental settings to relate quantities that are hard to measure with others that are more intuitive. Their real power is that they let us calculate how the entropy changes with pressure or volume, which we cannot measure directly, from how \(P\), \(V\), and \(T\) are related, which we can measure easily.
Let’s see an example. The third Maxwell relation tells us that \(\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_{T} = \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_{V}\). For an ideal gas, \(P=\frac{nRT}{V}\), and the right-hand side is easy to calculate: \(\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_{V}=\frac{nR}{V}\). Therefore, \(dS=\frac{nR}{V}dV\) at constant temperature, and integrating between \(V_i\) and \(V_f\):
\[
\Delta S = nR \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i} \qquad \text{(constant } T\text{)},
\tag{8.20}\]
which is exactly the result that we obtained in eq. 6.4, using the heat exchanged along a reversible path. With the Maxwell relation, we obtained it without ever thinking about heat, starting only from the ideal gas law.

Example 8.1 (Deriving a Maxwell relation) Derive the last Maxwell relation in eq. 8.19.
Solution: We can start our derivation from the definitions of \(V\) and \(S\) as partial derivatives of \(G\):
\[
V = \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P} \right)_{T,\{n_i\}} \qquad \text{and:} \qquad -S = \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}},
\]
and then take a second partial derivative of each quantity with respect to the second variable:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}} &=\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\left[ \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P} \right)_{T,\{n_i\}} \right]_{P,\{n_i\}} \\
\\
-\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P} \right)_{T,\{n_i\}} &=\frac{\partial}{\partial P}\left[ \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}} \right]_{T,\{n_i\}} \;.
\end{aligned}
\]
These two derivatives are mixed partial second derivatives of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) and \(P\), and therefore, according to Schwarz’s theorem, they are equal to each other:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\left[ \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P} \right)_{T,\{n_i\}} \right]_{P,\{n_i\}} &=
\frac{\partial}{\partial P}\left[ \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}} \right]_{T,\{n_i\}}, \\
\\
\text{hence:} \\
\\
\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}} &= -\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P} \right)_{T,\{n_i\}},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is the last of Maxwell relations, as defined in eq. 8.19. This relation is particularly useful because it connects the quantity \(\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P} \right)_{T,\{n_i\}}\)—which is impossible to measure in a lab—with the quantity \(\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}}\)—which is easier to measure from an experiment that determines isobaric volumetric thermal expansion coefficients.

title: 8  Thermodynamic Potentials
text:
8.5 Chapter Review

8.5.1 Key Ideas

Fundamental equation: \(dU = T\,dS - P\,dV + \sum_i \mu_i\,dn_i\). It contains only state functions, so it applies to reversible and irreversible processes alike.
Chemical potential: \(\mu_i\) measures how the energy changes when moles of species \(i\) are added.
Legendre transformations swap a variable with its conjugate, giving \(H = U + PV\), \(A = U - TS\), and \(G = U - TS + PV\), each with its own natural variables.
Spontaneity criteria: at constant \(T\) and \(V\), the Helmholtz energy decreases (\(dA < 0\)); at constant \(T\) and \(P\), the Gibbs energy decreases (\(dG < 0\)).
Maxwell relations follow from the equality of mixed second derivatives, and they turn hard-to-measure derivatives of \(S\) into easy-to-measure ones of \(P\), \(V\), and \(T\).



8.5.2 Study Questions
1. What is the fundamental equation of thermodynamics for a closed system?

\(dU = TdS + PdV\).
\(dU = đQ - PdV\) only for reversible processes.
\(dU = TdS - PdV\).
\(dU = SdT - VdP\).
\(dU = TdS - VdP\).


2. Why does the fundamental equation apply to irreversible processes too, even if it was derived for reversible ones?

Because it contains only state functions.
Because irreversible processes do not exist.
Because heat is a state function.
Because it contains the entropy.
Because it is an approximation.


3. What is the chemical potential?

The energy stored in chemical bonds.
The potential energy of a molecule.
The pressure of a chemical species.
The energy needed to break a molecule into atoms.
The amount of energy absorbed or released due to a change in the number of particles of a chemical species.


4. What are the natural variables of the internal energy?

\(T\), \(P\), \(\{n_i\}\).
\(S\), \(V\), \(\{n_i\}\).
\(T\), \(V\), \(\{n_i\}\).
\(S\), \(P\), \(\{n_i\}\).
\(U\), \(V\), \(T\).


5. What does a Legendre transformation do?

It adds heat to the system.
It removes all information from the original function.
It converts a path function into a state function.
It defines a new function by subtracting a product of conjugate variables, replacing one natural variable with its conjugate.
It changes the units of the energy.


6. What are the natural variables of the Gibbs energy?

\(T\), \(P\), \(\{n_i\}\).
\(S\), \(V\), \(\{n_i\}\).
\(T\), \(V\), \(\{n_i\}\).
\(S\), \(P\), \(\{n_i\}\).
\(G\), \(H\), \(S\).


7. What is the fundamental equation for the Helmholtz energy?

\(dA = TdS - PdV + \sum_i \mu_i dn_i\).
\(dA = -SdT + VdP + \sum_i \mu_i dn_i\).
\(dA = -SdT - PdV + \sum_i \mu_i dn_i\).
\(dA = TdS + VdP + \sum_i \mu_i dn_i\).
\(dA = SdT + PdV\).


8. What is the condition for a spontaneous process at constant temperature and pressure?

\(dA < 0\).
\(dS = 0\).
\(dH > 0\).
\(dG > 0\).
\(dG < 0\), until \(dG = 0\) at equilibrium.


9. From which mathematical property do the Maxwell relations follow?

The first law of thermodynamics.
The equality of the mixed second derivatives of a state function (Schwarz’s theorem).
The ideal gas law.
The definition of the chemical potential.
The Clausius inequality.


10. Why is the Maxwell relation \(\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = -\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T\) useful?

Because it shows that the entropy is constant.
Because it defines the temperature.
Because it is valid only for ideal gases.
Because it relates a quantity that is hard to measure (how \(S\) changes with \(P\)) to one that is easy to measure (thermal expansion).
Because it gives the value of the Gibbs energy.








TipAnswers





1.c, 2.a, 3.e, 4.b, 5.d, 6.a, 7.c, 8.e, 9.b, 10.d

title: 9  Gibbs Energy
text:
9.1 Gibbs Equation
In chapter 8, we found that, at constant temperature and pressure, a process is spontaneous if it decreases the Gibbs energy of the system. In this chapter, we will concentrate on chemical processes that happen at these conditions.1 We will learn how to calculate the Gibbs energy of a reaction from tabulated data, and how the Gibbs energy changes with temperature, pressure, and composition. These three dependencies will be the foundations of the next chapters on chemical equilibrium, phase equilibrium, and solutions.
Recalling from chapter 8, the definition of \(G\) is:
\[
G = U -TS +PV = H-TS,
\tag{9.1}\]
which, taking the differential at constant \(T\) and \(P\), becomes:
\[
dG = dH \; \overbrace{-SdT}^{=0} -TdS = dH -TdS.
\tag{9.2}\]
Integrating eq. 9.2 between the initial and final states of a process results in:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_i^f dG &= \int_i^f dH -T \int_i^f dS \\
\\
\Delta G &= \Delta H -T \Delta S
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.3}\]
which is the famous Gibbs equation for \(\Delta G\). Using Definition 8.2, we can use \(\Delta G\) to infer the spontaneity of a chemical process that happens at constant \(T\) and \(P\) using \(\Delta G \leq 0\). If we set ourselves at standard conditions, we can calculate the standard Gibbs energy of reaction, \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate\), for any reaction as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate &= \Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate -T \Delta_{\text{rxn}} S^\standardstate \\
\\
&= \sum_i \nu_i \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H_i^\standardstate - T \sum_i \nu_i S_i^\standardstate,
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.4}\]
where \(\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H_i^\standardstate\) are the standard enthalpies of formation, \(S_i^\standardstate\) are the standard entropies, and \(\nu_i\) are the stoichiometric coefficients for every species \(i\) involved in the reaction. All these quantities are commonly available, and we have already discussed their usage in chapter 7 and chapter 6, respectively.2
The following four options are possible for \(\Delta G^\standardstate\) of a chemical reaction:
Or, in other words:
The synthesis of ammonia is an example of the third case. Its standard Gibbs energy of reaction at \(298\;\text{K}\) is \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate = -91.8 - 298 \times (-0.1981) = -32.8\;\text{kJ/mol}\), the same number that we obtained from the entropy of the universe in section 7.7, and the same that we get from the tabulated Gibbs energy of formation of ammonia, \(2\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} G^\standardstate_{\mathrm{NH}_{3(g)}} = 2(-16.4)\;\text{kJ/mol}\). The reaction is spontaneous at room temperature, but it becomes non-spontaneous at high temperature, where the \(-T\Delta_{\text{rxn}}S^\standardstate\) term wins. If we assume that \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^\standardstate\) and \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}S^\standardstate\) do not depend on temperature, the switch happens where \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G^\standardstate=0\), at \(T = \frac{91.8\times 10^3}{198.1} \approx 463\;\text{K}\).
figure 9.1 shows the four cases as lines, since, if \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta S\) do not depend much on the temperature, \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) is a straight line with intercept \(\Delta H\) and slope \(-\Delta S\). In the two cases where the spontaneity depends on the temperature, the line crosses \(\Delta G=0\) at \(T=\frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}\), the temperature at which the reaction changes direction.
A simple criterion to estimate the sign of the entropy change of a reaction is to count the moles of gas among the reactants and the products. Gases have much larger entropies than liquids and solids, since their molecules can occupy a much larger volume. Therefore, if the reaction produces more moles of gas than it consumes, it will most likely increase the entropy. Vice versa, if the number of moles of gas decreases, the entropy will most likely decrease. For example, the combustion of methane, \(\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)} + 2\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(l)}\), goes from 3 moles of gas to 1, and its entropy change is indeed negative. This criterion is only a rule of thumb: when the number of moles of gas does not change, we need the tabulated entropies to decide.
As we saw in section 8.2, the natural variables of the Gibbs energy are the temperature, \(T\), the pressure, \(P\), and chemical composition, as the number of moles \(\{n_i\}\). The Gibbs energy can therefore be expressed using the total differential as (see also the last formula in eq. 8.17):
\[
dG(T,P,\{n_i\}) = \mkern-18mu \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}}}_{\text{temperature dependence}} \mkern-36mu dT + \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P} \right)_{T,\{n_i\}}}_{\text{pressure dependence}} \mkern-36mu dP + \sum_i \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,P,\{n_{j \neq i}\}}}_{\text{composition dependence}} \mkern-36mu dn_i.
\tag{9.5}\]
If we know the behavior of \(G\) as we vary each of the three natural variables independently of the other two, we can reconstruct the total differential \(dG\). Each of these terms represents a coefficient in eq. 9.5, which are given in eq. 8.18.
