title: 9  Gibbs Energy
text:
9.2 Temperature Dependence of \(\Delta G\)
\[
\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}}=-S
\]
Let’s analyze the first coefficient that gives the dependence of the Gibbs energy on temperature. Since this coefficient is equal to \(-S\) and the entropy is always positive, \(G\) must decrease when \(T\) increases at constant \(P\) and \(\{n_i\}\), and vice versa.
If we replace this coefficient for \(-S\) in the Gibbs equation, eq. 9.3, we obtain:
\[
\Delta G = \Delta H + T \left(\frac{\partial \Delta G}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}},
\tag{9.6}\]
and since eq. 9.6 includes both \(\Delta G\) and its partial derivative with respect to temperature \(\left(\frac{\partial \Delta G}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}}\) we need to rearrange it to include the temperature derivative only. To do so, we can start by evaluating the partial derivative of \(\left( \frac{\Delta G}{T} \right)\) using the product rule:
\[
\left[ \frac{\partial\left( \frac{\Delta G}{T} \right)}{\partial T} \right]_{P,\{n_i\}} = \frac{1}{T} \left(\frac{\partial \Delta G}{\partial T}  \right)_{P,\{n_i\}} - \frac{1}{T^2}\Delta G,
\tag{9.7}\]
which, replacing \(\Delta G\) from eq. 9.6 into eq. 9.7, becomes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left[ \frac{\partial\left( \frac{\Delta G}{T} \right)}{\partial T} \right]_{P,\{n_i\}} &= \frac{1}{T} \left(\frac{\partial \Delta G}{\partial T}  \right)_{P,\{n_i\}} - \frac{1}{T^2} \left[ \Delta H + T \left(\frac{\partial \Delta G}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}} \right] \\
&= \frac{1}{T} \left(\frac{\partial \Delta G}{\partial T}  \right)_{P,\{n_i\}}- \frac{\Delta H}{T^2}-\frac{1}{T} \left(\frac{\partial \Delta G}{\partial T}  \right)_{P,\{n_i\}},
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.8}\]
which simplifies to:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left[ \frac{\partial\left( \frac{\Delta G}{T} \right)}{\partial T} \right]_{P,\{n_i\}} &= - \frac{\Delta H}{T^2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.9}\]
Eq. 9.9 is known as the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation, and is useful in its integrated form to calculate the Gibbs energy for a chemical reaction at any temperature \(T\) by knowing just the standard Gibbs energy of formation and the standard enthalpy of formation for the individual species, which are usually reported at \(T=298\;\text{K}\). The integration is performed as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{T_i=298 \;\text{K}}^{T_f=T}  \frac{\partial\left( \frac{\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G}{T} \right)}{\partial T} &=  - \int_{T_i=298 \;\text{K}}^{T_f=T}  \frac{\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H}{T^2} \\ \\ \frac{\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate(T)}{T} &=  \frac{\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate}{298 \;\text{K}} + \Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate \left( \frac{1}{T} -\frac{1}{298 \;\text{K}} \right),
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.10}\]
giving the integrated Gibbs–Helmholtz equation:
\[
\frac{\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate(T)}{T} =  \frac{\sum_i \nu_i \Delta_{\text{f}} G_i^\standardstate}{298 \;\text{K}} + \sum_i \nu_i \Delta_{\text{f}} H_i^\standardstate \left( \frac{1}{T} -\frac{1}{298 \;\text{K}} \right)
\tag{9.11}\]

title: 9  Gibbs Energy
text:
9.3 Pressure Dependence of \(\Delta G\)
\[
\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P} \right)_{T,\{n_i\}}=V
\]
We can now turn our attention to the second coefficient that gives how the Gibbs energy changes when the pressure changes. To do this, we put the system at constant \(T\) and \(\{n_i\}\), and then we consider infinitesimal variations of \(G\). From eq. 8.9:
\[
dG = VdP -SdT +\sum_i\mu_i dn_i \quad \xrightarrow{\text{constant}\; T,\{n_i\}} \quad dG = VdP,
\tag{9.12}\]
which is the differential equation that we were looking for. To study changes of \(G\) for macroscopic changes in \(P\), we can integrate eq. 9.12 between initial and final pressures, and considering an ideal gas, we obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_i^f dG &= \int_i^f VdP \\
\Delta G &= nRT \int_i^f \frac{dP}{P} = nRT \ln \frac{P_f}{P_i}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.13}\]
If we take \(P_i = P^\standardstate = 1 \, \text{bar}\), we can rewrite eq. 9.13 as:
\[
G = G^\standardstate + nRT \ln \frac{P_f}{P^\standardstate},
\tag{9.14}\]
which is useful to convert standard Gibbs energies of formation to pressures different from standard pressure, using:
\[
\Delta_{\text{f}} G = \Delta_{\text{f}} G^\standardstate + nRT \ln \frac{P_f}{\underbrace{P^\standardstate}_{=1 \; \text{bar}}} = \Delta_{\text{f}} G^\standardstate + nRT \ln P_f
\tag{9.15}\]
For liquids and solids, \(V\) is essentially independent of \(P\) (liquids and solids are incompressible), and eq. 9.12 can be integrated as:
\[
\Delta G = \int_i^f VdP = V \int_i^f dP = V \Delta P.
\tag{9.16}\]
The plots in Figure 9.2 show the remarkable difference in the behaviors of \(\Delta_{\text{f}} G\) for a gas and for a liquid, as obtained from eq. 9.13 and eq. 9.16.






Figure 9.2: Pressure Dependence of the Gibbs Energy of Formation of Liquid and Gaseous Ethanol at T = 310 K. The Curves Cross at the Vapor Pressure of Liquid Ethanol at this Temperature, which is 0.15 bar.

title: 9  Gibbs Energy
text:
9.4 Composition Dependence of \(\Delta G\)
\[
\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,P}=\mu_i
\]
The third and final coefficient gives the chemical potential as the dependence of \(G\) on the chemical composition at constant \(T\) and \(P\). To understand what the chemical potential means, let’s consider a pure substance, and let’s imagine building a sample of it by adding small amounts, \(dn\), one after the other, at constant \(T\) and \(P\). Each small amount that we add is identical to what is already in the sample. Therefore, each of them changes the Gibbs energy by the same amount, \(dG=\mu^* dn\), where \(\mu^*\) indicates the chemical potential of the pure substance. In other words, \(\mu^*\) is an intensive property: it depends on \(T\) and \(P\), but not on how much substance we have. Since the Gibbs energy is extensive, when there is no substance there is also no Gibbs energy. We can then integrate from an empty sample (\(n=0\), \(G=0\)) to a sample with \(n\) moles and Gibbs energy \(G\):
\[
\int_0^G d G = \int_0^n \mu^* dn,
\tag{9.17}\]
and since \(\mu^*\) does not depend on the number of moles, we can take it out of the integral:
\[
\int_0^G d G = \mu^* \int_0^n dn \quad \rightarrow \quad G = \mu^* n \quad \rightarrow \quad \mu^* = \frac{G}{n},
\tag{9.18}\]
which gives a straightforward interpretation of the chemical potential of a pure substance as the molar Gibbs energy.
In a mixture, the chemical potential of a component is no longer simply \(G/n\), since its molecules are surrounded by molecules of other kinds. The derivative \(\mu_i = \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial n_i}\right)_{T,P,n_{j\neq i}}\) is an example of a partial molar quantity:

Definition 9.1 The partial molar quantity of component \(i\), \(\overline{X}_i = \left(\frac{\partial X}{\partial n_i}\right)_{T,P,n_{j\neq i}}\), is the change in the extensive property \(X\) per mole of \(i\) added to a mixture, at constant temperature, pressure, and amounts of all the other components.

The most intuitive example is the volume. Adding 1 mol of water (\(18\;\text{cm}^3\)) to a large amount of pure water increases the volume by \(18\;\text{cm}^3\), but adding it to a large amount of ethanol increases the volume by only about \(14\;\text{cm}^3\), because the water molecules pack tightly around the ethanol molecules. Partial molar quantities depend on the composition of the mixture. The chemical potential is the partial molar Gibbs energy, \(\mu_i = \overline{G}_i\).
Repeating the argument of eq. 9.17 for a mixture built by adding all the components at once, at constant composition, gives:
\[
G = \sum_i n_i \mu_i.
\tag{9.19}\]
Differentiating eq. 9.19 gives \(dG = \sum_i \mu_i dn_i + \sum_i n_i d\mu_i\), and at constant \(T\) and \(P\), eq. 8.17 gives \(dG = \sum_i \mu_i dn_i\). The two expressions agree only if:
\[
\sum_i n_i d\mu_i = 0 \qquad \text{(constant } T, P\text{)},
\tag{9.20}\]
which is the Gibbs–Duhem equation. It tells us that the chemical potentials of the components of a mixture cannot change independently. For a binary mixture, \(d\mu_{\text{B}} = -\frac{n_{\text{A}}}{n_{\text{B}}} d\mu_{\text{A}}\): if the chemical potential of one component increases, the other one must decrease.
We can start from eq. 9.14 and write for a pure substance that is brought from \(P_i=P^\standardstate\) to \(P_f=P\) at constant \(T\):
\[
G - G^\standardstate = nRT \ln \frac{P}{P^\standardstate},
\tag{9.21}\]
dividing both sides by \(n\), we obtain:
\[
\frac{G}{n} - \frac{G^\standardstate}{n} = RT \ln \frac{P}{P^\standardstate},
\tag{9.22}\]
which, for a pure substance at \(P^\standardstate = 1 \;\text{bar}\), becomes:
\[
\mu^* - \mu^\standardstate =      RT \ln P.
\tag{9.23}\]
Notice that, while we use the pressure of the gas inside the logarithm in eq. 9.23, the quantity is formally divided by the standard pressure \(P^\standardstate = 1 \;\text{bar}\), and therefore it is a dimensionless quantity, as it should be. For simplicity of notation, however, we will omit the division by \(P^\standardstate\) in the remainder of this textbook, especially wherever it does not create confusion. Let’s now consider a mixture of ideal gases, and let’s try to find out whether the chemical potential of a pure gas inside the mixture, \(\mu_i^{\text{mixture}}\), is the same as its chemical potential outside the mixture, \(\mu^*\). To do so, we can use eq. 9.23 and replace the pressure \(P\) with the partial pressure \(P_i\):
\[
\mu_i^{\text{mixture}} = \mu_i^\standardstate + RT \ln P_i,
\tag{9.24}\]
where the partial pressure \(P_i\) can be obtained from the simple relation that is known as Dalton’s Law:
\[
P_i = y_i P,
\tag{9.25}\]
with \(y_i\) being the concentration of gas \(i\) measured as a mole fraction in the gas phase \(y_i=\frac{n_i}{n_{\text{TOT}}} < 1\). Replacing eq. 9.25 into eq. 9.24, we obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_i^{\text{mixture}} &= \mu_i^\standardstate + RT \ln (y_i P) \\
&= \underbrace{\mu_i^\standardstate + RT \ln P}_{\mu_i^*} + RT \ln y_i,
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.26}\]
which then reduces to the following equation:
\[
\mu_i^{\text{mixture}} = \mu_i^* + RT \ln y_i.
\tag{9.27}\]
Analyzing eq. 9.27, we can immediately see that, since \(y_i < 1\):
\[
\mu_i^{\text{mixture}} < \mu_i^*,
\tag{9.28}\]
or, in other words, the chemical potential of a substance in the mixture is always lower than the chemical potential of the pure substance. If we consider a process where we start from two separate pure ideal gases and finish with a mixture of the two, we can calculate the change in Gibbs energy due to the mixing process with:
\[
\Delta_{\text{mixing}} G = \sum n_i \left( \mu_i^{\text{mixture}} - \mu_i^* \right)  < 0,
\tag{9.29}\]
or, in other words, the process is spontaneous under all circumstances, and pure ideal gases will always mix.

title: 9  Gibbs Energy
text:
9.5 Chapter Review

9.5.1 Key Ideas

Gibbs equation: at constant \(T\) and \(P\), \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\), which balances enthalpy and entropy.
Temperature dependence: \(\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T}\right)_{P} = -S\), and the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation gives \(\Delta G\) at other temperatures from \(\Delta H\).
Pressure dependence: \(\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P}\right)_{T} = V\). For an ideal gas, \(G = G^\standardstate + nRT\ln\frac{P}{P^\standardstate}\); for liquids and solids, \(G\) barely changes with \(P\).
Chemical potential: for a pure substance, \(\mu^* = G/n\); for an ideal gas in a mixture, \(\mu_i = \mu_i^\standardstate + RT\ln P_i\).
Partial molar quantities: in a mixture, \(\mu_i = \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial n_i}\right)_{T,P,n_{j\neq i}}\) is the partial molar Gibbs energy, \(G=\sum_i n_i\mu_i\), and the Gibbs–Duhem equation, \(\sum_i n_i\,d\mu_i = 0\), links the changes of the chemical potentials.
Mixing: ideal gases always mix spontaneously, since \(\Delta_{\text{mixing}}G < 0\).



9.5.2 Study Questions
1. Which equation gives the Gibbs energy change of a process at constant \(T\) and \(P\)?

\(\Delta G = \Delta H + T\Delta S\).
\(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\).
\(\Delta G = \Delta U - T\Delta S\).
\(\Delta G = T\Delta S - \Delta H\).
\(\Delta G = \Delta H \cdot \Delta S\).


2. An exothermic reaction decreases the entropy of the system. When is it spontaneous?

Always.
Never.
Only at high temperature.
Only at low temperature.
Only at high pressure.


3. An endothermic reaction increases the entropy of the system. When is it spontaneous?

Only at high temperature.
Only at low temperature.
Always.
Never.
Only at low pressure.


4. Since \(\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T}\right)_{P,\{n_i\}} = -S\), how does the Gibbs energy of a substance change when the temperature increases?

It increases, since the entropy is positive.
It stays constant.
It increases linearly with the volume.
It oscillates.
It decreases, since the entropy is positive.


5. What is the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation?

\(\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P}\right)_T = V\).
\(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\).
\(\left[\frac{\partial (\Delta G/T)}{\partial T}\right]_P = -\frac{\Delta H}{T^2}\).
\(\left[\frac{\partial (\Delta G/T)}{\partial T}\right]_P = \frac{\Delta S}{T^2}\).
\(\Delta G = -RT\ln K\).


6. What is the pressure dependence coefficient of the Gibbs energy?

\(\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P}\right)_{T,\{n_i\}} = -V\).
\(\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P}\right)_{T,\{n_i\}} = V\).
\(\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P}\right)_{T,\{n_i\}} = -S\).
\(\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P}\right)_{T,\{n_i\}} = H\).
\(\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial P}\right)_{T,\{n_i\}} = 0\).


7. How does the Gibbs energy of an ideal gas depend on the pressure at constant temperature?

\(G = G^{\standardstate} - nRT\ln\frac{P}{P^{\standardstate}}\).
\(G = G^{\standardstate} + nRT\frac{P}{P^{\standardstate}}\).
\(G = G^{\standardstate} + V\Delta P\).
\(G = G^{\standardstate} + nRT\ln\frac{P}{P^{\standardstate}}\).
\(G\) does not depend on \(P\).


8. Why does the Gibbs energy of a liquid change much less with pressure than that of a gas?

Because the molar volume of a liquid is small and almost independent of pressure.
Because liquids have zero entropy.
Because liquids are always at standard pressure.
Because the Gibbs energy of a liquid is zero.
Because liquids do not have a chemical potential.


9. What is the chemical potential of a pure substance?

Its enthalpy.
Its entropy per mole.
Its pressure divided by \(RT\).
Zero at standard conditions.
Its molar Gibbs energy, \(\mu^* = G/n\).


10. Two pure ideal gases are allowed to mix at constant \(T\) and \(P\). What is the sign of \(\Delta_{\text{mixing}}G\)?

Positive, so the gases do not mix.
Zero, since ideal gases do not interact.
Negative, so the gases always mix spontaneously.
It depends on the gases.
It depends on the temperature.








TipAnswers





1.b, 2.d, 3.a, 4.e, 5.c, 6.b, 7.d, 8.a, 9.e, 10.c

title: 10  Chemical Equilibrium
text:
10.1 Reaction Quotient and Equilibrium Constant
In chapter 9, we learned that the Gibbs energy decreases during a spontaneous process at constant temperature and pressure, and we found how it depends on the composition of a mixture. In this chapter, we will apply these results to chemical reactions. Most reactions do not go all the way to products: they stop at a mixture of reactants and products, the chemical equilibrium. We will see that the composition of this mixture is set by the minimum of the Gibbs energy, which leads us to the equilibrium constant that you know from general chemistry. We will then study how the equilibrium constant changes with temperature and pressure, which gives a mathematical form to Le Chatelier’s principle.
Let’s consider a prototypical reaction at constant \(T,P\):
\[
a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B} \rightarrow c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D}
\tag{10.1}\]
The Gibbs energy of the reaction is defined as:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G = G_{\text{products}} - G_{\text{reactants}} = G^{\text{C}} + G^{\text{D}} - G^{\text{A}}-G^{\text{B}},
\tag{10.2}\]
and replacing the absolute Gibbs energies with the chemical potentials \(\mu_i\), we obtain:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G = c \mu_{\text{C}} + d \mu_{\text{D}} - a \mu_{\text{A}}- b\mu_{\text{B}}.
\tag{10.3}\]
Assuming the reaction is happening in the gas phase, we can then use eq. 9.24 to replace the chemical potentials with their value in the reaction mixture, as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mkern-60mu \Delta_{\text{rxn}} G =& \; c (\mu_{\text{C}}^\standardstate +RT \ln P_{\text{C}}) + d (\mu_{\text{D}}^\standardstate +RT \ln P_{\text{D}}) +\\ & - a (\mu_{\text{A}}^\standardstate +RT \ln P_{\text{A}}) - b (\mu_{\text{B}}^\standardstate +RT \ln P_{\text{B}}) \\
  =& \; \underbrace{c \mu_{\text{C}}^\standardstate + d \mu_{\text{D}}^\standardstate - a \mu_{\text{A}}^\standardstate - b\mu_{\text{B}}^\standardstate}_{\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate}  +RT \ln \frac{P_{\text{C}}^c \cdot P_{\text{D}}^d}{P_{\text{A}}^a \cdot P_{\text{B}}^b}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.4}\]
We can define a new quantity called the reaction quotient as a function of the partial pressures of each substance:1
\[
Q_P = \frac{P_{\text{C}}^c \cdot P_{\text{D}}^d}{P_{\text{A}}^a \cdot P_{\text{B}}^b},
\tag{10.5}\]
and we can then simply rewrite eq. 10.4 using eq. 10.5 as:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G = \Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate + RT \ln Q_P.
\tag{10.6}\]
This equation tells us that the sign of \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G\) is influenced by the reaction quotient \(Q_P\). For a spontaneous reaction at the beginning, the partial pressures of the reactants are much higher than the partial pressures of the products, therefore \(Q_P \ll 1\) and \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G < 0\), as we expect. As the reaction proceeds, the partial pressures of the products will increase, while the partial pressures of the reactants will decrease. Consequently, both \(Q_P\) and \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G\) will increase. The reaction will completely stop when \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G = 0\), which is the chemical equilibrium point. At the reaction equilibrium:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G = 0 = \Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate + RT \ln K_P,
\tag{10.7}\]
where we have defined a new quantity called equilibrium constant, as the value the reaction quotient assumes when the reaction reaches equilibrium, and we have denoted it with the symbol \(K_P\).2 From eq. 10.7 we can derive the following fundamental equation on the standard Gibbs energy of reaction:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate = - RT \ln K_P.
\tag{10.8}\]
To extend the concept of \(K_P\) beyond the four species in the prototypical reaction eq. 10.1, we can use the product of a series symbol \(\left( \prod_i \right)\), and write:
\[
K_P=\prod_i P_{i,\text{eq}}^{\nu_i},
\tag{10.9}\]
where \(P_{i,\text{eq}}\) are the partial pressures of each species at equilibrium. Eq. 10.9 is in principle valid for ideal gases only. However, reactions involving ideal gases are pretty rare. As such, we can further extend the concept of equilibrium constant and write:
\[
K_{\text{eq}} =\prod_i a_{i,\text{eq}}^{\nu_i},
\tag{10.10}\]
where we have replaced the partial pressure at equilibrium, \(P_{i,\text{eq}}\), with a new concept introduced initially by Gilbert Newton Lewis (1875–1946),3 that he termed activity, and represented by the letter \(a\). The activity is a dimensionless “effective concentration” that tells us how much each species contributes to the equilibrium. Its expression depends on the state of the species:
For now, it is interesting to use the activity to write the definition of the following two constants:
\[
K_y =\prod_i \left( y_{i,\text{eq}} \right)^{\nu_i} \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad K_C =\prod_i \left( [i]_{\text{eq}}/[i]^\standardstate \right)^{\nu_i},
\tag{10.11}\]
which can then be related with \(K_P\) for a mixture of ideal gases using:
\[
P_i = y_i P \qquad \qquad \qquad P_i=\frac{n_i}{V}RT=[i]RT,
\tag{10.12}\]
which then results in:
\[
K_P = K_y\cdot \left(\frac{P}{P^\standardstate}\right)^{\Delta \nu} \qquad \qquad K_P = K_C \left( \frac{[i]^\standardstate RT}{P^\standardstate} \right)^{\Delta \nu},
\tag{10.13}\]
with \(\Delta \nu =\sum_i \nu_i\).
Using the general equilibrium constant, \(K_{\text{eq}}\), we can also rewrite the fundamental equation on \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate\) that we derived in eq. 10.8 to be applicable at most conditions, as:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate = - RT \ln K_{\text{eq}},
\tag{10.14}\]
and since \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate\) depends on \(T,P\) and \(\{n_i\}\), it is useful to explore how \(K_{\text{eq}}\) depends on those variables as well.

title: 10  Chemical Equilibrium
text:
Ideal gases: the activity is the partial pressure divided by the standard pressure, \(a_i=P_i/P^\standardstate\), as in eq. 10.9.
Non-ideal gases: the pressure is replaced by an “effective pressure,” the fugacity, \(a_i=f_i/P^\standardstate\), which we will introduce in chapter 11.
Pure liquids and solids: the activity is simply \(a_i=1\). This is why pure solids and liquids do not appear in the equilibrium constants that you wrote in general chemistry.
Solutions: for dilute solutions, the activity is approximately equal to a measured concentration, such as the mole fraction, or the molar concentration divided by the standard one, \([i]/[i]^\standardstate\) with \([i]^\standardstate = 1\;\text{mol/L}\). For concentrated solutions, a correction factor is needed. We will derive the activity of solutions in chapter 13.

title: 10  Chemical Equilibrium
section: 10.2 Extent of Reaction and the Minimum of the Gibbs Energy
text:
10.2 Extent of Reaction and the Minimum of the Gibbs Energy
We said that a reaction stops when \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G = 0\). But what exactly is \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G\) while a reaction is still going? It is not the difference between two finished states, as the \(\Delta\) symbol might suggest. To see what it really is, we need a variable that tells us how far a reaction has gone.
Let’s go back to our prototypical reaction, eq. 10.1. Every time the reaction proceeds, the amounts of all species change together, in the ratios set by the stoichiometric coefficients: if \(a\) moles of \(\mathrm{A}\) disappear, \(c\) moles of \(\mathrm{C}\) must appear. We can capture all these changes with a single variable, the extent of reaction, \(\xi\) (the Greek letter “xi”), defined by:
\[
dn_i = \nu_i \, d\xi \qquad \text{or, after integration,} \qquad n_i = n_{i,0} + \nu_i \, \xi,
\tag{10.15}\]
where \(n_{i,0}\) is the amount of species \(i\) at the start, and \(\nu_i\) is its stoichiometric number (negative for reactants, positive for products, as in definition 6.3). The extent of reaction is measured in moles, and it is the same number for every species: \(\xi=0\) at the start, and \(\xi = 1\;\text{mol}\) when the reaction has gone “once” as written, with \(a\) moles of \(\mathrm{A}\) and \(b\) moles of \(\mathrm{B}\) turned into \(c\) moles of \(\mathrm{C}\) and \(d\) moles of \(\mathrm{D}\).
At constant \(T\) and \(P\), the change in Gibbs energy of the reacting mixture is given by the last line of eq. 8.16 with \(dT=dP=0\). Replacing \(dn_i\) with eq. 10.15, we get:
\[
dG = \sum_i \mu_i \, dn_i = \left( \sum_i \nu_i \mu_i \right) d\xi
\quad \longrightarrow \quad
\left( \frac{\partial G}{\partial \xi} \right)_{T,P} = \sum_i \nu_i \mu_i = \Delta_{\text{rxn}} G,
\tag{10.16}\]
where in the last step we recognized the same combination of chemical potentials that appears in eq. 10.3. This is the meaning of \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G\): it is the slope of the Gibbs energy of the mixture as a function of the extent of reaction. Its value changes as the reaction proceeds, because the chemical potentials depend on the composition.






Figure 10.1: Gibbs energy of the mixture as a function of the extent of reaction for \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}_{(g)} \rightleftarrows 2\,\mathrm{NO_2}_{(g)}\) at 298 K and 1 bar, starting from 1 mol of \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}\), computed from the standard Gibbs energies of formation in the appendix. The dashed line is the Gibbs energy if reactants and products were kept separate. Mixing lowers the Gibbs energy and creates a minimum, at the equilibrium extent of reaction.



Let’s look at what figure 10.1 tells us about the dissociation of dinitrogen tetroxide into nitrogen dioxide:

The slope decides the direction. To the left of the minimum, the slope is negative, \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G<0\), and the Gibbs energy decreases if the reaction moves forward. To the right of the minimum, the slope is positive, and the reaction runs spontaneously in reverse. Either way, the mixture slides downhill toward the bottom of the curve.
Equilibrium is the bottom of the curve. At the minimum, the slope is zero, \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G = 0\), and the reaction has no reason to go in either direction. This is the chemical equilibrium of eq. 10.7, and its position, \(\xi_{\text{eq}}\), gives the equilibrium composition.
Mixing is what makes a minimum. If reactants and products stayed separate, the Gibbs energy would follow the dashed straight line, and the reaction would go either all the way or not at all, depending on the sign of \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate\). Because the gases mix, the Gibbs energy drops below this line by the Gibbs energy of mixing, which is always negative (eq. 9.29). This is why some products always form, even when \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate>0\), as in this case, and why most reactions stop at a mixture instead of going to completion.
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate\) is the slope of the dashed line, that is, the Gibbs energy difference between the pure products and the pure reactants, each at standard pressure. It decides where the minimum falls, through \(K_{\text{eq}}\), but it is not the quantity that drives the reaction at a given moment: that is \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G\).


Example 10.1 (Equilibrium composition of dinitrogen tetroxide) One mole of \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}_{(g)}\) is kept at \(298\;\text{K}\) and a total pressure of \(1\;\text{bar}\), where it partially dissociates into \(\mathrm{NO_2}_{(g)}\). Using \(\Delta_{\text{f}} G^\standardstate = 99.8\;\text{kJ/mol}\) for \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}_{(g)}\) and \(51.3\;\text{kJ/mol}\) for \(\mathrm{NO_2}_{(g)}\), find the extent of reaction and the composition at equilibrium.
Solution: The standard Gibbs energy of reaction is:
\[
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate = 2(51.3) - 99.8 = 2.8\;\text{kJ/mol},
\]
and from eq. 10.8:
\[
K_P = \exp\left(-\frac{\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate}{RT}\right) = \exp\left(-\frac{2\,800}{8.314 \times 298}\right) = 0.323.
\]
Using eq. 10.15 with \(n_{\mathrm{N_2O_4},0}=1\;\text{mol}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{NO_2},0}=0\), at a generic extent of reaction we have \(n_{\mathrm{N_2O_4}} = 1-\xi\), \(n_{\mathrm{NO_2}} = 2\xi\), and a total of \(1+\xi\) moles of gas. With a total pressure of \(1\;\text{bar}\), the partial pressures are equal to the mole fractions, and the equilibrium constant becomes:
\[
K_P = \frac{P_{\mathrm{NO_2}}^2}{P_{\mathrm{N_2O_4}}} = \frac{\left(\frac{2\xi}{1+\xi}\right)^2}{\frac{1-\xi}{1+\xi}} = \frac{4\xi^2}{1-\xi^2}.
\]
Solving for \(\xi\) gives:
\[
\xi_{\text{eq}} = \sqrt{\frac{K_P}{4+K_P}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.323}{4.323}} = 0.273\;\text{mol}.
\]
At equilibrium, we have \(0.727\;\text{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}\) and \(0.546\;\text{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NO_2}\), with mole fractions \(y_{\mathrm{N_2O_4}} = 0.571\) and \(y_{\mathrm{NO_2}}=0.429\). This is exactly the position of the minimum in figure 10.1. Even though \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate\) is positive, more than a quarter of the \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}\) dissociates, thanks to the Gibbs energy of mixing.

title: 10  Chemical Equilibrium
text:
10.3 Temperature Dependence of \(K_{\text{eq}}\)
To study the temperature dependence of \(K_{\text{eq}}\) we can use eq. 10.14 for the general equilibrium constant and write:
\[
\ln K_{\text{eq}} = -\frac{\Delta G^\standardstate}{RT},
\tag{10.17}\]
which we can then differentiate with respect to temperature at constant \(P,\{n_i\}\) on both sides:
\[
\left( \frac{\partial \ln K_{\text{eq}}}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}} = -\frac{1}{R}  \left[ \frac{\partial \left( \frac{\Delta G^\standardstate}{T} \right)}{\partial T} \right]_{P,\{n_i\}},
\tag{10.18}\]
and, using the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation (eq. 9.9) to simplify the right-hand side, becomes:
\[
\left( \frac{\partial \ln K_{\text{eq}}}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\{n_i\}} = -\frac{1}{R} \left( -\frac{\Delta H^\standardstate}{T^2} \right) = \frac{\Delta H^\standardstate}{RT^2},
\tag{10.19}\]
which gives the dependence of \(\ln K_{\text{eq}}\) on \(T\) that we were looking for. Eq. 10.19 is also called van ’t Hoff equation,4 and it is the mathematical expression of Le Chatelier’s principle. The simplest interpretation is as follows:

For an exothermic reaction (\(\Delta H^\standardstate < 0\)): \(K_{\text{eq}}\) will decrease as the temperature increases.
For an endothermic reaction (\(\Delta H^\standardstate > 0\)): \(K_{\text{eq}}\) will increase as the temperature increases.

If we integrate the van ’t Hoff equation between two arbitrary points at constant \(P\), and assuming constant \(\Delta H^\standardstate\), we obtain the following:
\[
\int_1^2 d \ln K_{\text{eq}} = \frac{\Delta H^\standardstate}{R} \int_1^2 \frac{dT}{T^2},
\tag{10.20}\]
which leads to the linear equation:
\[
\ln K_{\text{eq}}(2) = \ln K_{\text{eq}}(1) - \frac{\Delta H^\standardstate}{R} \left( \frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1} \right),
\tag{10.21}\]
which is the equation that produces the so-called van ’t Hoff plots, from which \(\Delta H^\standardstate\) can be experimentally determined:






Figure 10.2: Van ’t Hoff Plots for an Endothermic (Left, Blue) and an Exothermic (Right, Red) Reaction at Constant P.
crumbs: The Live Textbook of Physical Chemistry 1

title: 10  Chemical Equilibrium
text:
10.4 Pressure and Composition Dependence of \(K_{\text{eq}}\)
While \(K_P\) is independent of both total pressure and number of moles for an ideal gas, the same is not necessarily true for the other equilibrium constants.
\[
\left( \frac{\partial K_P}{\partial P} \right)_{T,\{n_i\}} = 0 \qquad \qquad \left( \frac{\partial K_P}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,P} =0.
\tag{10.22}\]
For example, it is easy to look at eq. 10.13 and determine that \(K_y\) usually depends on \(P\).5 Using Dalton’s Law, eq. 9.25, we can also notice that the equilibrium partial pressures of the reactants and products in a gas-phase reaction can be expressed in terms of their equilibrium mole fractions \(y_i\) and the total pressure \(P\). As such, we can use \(K_y\) to demonstrate that the equilibrium mole fractions will change when \(P\) changes,6 as it is demonstrated by the following exercise.

Example 10.2 (Dissociation of chlorine under pressure) Calculate the mole fraction change for the dissociation of \(\mathrm{Cl}_{2(g)}\) when the pressure is increased from \(P^\standardstate\) to \(P_f=2.5 \;\text{bar}\) at constant \(T=2\,298\;\mathrm{K}\), knowing that \(\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} G^\standardstate_{\mathrm{Cl}_{(g)}} = 105.3 \;\text{kJ/mol}\) and \(\Delta_{\mathrm{f}} H^\standardstate_{\mathrm{Cl}_{(g)}} = 121.3 \;\text{kJ/mol}\), and remembering that both of these values are tabulated at \(T=298\;\text{K}\).
Solution: Let’s consider the reaction: \[
\mathrm{Cl}_{2(g)} \rightleftarrows 2 \mathrm{Cl}_{(g)}
\]
We can divide the exercise into two parts. In the first one, we will deal with calculating the equilibrium constant at \(T=2\,298\;\mathrm{K}\) from the data at \(T=298\;\mathrm{K}\). In the second one, we will calculate the change in mole fraction when the pressure is increased from \(P^\standardstate=1\;\text{bar}\) to \(P_f=2.5 \;\text{bar}\).

Let’s begin the first part by calculating \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate\) and \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate\) from: \[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate &= 2 \Delta_{\text{f}} G^\standardstate_{\text{Cl}_{(g)}} - \Delta_{\text{f}} G^\standardstate_{\text{Cl}_{2(g)}} \\
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate &= 2 \Delta_{\text{f}} H^\standardstate_{\text{Cl}_{(g)}} - \Delta_{\text{f}} H^\standardstate_{\text{Cl}_{2(g)}},
\end{aligned}
\] and since \(\text{Cl}_{2(g)}\) is an element in its most stable form at \(T=298\;\mathrm{K}\), its standard enthalpy and Gibbs energy of formation are \(\Delta_{\text{f}} H^\standardstate_{\text{Cl}_{2(g)}} = \Delta_{\text{f}} G^\standardstate_{\text{Cl}_{2(g)}} = 0\). Therefore:7 \[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate &= 2 \cdot 105.3 - 0 = 210.6 \;\text{kJ/mol} \\
\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate &= 2 \cdot 121.3 - 0 = 242.6\;\text{kJ/mol}.
\end{aligned}
\] Using eq. 10.8 to calculate \(K_P (P^\standardstate,298\;\text{K})\), we obtain:8 \[
\ln [ K_P (P^\standardstate,298\;\text{K}) ] =  \frac{ - \Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^\standardstate}{RT}  =  \frac{-210.6\times10^3}{8.31 \cdot 298} = - 85.0.
\] We can now use the integrated van ’t Hoff equation, eq. 10.21, to calculate \(K_P\) at \(T=2\,298\;\text{K}\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\ln [K_P (P^\standardstate,&2\,298\;\text{K})] = \ln [K_P (P^\standardstate,298\;\text{K})] \;+ \\ &-\frac{\Delta_{\text{rxn}} H^\standardstate}{R} \left(\frac{1}{2\,298}-\frac{1}{298} \right),
\end{aligned}
\] which becomes: \[
\begin{aligned}
\ln [K_P (P^\standardstate,&2\,298\;\text{K})] = - 85.0 \;+\\&-\frac{242.6\times 10^{3}}{8.31} \left(\frac{1}{2\,298}-\frac{1}{298} \right) = 0.262\;,
\end{aligned}
\] which corresponds to: \[
K_P (P^\standardstate,2\,298\;\text{K}) = \exp (0.262)=1.30.
\]
Let’s now move to the second part of the exercise, where we increase the pressure from \(1\;\text{bar}\) to \(2.5\;\text{bar}\) at constant \(T=2\,298\;\text{K}\). We start by writing the definition of \(K_P\) and \(K_y\): \[
K_P=\frac{P_\mathrm{Cl_{(g)}}^2}{P_{\mathrm{Cl}_{2(g)}}} \qquad \qquad  K_y=\frac{y_\mathrm{Cl_{(g)}}^2}{y_{\mathrm{Cl}_{2(g)}}},
\] and using eq. 10.13: \[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta \nu &= 2 - 1 = 1 \\
K_P &= K_y \cdot \frac{P}{P^\standardstate} \quad \xrightarrow \qquad K_y=K_P \left( \frac{P}{P^\standardstate} \right)^{-1},
\end{aligned}
\] we can calculate the initial \(K_y\) at \(P_i=P^\standardstate\), using: \[
K_y (P^\standardstate,2\,298\;\text{K}) = 1.30 =\frac{1.30}{1}.
\] and calculate the initial concentration of \(\mathrm{Cl}_{2(g)}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}_{(g)}\) at \(P^\standardstate\), recalling that \(y_{\mathrm{Cl}_{2(g)}}=1-y_{\mathrm{Cl}_{(g)}}:\) \[
K_y (P_i,2\,298\;\text{K})=\frac{\left(y^i_{\mathrm{Cl}_{(g)}}\right)^2}{1-y^i_{\mathrm{Cl}_{(g)}}} = 1.30.
\] Solving the quadratic equation, we obtain one negative answer—which is unphysical—,9 and: \[
y_{\mathrm{Cl}_{(g)}}^i= 0.662 \quad \xrightarrow \qquad y_{\mathrm{Cl}_{2(g)}}^i=1-0.662 = 0.338.
\] At the end of the process, \(P_f=2.5\;\text{bar}\), and we obtain: \[
K_y (P_f,2\,298\;\text{K}) = 0.520 = K_P \frac{P^\standardstate}{P_f} = \frac{1.30}{2.5},
\] and, using the same technique used before to solve the quadratic equation: \[
K_y (P_f,2\,298\;\text{K})=\frac{\left(y^f_{\mathrm{Cl}_{(g)}}\right)^2}{1-y^f_{\mathrm{Cl}_{(g)}}} = 0.520,
\] gives: \[
y_{\mathrm{Cl}_{(g)}}^f=0.507 \quad \xrightarrow \qquad y_{\mathrm{Cl}_{2(g)}}^f=1-0.507 = 0.493.
\] To summarize, when we increase the pressure from \(1\;\text{bar}\) to \(2.5\;\text{bar}\) at \(T=2\,298\;\text{K}\), the equilibrium constant in terms of the mole fraction decreases from \(K_y(P^\standardstate,2\,298\;\text{K})=1.30\) to \(K_y(P_f=2.5\;\text{bar},2\,298\;\text{K})=0.520\). This reduction is causing a shift of the equilibrium towards the reactants, with the concentration of \(\text{Cl}_{2(g)}\) increasing from \(y_{\text{Cl}_{2(g)}}^i = 0.338\) to \(y_{\text{Cl}_{2(g)}}^f = 0.493\) and the concentration of \(\text{Cl}_{(g)}\) decreasing from \(y_{\text{Cl}_{(g)}}^i = 0.662\) to \(y_{\text{Cl}_{(g)}}^f = 0.507\).


The dependence of \(K_{\text{eq}}\) on \(P\) highlighted above is another mathematical expression of Le Chatelier’s principle, on this occasion, for changes in pressure. The interpretation for a reaction happening in the gas phase is as follows:

If the total pressure increases, the equilibrium will shift towards the side of the chemical equation that contains the smallest total number of moles of gas (the equilibrium in example 10.2 shifts toward the reactant).

title: 10  Chemical Equilibrium
text:
10.5 Chapter Review

10.5.1 Key Ideas

Reaction Gibbs energy: \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}G^\standardstate + RT\ln Q\), which changes as the reaction proceeds.
Extent of reaction: \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G = \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial \xi}\right)_{T,P}\) is the slope of the Gibbs energy of the mixture; equilibrium is the minimum, where \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G = 0\). Mixing is what creates the minimum.
Equilibrium constant: \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G^\standardstate = -RT\ln K_{\text{eq}}\), with \(K_{\text{eq}} = \prod_i a_{i,\text{eq}}^{\nu_i}\); pure liquids and solids have \(a=1\).
Temperature: the van ’t Hoff equation, \(\frac{d\ln K_{\text{eq}}}{dT} = \frac{\Delta_{\text{rxn}}H^\standardstate}{RT^2}\), says that \(K\) increases with \(T\) for endothermic reactions and decreases for exothermic ones.
Pressure: \(K_P\) does not depend on the pressure, but the composition does, through \(K_P = K_y \left(P/P^\standardstate\right)^{\Delta\nu}\). This is Le Chatelier’s principle in mathematical form.



10.5.2 Study Questions
1. How is the Gibbs energy of a reaction related to the reaction quotient?

\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}G^{\standardstate} + RT\ln Q\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}G^{\standardstate} - RT\ln Q\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G = RTQ\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G = \Delta_{\text{rxn}}G^{\standardstate}\,Q\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G = -RT\ln K\).


2. What is true at chemical equilibrium?

\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G^{\standardstate} = 0\).
\(Q = 1\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G = 0\), and the reaction quotient equals the equilibrium constant.
The reaction stops because the reactants are used up.
\(K = 0\).


3. How is the standard Gibbs energy of reaction related to the equilibrium constant?

\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G^{\standardstate} = RT\ln K_{\text{eq}}\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G^{\standardstate} = K_{\text{eq}}/RT\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G^{\standardstate} = RTK_{\text{eq}}\).
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G^{\standardstate} = 0\) at equilibrium.
\(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G^{\standardstate} = -RT\ln K_{\text{eq}}\).


4. The dissociation of \(\mathrm{Cl}_{2(g)}\) has a large positive \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G^{\standardstate}\) at 298 K. What does this tell us about its equilibrium constant?

It is very large.
It is very small.
It is equal to 1.
It is negative.
It cannot be defined.


5. What is the activity of a pure liquid or solid?

Its mole fraction.
Its molar concentration.
Its vapor pressure.








6. What is the meaning of \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}}G\) in terms of the extent of reaction, \(\xi\)?

It is the slope of the Gibbs energy of the reacting mixture, \(\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial \xi}\right)_{T,P}\), which is zero at equilibrium.
It is the difference between the Gibbs energies of the pure products and the pure reactants, which never changes during the reaction.
It is the total Gibbs energy of the mixture at the end of the reaction.
It is equal to \(\xi\) multiplied by \(RT\).
It is the Gibbs energy of mixing, which is always positive.


7. What is the van ’t Hoff equation?

\(\left(\frac{\partial \ln K_{\text{eq}}}{\partial T}\right)_P = -\frac{\Delta H^{\standardstate}}{RT^2}\).
\(\left(\frac{\partial \ln K_{\text{eq}}}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{\Delta S^{\standardstate}}{R}\).
\(\left(\frac{\partial \ln K_{\text{eq}}}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{\Delta H^{\standardstate}}{RT^2}\).
\(\left(\frac{\partial K_{\text{eq}}}{\partial P}\right)_T = 0\).
\(\ln K_{\text{eq}} = -\frac{\Delta G^{\standardstate}}{R}\).


8. How does the equilibrium constant of an exothermic reaction change when the temperature increases?

It increases.
It stays constant.
It becomes negative.
It first increases, then decreases.
It decreases.


9. In a van ’t Hoff plot of \(\ln K\) versus \(1/T\), what is the slope of the line?

\(\frac{\Delta H^{\standardstate}}{R}\).
\(-\frac{\Delta H^{\standardstate}}{R}\).
\(\frac{\Delta S^{\standardstate}}{R}\).
\(-\Delta G^{\standardstate}\).
\(RT\).


10. What happens when the total pressure of a gas-phase reaction at equilibrium is increased, if the number of moles of gas changes in the reaction?

\(K_P\) increases, and the equilibrium shifts towards the products.
\(K_P\) decreases, and the equilibrium shifts towards the reactants.
Nothing changes.
\(K_P\) does not change, but the equilibrium shifts towards the side with fewer moles of gas.
The equilibrium shifts towards the side with more moles of gas.








TipAnswers





1.a, 2.c, 3.e, 4.b, 5.d, 6.a, 7.c, 8.e, 9.b, 10.d

title: 11  Ideal and Non-Ideal Gases
text:
11.1 The Ideal Gas Equation
Up to this point, we have used the ideal gas as our main example, and in chapter 10 we wrote equilibrium constants in terms of the partial pressures of ideal gases. Real gases, however, are not ideal: their molecules occupy some space, and they attract each other. In this chapter, we will first look back at how the ideal gas law was discovered, and then we will study what happens when its assumptions break down. We will see that non-ideal behavior is responsible for some very useful phenomena, such as the cooling of a gas when it expands and the liquefaction of gases, and we will introduce the fugacity, a quantity that allows us to keep using our thermodynamic formulas for non-ideal gases.
The concept of an ideal gas is a theoretical construct that allows for straightforward treatment and interpretation of gases’ behavior. As such, the ideal gas is a simplified model that we use to understand nature, and it does not correspond to any real system. In typical “spherical cow” spirit, the ideal gas model strips away many real-world complications so we can focus on the core relationships between pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of gas. The following two assumptions define the ideal gas model:
Because of its simplicity, the ideal gas model has been the historical foundation of thermodynamics and of science in general. The first studies of the ideal gas behavior date back to the seventeenth century, and the scientists that performed them are among the founders of modern science.

title: 11  Ideal and Non-Ideal Gases
text:
Definition 11.1  

The particles that compose an ideal gas do not occupy any volume.
The particles that compose an ideal gas do not interact with each other.




11.1.1 Boyle’s Law
In 1662 Robert Boyle (1627–1691) found that the pressure and the volume of an ideal gas are inversely related at constant temperature. Boyle’s Law has the following mathematical description:
\[
P\propto\frac{1}{V}\quad\text{at const.}\;T,
\tag{11.1}\]
or, in other terms:
\[
PV=k_1\quad\text{at const.}\;T,
\tag{11.2}\]
which results in the familiar \(PV\) plots of Figure 11.1. As we already discussed in chapter 2, each of the curves in Figure 11.1 is obtained at constant temperature, and it is therefore called “isotherm.”






Figure 11.1: PV-Diagram of 1 mol of an Ideal Gas.





11.1.2 Charles’s and Gay-Lussac’s Laws
It took scientists more than a century to expand Boyle’s work and study the relationship between volume and temperature. In 1787 Jacques Alexandre César Charles (1746–1823) wrote the relationship known as Charles’s Law:
\[
V\propto T\quad\text{at const.}\;P,
\tag{11.3}\]
or, in other terms:
\[
V=k_2 T\quad\text{at const.}\;P,
\tag{11.4}\]
which results in the plots of Figure 11.2. Each of the curves is obtained at constant pressure, and it is termed “isobar.”






Figure 11.2: VT-Diagram of 1 mol of an Ideal Gas.



The interesting thing about isobars is that each line seems to converge to a specific point along the temperature line when we extrapolate them to \(V\rightarrow 0\). As we anticipated in chapter 2, this observation led to the introduction of the absolute temperature scale, suggesting that the temperature will never get smaller than \(-273.15^\circ\mathrm{C}\). Charles’s law in the form of eq. 11.4 holds only if \(T\) is measured from this point, in kelvin.
Why do all gases point to the same temperature? Because all of them approach the ideal gas at low pressure, and the ideal gas is made of point-like molecules that occupy no volume. Its volume, \(V = \frac{nRT}{P}\), can therefore shrink all the way to zero, and it does so only at \(T=0\), whatever the gas and whatever the pressure. A real gas never gets there: its molecules have a finite size and attract each other, and it liquefies and then solidifies long before absolute zero, as we will see later in this chapter. The point at \(-273.15^\circ\mathrm{C}\) is therefore an extrapolation of ideal behavior, not a measurement. That it coincides with the zero of the thermodynamic scale, which does not depend on any substance (chapter 4), is what makes the ideal gas such a good thermometer.
It took an additional 21 years to write a formal relationship between pressure and temperature. The following relationships were proposed by Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac (1778–1850) in 1808:
\[
P\propto T\quad\text{at const.}\;V,
\tag{11.5}\]
or, in other terms:
\[
P=k_3 T\quad\text{at const.}\;V,
\tag{11.6}\]
which results in the plots of Figure 11.3. Each of the curves is obtained at constant volume, and it is termed “isochor.”






Figure 11.3: PT-Diagram of 1 mol of an Ideal Gas.





11.1.3 Avogadro’s Law
Three years later, in 1811, Amedeo Avogadro (1776–1856) discovered a seemingly unrelated principle by studying the composition of matter. His Avogadro’s Law encodes the relationship between the number of moles in an ideal gas and its volume as:
\[
V\propto n\quad\text{at const.}\;P,T,
\tag{11.7}\]
or in other terms:
\[
V=k_4 n\quad\text{at const.}\;P,T,
\tag{11.8}\]
which results in the straight lines of Figure 11.4.






Figure 11.4: Vn-Diagram of an Ideal Gas at Constant Pressure (1 bar).





11.1.4 The Ideal Gas Law
Despite all of the ingredients being available for more than 20 years, it’s only in 1834 that Benoît Paul Émile Clapeyron (1799–1864) was finally able to combine them into what is now known as the ideal gas Law. Using the same formulas obtained above, we can write:
\[
PV=\underbrace{k_3 T}_{\text{from Gay-Lussac's}} \cdot \underbrace{k_4 n,}_{\text{from Avogadro's}}
\tag{11.9}\]
which by renaming the product of the two constants \(k_3\) and \(k_4\) as \(R\), becomes:
\[
PV=nRT
\tag{11.10}\]
The value of the constant \(R\) can be determined experimentally by measuring the volume that 1 mol of an ideal gas occupies at a constant temperature (e.g., at \(T=0^\circ\mathrm{C}\)) and a constant pressure (e.g., atmospheric pressure \(P=1\;\mathrm{atm}\)). At those conditions, the volume is measured at 22.4 L, resulting in the following value of \(R\):
\[
R=\frac{VP}{nT}=\frac{22.4 \cdot 1}{1 \cdot 273}=0.082 \;\frac{\text{L atm}}{\text{mol K}},
\tag{11.11}\]
which a simple conversion to SI units transforms into:
\[
R=8.31\;\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol K}}.
\tag{11.12}\]

title: 11  Ideal and Non-Ideal Gases
text:
11.2 Behaviors of Non-Ideal Gases
Non-ideal gases (sometimes also referred to as “real gases”), do not behave as ideal gases because at least one of the assumptions in definition 11.1 is violated. What characterizes non-ideal gases is that there is no unique equation that we can use to describe their behavior. For this reason, we have a plethora of several experimental models, none of which is superior to the other. The van der Waals (vdW) equation is the only model that we will analyze in detail because of its simple interpretation. However, it is far from universal, and for several non-ideal gases, it is severely inaccurate. Other popular non-ideal gas equations are the Clausius equation, the virial equation, the Redlich–Kwong equation and several others.1

11.2.1 The van der Waals Equation
One of the simplest empirical equations that describe non-ideal gases was obtained in 1873 by Johannes Diderik van der Waals (1837–1923). The vdW equation includes two empirical parameters (\(a\) and \(b\)) with different values for different non-ideal gases. Each of the parameters corresponds to a correction for the breaking of one of the two conditions that define the ideal gas behavior (definition 11.1). The vdW equation is obtained from the ideal gas equation performing the following simple substitutions:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P & \;\rightarrow\;\left( P + \frac{a}{\overline{V}^2} \right)\\
\overline{V} & \;\rightarrow\;\left( \overline{V} - b\right),\\
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.13}\]
which results in:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P\overline{V} &=RT \; \rightarrow \; \left( P + \frac{a}{\overline{V}^2} \right)\left( \overline{V} - b\right)=RT\\
P &=\frac{RT}{\overline{V} - b}-\frac{a}{\overline{V}^2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.14}\]
The parameter \(a\) accounts for the presence of intermolecular interactions, while the parameter \(b\) accounts for the non-negligible volume of the gas molecules. Despite the parameters having simple interpretations, their values for each gas must be determined experimentally. Values for these parameters for some significant non-ideal gases are reported below:

11.2.2 Joule–Thomson Effect






Figure 11.5: The Joule–Thomson Experiment.



We have already met William Thomson, also known as Lord Kelvin, and his seminal work on the second law of thermodynamics. In conjunction with that work, Thomson is famous for developing a sensitive method for measuring the temperature changes related to the expansion of a gas. These experiments improved on the earlier work by James Joule, and Lord Kelvin’s improved instrument depicted in Figure 11.5 is named the Joule–Thomson apparatus. The apparatus is composed of two chambers, each with its own mobile piston. The chambers are connected via a valve or a porous plug. The entire equipment is also thermally isolated from the surroundings. This instrument is a more sensitive version of the Joule expansion apparatus that we already described in chapter 3 (compare with Figure 3.1).
Thomson realized that a gas flowing through an obstruction experiences a drop in pressure. If the entire apparatus is insulated, it will not exchange heat with its surroundings (\(Q=0\)), and each transformation will happen at adiabatic conditions. Let’s consider an initial condition with 1 mol of gas in the left chamber, occupying a volume \(V_l\), and a completely closed right chamber, for which \(V_r^i=0\). After the process completes, the volume of the left chamber will reduce to \(V_l^f=0\), while the volume of the right chamber will be \(V_r\). Using the first law of thermodynamics, we can write:
\[
\Delta U=U_r-U_l=\underbrace{Q}_{=0}+W=W_l+W_r,
\tag{11.15}\]
with:
\[
\begin{aligned}
W_l &=-\int_{V_l}^0 P_l dV = P_l V_l\\
W_r &=-\int_0^{V_r} P_r dV = - P_r V_r.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.16}\]
Replacing eq. 11.16 into eq. 11.15, results in:
\[
\begin{aligned}
U_r-U_l &=P_l V_l-P_r V_r \\
\underbrace{U_r+P_r V_r}_{H_r} &= \underbrace{U_l + P_l V_l}_{H_l},
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.17}\]
which, replacing the definition of enthalpy \(H=U+PV\), we obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_r &=H_l \\
\Delta H &=0,
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.18}\]
or, in other words, the process is isenthalpic. Using the total differential of \(H\):
\[
dH=\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T} \right)_P dT + \left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial P} \right)_T dP = C_P dT + \left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial P} \right)_T dP,
\tag{11.19}\]
we obtain:
\[
\Delta H=\int dH = \int C_P dT + \int \left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial P} \right)_T dP =0,
\tag{11.20}\]
or, in purely differential form:
\[
dH = C_P dT + \left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial P} \right)_T dP =0.
\tag{11.21}\]
From eq. 11.21 we can define a new coefficient, called the Joule–Thomson coefficient, \(\mu_{\mathrm{JT}}\), that measures the rate of change of temperature of a gas with respect to pressure in the Joule–Thomson process:
\[
\mu_{\mathrm{JT}}=\left( \frac{\partial T}{\partial P} \right)_H=-\frac{1}{C_P} \left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial P} \right)_T.
\tag{11.22}\]
The value of \(\mu_{\mathrm{JT}}\) depends on the type of gas, the temperature and pressure before expansion, and the heat capacity at constant pressure of the gas. The temperature at which \(\mu_{\mathrm{JT}}\) changes sign is called the “Joule–Thomson inversion temperature.” Since the pressure decreases during an expansion, \(\partial P\) is negative by definition, and the following possibilities are available for \(\mu_{\mathrm{JT}}\):

For example, helium has a very low Joule–Thomson inversion temperature at standard pressure \((T=45\;\text{K})\), and it warms when expanded at constant enthalpy at typical room temperatures. The only other gases that have standard inversion temperature lower than room temperature are hydrogen and neon. On the other hand, nitrogen and oxygen have high inversion temperatures (\(T=621\;\text{K}\) and \(T=764\;\text{K}\), respectively), and they both cool when expanded at room temperature. Therefore, it is possible to use the Joule–Thomson effect in refrigeration processes such as air conditioning.2 As we already discussed in chapter 3, the temperature of an ideal gas stays constant in an adiabatic expansion, therefore its Joule–Thomson coefficient is always equal to zero.

title: 11  Ideal and Non-Ideal Gases
text:
11.3 Critical Phenomena

11.3.1 Compressibility Factors
The compressibility factor is a correction coefficient that describes the deviation of a real gas from ideal gas behavior. It is usually represented with the symbol \(z\), and is calculated as:
\[
z=\frac{\overline{V}}{\overline{V}_{\text{ideal}}} = \frac{P \overline{V}}{RT}.
\tag{11.23}\]
It is evident from eq. 11.23 that the compressibility factor is dependent on the pressure, and for an ideal gas \(z=1\) always. For a non-ideal gas at any given pressure, \(z\) can be higher or lower than one, separating the behavior of non-ideal gases into two possibilities. The dependence of the compressibility factor against pressure is represented for \(\mathrm{H}_2\) and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) in Figure 11.6.






Figure 11.6: Compressibility Factor of Hydrogen (Type I) and Carbon Dioxide (Type II) at 350 K, Computed with the van der Waals Equation.



The two types of possible behaviors are differentiated based on the compressibility factor at \(P\rightarrow 0\). To analyze these situations we can use the vdW equation to calculate the compressibility factor as:
\[
z= \frac{\overline{V}}{RT} \left( \frac{RT}{\overline{V}-b} -\frac{a}{\overline{V}^2} \right),
\tag{11.24}\]
which can be simplified as \(z=\frac{\overline{V}}{\overline{V}-b}-\frac{a}{RT\overline{V}}\). We are interested in what happens at low pressure, where the molar volume is very large compared to \(b\). In this case, we can use the approximation \(\frac{\overline{V}}{\overline{V}-b}=\frac{1}{1-b/\overline{V}} \approx 1+\frac{b}{\overline{V}}\), which gives:
\[
z \approx 1 + \frac{1}{\overline{V}}\left(b-\frac{a}{RT}\right) \approx 1 + \frac{P}{RT}\left(b-\frac{a}{RT}\right),
\tag{11.25}\]
where in the last step we used the ideal gas law, \(\frac{1}{\overline{V}} \approx \frac{P}{RT}\), which is a good approximation at low pressure. Eq. 11.25 is a straight line in \(P\), and its slope gives the behavior of the compressibility factor near \(P=0\):
\[
\left. \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial P}\right)_T \right|_{P=0} = \frac{1}{RT} \left( b -\frac{a}{RT} \right),
\tag{11.26}\]
which is then interpreted as follows:

Type I gases: \(b>\frac{a}{RT} \; \Rightarrow \; \frac{\partial z}{\partial P} > 0\) molecular size dominates (\(\mathrm{H}_2-\)like behavior).
Type II gases: \(b<\frac{a}{RT} \; \Rightarrow \; \frac{\partial z}{\partial P} < 0\) attractive forces dominate (\(\mathrm{CO}_2-\)like behavior).

The dependence of the compressibility factor as a function of temperature (Figure 11.7) results in different plots for each of the two types of behavior.






Figure 11.7: Temperature Dependence of the Compressibility Factor, Computed with the van der Waals Equation. The van der Waals Boyle temperature of CO\(_2\) (about 1030 K) is higher than the experimental value of 713 K, since the van der Waals equation is only an approximate model.



Both type I and type II non-ideal gases will approach the ideal gas behavior as \(T\rightarrow \infty\), because \(\frac{1}{RT}\rightarrow 0\) as \(T\rightarrow \infty\). For type II gases, there are three interesting situations:

At low \(T\): \(b<\frac{a}{RT} \; \Rightarrow \; \frac{\partial z}{\partial P} < 0,\) which is the behavior described above.
At high \(T\): \(b>\frac{a}{RT} \; \Rightarrow \; \frac{\partial z}{\partial P} > 0,\) which is the same behavior of type I gases.
At a very specific temperature, inversion will occur (i.e., at \(T=713 \; \mathrm{K}\) for \(\mathrm{CO}_2\)). This temperature is called the Boyle temperature, \(T_{\mathrm{B}}\), and is the temperature at which the attractive and repulsive forces balance out. It can be calculated from the vdW equation, since \(b-\frac{a}{RT_{\mathrm{B}}}=0 \; \Rightarrow \; T_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{a}{bR}.\) At the Boyle temperature a type II gas shows ideal gas behavior over a large range of pressure.



11.3.2 Phase Diagram of a Non-Ideal Gas






Figure 11.8: The Pressure–Volume Diagram of a Non-Ideal Gas, Computed with the van der Waals Equation in Reduced Units (\(P/P_c\) and \(\overline{V}/\overline{V}_c\)). Below the Critical Temperature, the Flat Segments Inside the Green Region Mark the Coexistence of Liquid and Vapor.



Let’s now turn our attention to the \(PV\) phase diagram of a non-ideal gas, reported in Figure 11.8. We can start the analysis from an isotherm at a high temperature. Since every gas will behave as an ideal gas at those conditions, the corresponding isotherms will look similar to those of an ideal gas (\(T_5\) and \(T_4\) in Figure 11.8). Lowering the temperature, we start to see the deviation from ideality getting more prominent (\(T_3\) in Figure 11.8) until we reach a particular temperature called the critical temperature, \(T_c\).

Definition 11.2 Critical Temperature: The temperature above which no appearance of a second phase is observed, regardless of how high the pressure becomes.

At the critical temperature and below, the gas liquefies when the pressure is increased. For this reason, the liquefaction of a gas is called a critical phenomenon.
The critical temperature is the coordinate of a unique point, called the critical point, that can be visualized in the three-dimensional \(T,P,V\) diagram of each gas (a surface whose slices at constant temperature are the isotherms of Figure 11.8).
The critical point has coordinates \(\{T_c,P_c, \overline{V}_c\}\). These critical coordinates can be determined from the vdW equation at \(T_c\), as:
\[
T_c=\frac{8a}{27Rb} \qquad P_c=\frac{a}{27b^2} \qquad \overline{V}_c=3b.
\tag{11.27}\]
These relations are used, in practice, to determine the vdW constants \(a,b\) from the experimentally measured critical isotherms.
The critical compressibility factor, \(z_c\), is predicted from the vdW equation at:
\[
z_c=\frac{P_c \overline{V}_c}{R T_c}=\left( \frac{a}{27b^2} \right) \left( \frac{3b}{R} \right) \left( \frac{27Rb}{8a} \right) = \frac{3}{8} = 0.375,
\tag{11.28}\]
a value that is independent of the gas. Experimentally measured values of \(z_c\) for different non-ideal gases are in the range of 0.2–0.3. These values can be used to infer the accuracy of the vdW equation for each non-ideal gas. Since the experimental \(z_c\) is usually lower than the one calculated from the vdW equation, we can deduce that the vdW equation overestimates the critical molar volume.
Notice how slicing the \(PT\overline{V}\) diagram at constant \(T\) results in the \(PV\) diagram that we reported in Figure 11.8. On the other hand, slicing the \(PT\overline{V}\) diagram at constant \(\overline{V}\) results in a \(PT\) diagram, similar to the one that we will examine in detail in the next chapter.

title: 11  Ideal and Non-Ideal Gases
text:
11.4 Fugacity
The chemical potential of a pure ideal gas can be calculated using eq. 9.23. Since we are not interested in a mixture, we can drop the asterisk in \(\mu^*\), and rewrite eq. 9.23 as:
\[
\mu_{\text{ideal}} = \mu^\standardstate + RT \ln \frac{P}{P^\standardstate}.
\tag{11.29}\]
For a non-ideal gas, the pressure cannot be used in eq. 11.29 because the response of each gas to changes in pressure is not universal. We can, however, define a new variable to replace the pressure in eq. 11.29 and call it fugacity (\(f\)).

Definition 11.3 Fugacity: The effective pressure of a non-ideal gas that corresponds to the pressure of an ideal gas with the same temperature and chemical potential of the non-ideal one.

Eq. 11.29 then becomes:
\[
\mu_{\text{non-ideal}} = \mu^\standardstate + RT \ln \frac{f}{P^\standardstate}.
\tag{11.30}\]
To complete the definition of the fugacity, we need to decide how it relates to the pressure. At very low pressure, the molecules of any gas are so far apart that their volume and their interactions become negligible, and every gas behaves ideally. In this limit, the chemical potential of the non-ideal gas, eq. 11.30, must become equal to that of the ideal gas, eq. 11.29, which is possible only if the fugacity becomes equal to the pressure:
\[
\lim_{P\rightarrow 0} \frac{f}{P} = 1,
\tag{11.31}\]
in other words, the fugacity is defined so that any non-ideal gas approaches the ideal gas behavior as \(P\rightarrow 0\). This condition, in conjunction with the \(T\rightarrow \infty\) behavior obtained in the previous section, results in the following statement:

The highest chances for any gas to behave ideally happen at high temperature and low pressure.

We can now return our attention to the definition of fugacity. Remembering that the chemical potential is the molar Gibbs energy of a substance, we can write:
\[
d \mu_{\text{ideal}} = \overline{V}_{\text{ideal}}dP,
\tag{11.32}\]
and:
\[
d \mu_{\text{non-ideal}} = \overline{V}_{\text{non-ideal}}dP.
\tag{11.33}\]
Subtracting eq. 11.32 from eq. 11.33, we obtain:
\[
d \mu_{\text{non-ideal}}-d \mu_{\text{ideal}} = \left(\overline{V}_{\text{non-ideal}}-\overline{V}_{\text{ideal}} \right) dP,
\tag{11.34}\]
which we can then integrate between \(0\) and \(P\):
\[
\mu_{\text{non-ideal}}-\mu_{\text{ideal}} = \int_0^P \left(\overline{V}_{\text{non-ideal}}-\overline{V}_{\text{ideal}} \right) dP.
\tag{11.35}\]
Using eq. 11.29 and eq. 11.30 we can then replace the definition of chemical potentials, resulting in:
\[
\ln f - \ln P = \frac{1}{RT} \int_0^P \left(\overline{V}_{\text{non-ideal}} - \overline{V}_{\text{ideal}} \right) dP,
\tag{11.36}\]
which gives us a mathematical definition of the fugacity, as:
\[
f = P \cdot \underbrace{\exp\left[ \frac{1}{RT} \int_0^P \left(\overline{V}_{\text{non-ideal}}-\overline{V}_{\text{ideal}} \right) dP \right]}_{\text{fugacity coefficient, }\phi(T,P)}.
\tag{11.37}\]
The exponential term in eq. 11.37 is complicated to write, but it can be interpreted as a coefficient—unique to each non-ideal gas—that can be measured experimentally. Such coefficients are dependent on pressure and temperature and are called the fugacity coefficients. Using letter \(\phi\) to represent the fugacity coefficient, we can rewrite eq. 11.37 as:
\[
f = \phi P,
\tag{11.38}\]
which gives us a straightforward interpretation of the fugacity as an effective pressure. As such, the fugacity will have the same unit as the pressure, while the fugacity coefficients will be dimensionless.
As we already saw in chapter 10, the fugacity can be used to replace the pressure in the definition of the equilibrium constant for reactions that involve non-ideal gases. The new constant is usually called \(K_f\), and is obtained from:
\[
K_f=\prod_i f_{i,\text{eq}}^{\nu_i} = K_P \prod_i \phi_{i}^{\nu_i}.
\tag{11.39}\]

title: 11  Ideal and Non-Ideal Gases
text:
11.5 Chapter Review

11.5.1 Key Ideas

Ideal gas: molecules with no volume and no interactions, \(PV = nRT\), combining Boyle’s, Charles’s, Gay-Lussac’s, and Avogadro’s laws.
Absolute zero: all isobars extrapolate to zero volume at \(-273.15\;^\circ\text{C}\), the origin of the Kelvin scale.
Van der Waals equation: \(\left(P + a\frac{n^2}{V^2}\right)\left(V - nb\right) = nRT\), where \(a\) accounts for attractions and \(b\) for the volume of the molecules.
Compressibility factor: \(z = \frac{P\overline{V}}{RT}\) measures deviations from ideality, and \(z=1\) for an ideal gas.
Joule–Thomson effect: an expansion at constant enthalpy cools a real gas below its inversion temperature.
Critical point: above \(T_c\), a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone.
Fugacity: the effective pressure of a real gas, \(f = \phi P\), with \(\phi \rightarrow 1\) as \(P \rightarrow 0\).



11.5.2 Study Questions
1. Which two assumptions define the ideal gas model?

The particles are spheres, and they move slowly.
The particles have the same mass, and they collide elastically.
The particles do not occupy any volume, and they do not interact with each other.
The particles are at rest, and they attract each other.
The gas is at low temperature and high pressure.


2. How did Charles’s isobars lead to the idea of an absolute temperature scale?

When extrapolated to zero volume, all isobars meet at the same temperature, \(-273.15\;^\circ\text{C}\).
They show that the volume is constant.
They are horizontal lines.
They meet at 0 °C.
They show that the pressure can be negative.


3. What does the parameter \(a\) in the van der Waals equation account for?

The volume of the gas molecules.
The temperature of the gas.
The number of moles.
The molar mass of the gas.
The attractive interactions between the gas molecules.


4. What quantity stays constant in a Joule–Thomson expansion?

The temperature.
The enthalpy.
The pressure.
The volume.
The internal energy.


5. When does a gas cool down in a Joule–Thomson expansion?

Always.
Never.
Only if it is an ideal gas.
When its temperature is below its inversion temperature (\(\mu_{\mathrm{JT}}>0\)).
When its temperature is above its inversion temperature.


6. What is the compressibility factor of an ideal gas?

\(z = 1\) at all conditions.
\(z = 0\).
\(z > 1\) at high pressure.
\(z < 1\) at low temperature.
\(z = 3/8\).


7. How is the Boyle temperature obtained from the van der Waals parameters?

\(T_{\text{B}} = \frac{8a}{27Rb}\).
\(T_{\text{B}} = \frac{bR}{a}\).
\(T_{\text{B}} = \frac{a}{bR}\).
\(T_{\text{B}} = \frac{a}{27b^2}\).
\(T_{\text{B}} = 3b\).


8. What is the critical temperature of a gas?

The temperature at which the gas freezes.
The temperature at which the gas behaves ideally.
The boiling temperature at 1 bar.
The temperature at which the compressibility factor is zero.
The temperature above which the gas cannot be liquefied, no matter how high the pressure.


9. The van der Waals equation predicts a critical compressibility factor \(z_c=3/8=0.375\), while experiments give 0.2–0.3. What does this tell us?

That the experiments are wrong.
That the van der Waals equation is only an approximate model.
That all gases are ideal at the critical point.
That the van der Waals equation is exact.
That the critical point does not exist.


10. What is the value of the fugacity coefficient, \(\phi = f/P\), of any gas as \(P\rightarrow 0\)?




Infinity.
3/8.



It depends on the gas.








TipAnswers





1.c, 2.a, 3.e, 4.b, 5.d, 6.a, 7.c, 8.e, 9.b, 10.d

title: 12  Phase Equilibrium
text:
12.1 Phase Stability
In chapter 11, we saw that a non-ideal gas can be liquefied, and that the liquid and the gas can coexist under certain conditions. In chapter 9, we introduced the chemical potential, the molar Gibbs energy of a substance, and we learned how it changes with temperature and pressure. In this chapter, we will put these two ideas together to understand when a pure substance is solid, liquid, or gas, and what happens at the boundaries between these phases. We will build the phase diagrams that chemists use every day, and we will derive the equations that tell us how melting and boiling points change with pressure.
We have already encountered the gas, liquid, and solid phases and already discussed some of their properties. These terms are intuitive since these are the three most common states of matter.1 For this reason, we have previously used the terms without the necessity of formally defining their meaning. However, a formal definition of “phase” is necessary to discuss several concepts in this chapter and the following ones:
Let’s now use the total differential of the chemical potential and the definition of molar Gibbs energy for one component:
\[
\begin{aligned}
d\mu &= \left( \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial T} \right)_P dT + \left( \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial P} \right)_T dP \\
d\mu &= -SdT+\overline{V}dP,
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.1}\]
to write:
\[
\left( \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial T} \right)_P=-S \qquad \left( \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial P} \right)_T =\overline{V}.
\tag{12.2}\]
We can use these definitions to study the dependence of the chemical potential with respect to changes in pressure and temperature. If we plot \(\mu\) as a function of \(T\) using the first coefficient in eq. 12.2, we obtain the diagram in Figure 12.1. The diagram presents three curves, each corresponding to one of the three most common states of matter – solid, liquid, and gas. As we saw in several previous chapters, the entropy of a phase is almost constant with respect to temperature,2 and therefore the three curves are essentially straight, with negative slopes equal to \(-S\). Since the solid has the smallest entropy of the three phases, its line is the least steep.3 The difference between the slopes of the three lines is explained by the fact that each of these states has a different value of entropy:
\[
\left( \frac{\partial \mu_{\text{solid}}}{\partial T} \right)_P =-S_{\text{s}} \qquad \left( \frac{\partial \mu_{\text{liquid}}}{\partial T} \right)_P =-S_{\text{l}} \qquad \left( \frac{\partial \mu_{\text{gas}}}{\partial T} \right)_P =-S_{\text{g}},
\tag{12.3}\]
and since the entropy of a gas is always bigger than the entropy of a liquid, which in turn, is yet bigger than the entropy of a solid (\(S_{\text{g}} \gg S_{\text{l}}>S_{\text{s}}\)), we obtain three lines with different slopes that intersect each other, as in Figure 12.1. What can we read from this diagram?
The effects of pressure on this diagram can be studied using the second coefficient in eq. 12.2. For the majority of substances, \(\overline{V}_{\text{g}} \gg \overline{V}_{\text{l}} > \overline{V}_{\text{s}}\), hence the curves will shift to lower values when the pressure is reduced, as in Figure 12.2. Notice also that since \(\overline{V}_{\text{l}} \cong \overline{V}_{\text{s}}\), the shifts for both the solid and liquid lines are much smaller than the shift for the gas line. These shifts also translate to different values of the junctions, which means the phase changes will occur at different temperatures. Therefore both the melting point and the boiling point in general increase when pressure is increased (and vice versa). Notice how the change for the melting point is always much smaller than the change for the boiling point. Water is a noticeable exception to this trend because \(\overline{V}_{\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O,l}} < \overline{V}_{\text{ice}}\). This explains the experimental observation that increasing the pressure on ice lowers its melting point.4
Considering the intersections between two lines, two phases are in equilibrium with each other at each of these points. For two or more phases to be in equilibrium, their chemical potentials must be equal:
\[
\mu_{\alpha} = \mu_{\beta}.
\tag{12.4}\]
If we now change either the temperature or the pressure, the location of the intersection will be shifted (see again Figure 12.2 and the discussion above). For infinitesimal changes in variables, the new location will be:
\[
\mu_{\alpha} + d\mu_{\alpha}= \mu_{\beta}+d\mu_{\beta},
\tag{12.5}\]
which using eq. 12.4, simply becomes:
\[
d\mu_{\alpha}= d\mu_{\beta}.
\tag{12.6}\]
Replacing the differential with the definition of chemical potential in eq. 12.1, we obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
-S_{\alpha}dT+\overline{V}_{\alpha}dP &= -S_{\beta}dT+\overline{V}_{\beta}dP \\
\underbrace{\left(S_{\beta}-S_{\alpha}\right)}_{\Delta S} dT &= \underbrace{\left( \overline{V}_{\beta}-\overline{V}_{\alpha}\right)}_{\Delta \overline{V}}dP,
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.7}\]
which can be rearranged into:
\[
\frac{dP}{dT}=\frac{\Delta S}{\Delta \overline{V}}.
\tag{12.8}\]
This equation is known as the Clapeyron equation, and it is the mathematical relation at the basis of the pressure-temperature phase diagrams. Plotting the results of eq. 12.8 on a \(PT\) phase diagram for common substances results in three lines representing the equilibrium between two different phases. Let’s see what eq. 12.8 tells us about each line:

title: 12  Phase Equilibrium
text:
Definition 12.1 Phase: A region of the system with homogeneous chemical composition and physical state.









The most stable phase has the lowest chemical potential. At each temperature, the phase whose line is the lowest is the stable one (red segments in Figure 12.1). Just as a ball rolls downhill, matter moves spontaneously towards the phase with the lowest chemical potential, since this lowers the Gibbs energy at constant \(T\) and \(P\).
Phase changes happen where two lines cross. At each intersection, the two phases have the same chemical potential, and they coexist. At the crossing between the solid and the liquid lines, the fusion (fus) process occurs, at the melting point \(T_{\text{m}}\). At the crossing between the liquid and the gas lines, the vaporization (vap) process occurs, at the boiling point \(T_{\text{b}}\).
Heating favors the phases with higher entropy. Since the gas line is the steepest, the gas always wins at high enough temperature, while the solid always wins at low enough temperature.
The liquid can be skipped. Depending on the substance and on the pressure, the solid line might intersect the gas line before the liquid line. When that occurs, the liquid phase is never observed, and the solid turns directly into gas, at the sublimation (subl) point \(T_{\text{subl}}\).







Figure 12.1: Dependence of the Chemical Potentials of Solid, Liquid, and Gas Phases on Temperature at Constant Pressure.










Figure 12.2: Effect of Pressure on the Chemical Potential Diagram.















The slope of a phase boundary is the ratio between two differences. It depends only on how much the entropy and the molar volume change when we go from one phase to the other.
The sign of the slope is decided by the volume change. Going from a lower-temperature phase to a higher-temperature one, the entropy always increases (\(\Delta S>0\)). Therefore, the line slopes up if the volume increases (\(\Delta\overline{V}>0\)), and down if it decreases.
Small volume changes give steep lines. When the two phases have almost the same molar volume, as for a solid and a liquid, \(\Delta\overline{V}\) is small, and the line is almost vertical. When one of the phases is a gas, \(\Delta\overline{V}\) is large, and the line is much flatter.

title: 12  Phase Equilibrium
text:
12.2 Gibbs Phase Rule
In chapter 1, we have already seen that the number of independent variables required to describe an ideal gas is two. This number was derived by counting the total number of variables \((3: P,\overline{V},T)\), and reducing it by one because the ideal gas law constrains the value of one of them, once the other two are fixed. For a generic system potentially containing more than one chemical substance in several different phases, however, the number of independent variables can be different than two. For a system composed of \(c\) components (chemical substances) and \(p\) phases, the number of independent variables, \(f\), is given by the Gibbs phase rule:
\[
f=c-p+2.
\tag{12.9}\]
The Gibbs phase rule derives from the fact that different phases are in equilibrium with each other at some conditions, resulting in the reduction of the number of independent variables at those conditions. More rigorously, when two phases are in thermodynamic equilibrium, their chemical potentials are equal (see eq. 12.4). For each equality, the number of independent variables—also called the number of degrees of freedom—is reduced by one. For example, the chemical potentials of the liquid and its vapor depend on both \(T\) and \(P\). But when these phases are in equilibrium with each other, their chemical potentials must be equal. If either the pressure or the temperature is fixed, the other variable will be uniquely determined by the equality relation. In other terms, when a liquid is in equilibrium with its vapor at a given pressure, the temperature is determined by the fact that the chemical potentials of the two phases are the same, and is denoted as the boiling temperature \(T_{\text{b}}\). Similarly, at a given temperature, the pressure of the vapor is uniquely determined by the same equality relation and is denoted as the vapor pressure, \(P^*\).
The Gibbs phase rule is obtained considering that the number of independent variables is given by the total number of variables minus the constraints. The total number of variables is given by temperature, pressure, plus all the variables required to describe each of the phases. The composition of each phase is determined by \((c-1)\) variables.5 The number of constraints is determined by the number of possible equilibrium relations, which is \(c(p-1)\) since the chemical potential of each component must be equal in all phases. The number of degrees of freedom \(f\) is then given by \(f=(c-1)p+2-c(p-1)\) \(=c-p+2\), which is the Gibbs phase rule, as in eq. 12.9.
For a pure substance (\(c=1\), so \(f=3-p\)), eq. 12.9 gives:

One phase, \(f=2\). We can change both \(T\) and \(P\) independently, and the substance stays in the same phase. In a \(PT\) diagram, single phases are areas.
Two phases, \(f=1\). If we choose the temperature, the pressure at which the two phases coexist is fixed, and vice versa. Two-phase equilibria are lines.
Three phases, \(f=0\). Nothing can be chosen: three phases can coexist only at a single temperature and pressure. Three-phase equilibria are points.
